title: Where will you spend eternity?
q: If I died tonight, where would I be?

b.x: Welcome, everyone. I’m glad you’re here. Tonight we’re going to talk about something most people avoid. I promise we’ll do it gently, and honestly, and nobody has to say anything they don’t want to.
Has a funeral ever made you stop and think?
Give people time. Some will answer quickly, and some will need a moment.

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together. Keep it simple.
b.x: Father, thank You that we can be here together. Open our hearts to hear what You want to say to us tonight. Amen.

Most of us avoid thinking about death until we have to. Tonight I’d like us to think about it together. I don’t want to scare anyone. I want us to see why God Himself brings it up, and what He wants for each of us. Here’s the question we’ll work on: if I died tonight, where would I be?
Everyone dies, and then comes judgment

Let’s start with something we all agree on. Everybody dies. It can happen to anyone, at any age, at any time of day. A child or an old man, rich or poor, in an accident or after a long sickness. Doctors can delay it, and healthy living can delay it. Nobody can stop it.
Hebrews 9:27

The Bible tells us people die once, and after that comes judgment. That’s a heavy word, so let me say what it means. Judgment is the moment God decides whether a person comes into His kingdom. Each of us will stand before Him and answer for the life we lived.
Revelation 20:12 and 15

In this vision, books are opened and the dead are judged by what they did. Anyone whose name isn’t written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire. So death isn’t the end of the story. It’s a door, and what’s on the other side matters.
Two places
The Bible talks about two places after death, heaven and hell. It doesn’t describe anywhere in between. (Luke 16:19-23)

Let’s take hell first, because it’s the hard one. Jesus called it the place prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). It’s described as a place of pain, weeping and regret (Mark 9:47-48; Matthew 25:30). A person there remembers their life on earth (Luke 16:25). And the most serious thing of all is that it means being cut off from God and from His presence for good (2 Thessalonians 1:9).
I know that’s hard to hear. Hold on to it for a moment, because heaven is the opposite.

In heaven, God will wipe away every tear. There will be no more death, no mourning, no crying and no pain (Revelation 21:4). Nothing wrong or deceitful will ever enter it, and the people who live there are the ones whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27). And best of all, God Himself will live with His people. He’ll be their God, and they’ll be His (Revelation 21:3). Heaven is more than a beautiful place. It’s home, and God is there.
A story Jesus told
Jesus told a story that shows how real this is.
Luke 16:19-31. Three readers work well: a narrator, the rich man, and Abraham

A rich man lived in comfort every day. A poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered in sores. They both died. Lazarus was carried to be with Abraham, and the rich man found himself in torment. I want you to notice three things.
First, the rich man remembers. He remembers his life on earth, and he’s full of regret. But the time to change is over.
Second, he doesn’t ask for himself. He asks for his five brothers. He wants someone to go and warn them.

Third, Abraham’s answer. They already have Moses and the Prophets, he says, meaning the Scriptures. Let them listen to those. The rich man says, but if someone comes back from the dead, they’ll change. And Abraham says, if they won’t listen to the Scriptures, they won’t be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

So what does this mean for us? It means the time to get ready is now, while we’re still alive. And God has already given us what we need to hear: His Word, and people who care enough to tell us the truth.
Why God tells us this
Why would God tell us all this? Because a warning is a loving thing to give. If you saw a friend about to walk into a flood, you wouldn’t stay quiet to keep things pleasant.
Matthew 7:13-14

Jesus said the road that leads to destruction is wide, and many take it, while the road to life is narrow, and few find it. He wasn’t trying to frighten us. He was showing us where each road goes while there’s still time to choose. And Paul reminds believers that our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). That’s where God wants us to end up.

Nobody is being asked to decide anything tonight. I’m only asking you to take it seriously. Over the coming weeks we’ll look at how God made a way, and by the end, the question we started with will have an answer.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds. People often need that time before they say something real.

x: Which feels more real to you, heaven or hell? Why?
Does thinking about hell scare you? Why or why not?
If you died today, are you sure where you’d go? What makes you think so?
Has anyone ever been honest with you about God? How did it land?

b.x: Don’t correct people’s answers tonight. If someone says they’re sure of heaven because they’re a good person, thank them and say you’ll come back to that in lessons 2 and 3. Your job tonight is to get people thinking, and to make it safe for them to say what they really think.
This week I’d like to ask you to do three small things.

x: Read Luke 16:19-31 on your own.
Pray for one person by name, someone you’d want to hear the good news.
Write down any question you’d like to ask next time.

b.x: Hebrews 9:27

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for telling us the truth because You love us. Help each person here take it seriously and not put it off. Keep us listening. Amen.
Why does God sometimes feel so far away?
Thinking of you. Did you get a chance to read Luke 16?

x.q: What about someone I love who has died?
x.a: Don’t give a verdict, and don’t guess. Tell them it’s right to grieve and right to ask, that God is just and loving, and that you’ll leave that person with Him. Then bring the conversation back to the person asking.

x.q: What about babies and young children who die?
x.a: Read Matthew 19:14 gently: the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

x.q: Isn’t that harsh for a loving God?
x.a: Go back to Luke 16 and Matthew 7:13-14. The warning is the love. Even the rich man, in torment, wanted his brothers to hear it.

x.q: What about people who’ve never heard?
x.a: Tell them it’s a fair question, that this lesson doesn’t answer it, and that you’ll ask your pastor and bring back an answer.

title: Made for God, separated by sin
q: Why does God sometimes feel so far away?

b.x: Welcome back. It’s good to see you again. Last week we talked about something hard, what happens after we die, and I appreciate how honest you were.
Did anyone get to read Luke 16 this week? What stood out to you?
Then ask whether anyone wrote down a question. Take one or two, and keep a list of the rest to come back to. If you promised someone an answer last week, give it now.
Hebrews 9:27
Tonight’s question is one many of us have asked quietly: why does God sometimes feel so far away?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to know You, and sometimes You feel far away. Meet us here tonight and help us understand why. Amen.

Have you ever felt like God was far away? Most of us have. Tonight we’ll look at where that distance came from, and what God thinks about it. Here’s the short version. God made us to know Him. Something went wrong. And God has never stopped coming after us.
God made us to know Him
Let’s go back to the beginning. Why did God make people at all?
Isaiah 43:21

God says, these are the people I formed for myself. He made us for a relationship with Him. He had already made the angels, the animals, the birds and the fish, and the Bible says all of it was good. But none of them were made in His image. When God made people, He said, let us make man in our image (Genesis 1:26). God thinks, God feels, and God makes choices, and so do we. He made us like Himself so that we could truly know Him and be close to Him.
Genesis 1:26 and 28

God also gave us a job. He told the first man and woman to rule over the earth and look after it. God can’t be seen, because He is Spirit, and in a way people are how He shows up in the world. So we were made for two things: to know God, and to look after what He made.
Something went wrong
So what happened? Why do we feel that distance?
Genesis 2:16-17

In the garden of Eden, God gave Adam and Eve almost everything. They could eat from any tree except one. That one tree was a test of obedience. Jesus said later, if you love me, you will obey me (John 14:15). Love shows itself in obeying.
Genesis 3:1-13

The serpent, which is the devil, deceived Eve. Adam knew exactly what he was doing and ate anyway (1 Timothy 2:14). And when God gave him a chance to own up, Adam blamed his wife. Three things changed that day.
First, the glory that had covered them was gone. Before they sinned, they felt no shame (Genesis 2:25). Afterward they saw they were exposed, and shame, fear and emptiness moved in (Genesis 3:7).
Second, they were afraid of God. They hid. Before, they had enjoyed His company freely. Now His presence frightened them (Genesis 3:10).
Third, life itself came under a curse. Work, relationships and life in general became harder and more painful (Genesis 3:16-19).
God sent them out of the garden. That sounds harsh, but there was mercy in it. He stopped them from eating from the tree of life and living forever in that broken state (Genesis 3:22-24).
Sin builds the wall
That’s the story of the first two people, but it’s also ours. The Bible says all of us have sinned.
Romans 3:23
Sin is what puts the distance between us and God.
Isaiah 59:2

Our sins have separated us from our God, and they’ve hidden His face from us. God is holy, and we are sinners. The gap isn’t a physical one, so no physical effort can cross it. That’s why religion, good deeds and trying harder can’t close it. And the Bible says the payment for sin is death, which means separation from God (Romans 6:23).

Last week, someone might have said, I’m going to heaven because I’m a good person. Tonight we can see why that doesn’t work. The problem was never that we aren’t nice enough. The problem is the separation, and it’s too wide for us to cross.
God came after us
Here’s the good news, and it starts right in the garden.
Genesis 3:15
Right after the fall, God promised that someone would come and defeat the enemy. From the very start, He had a plan to bring people home.
2 Corinthians 5:18-19

God was in Christ, bringing the world back to Himself, and not counting people’s sins against them. That’s what reconciling means: bringing people back together. So the distance you feel isn’t a sign that God doesn’t care. It’s the very thing He sent Jesus to fix.
To sum up: God made us to know Him. Sin separated us from Him. And God has been working to bring us home. Next week we’ll see how He did it.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Where do you notice that distance from God, in your own life or in the people around you?
Why do so many of us believe being good enough will fix it?
Adam and Eve hid from God. Have you ever hidden from Him? What was that like?
Is it important to you that your life fits God’s purpose? Why?

b.x: Some people may share something painful tonight. Don’t rush to fix it. If someone says they’ve done too much for God to forgive, tell them the next two lessons are for them, and ask them to stay with the group.
This week I’d like to ask you to do three small things.

x: Write down one way you’ve tried to earn God’s approval.
Read Genesis 3:8-13 and notice what God does when Adam and Eve hide.
Keep praying for the person you named last week.

b.x: Romans 3:23

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You made us to know You. We admit the distance is real, and that we can’t close it ourselves. Thank You that You’ve been coming after us all along. Help us be ready to hear what You did about it. Amen.
What did God do about it?
Thinking of you this week. How’s the reading going?

x.q: Why did God put the tree there if He knew they’d eat from it?
x.a: That’s an old question. The Bible tells us the tree was a test of love and obedience, and that God had a rescue plan from the start (Genesis 3:15). If someone wants to go deeper, take it to your pastor.

x.q: Is it fair that we suffer because of what Adam did?
x.a: The Bible says sin spread to everyone through Adam (Romans 5:12), and also that each of us has sinned (Romans 3:23). The good news over the coming weeks is that God has dealt with it.

x.q: I don’t feel far from God. Does that mean I’m fine?
x.a: Some people feel close to God and some feel nothing, and feelings can’t settle it either way. What the Bible says about sin applies to everyone (Romans 3:23). The coming lessons show how to be sure.

x.q: Can’t I make up for it by doing good?
x.a: Tell them it’s what most of us try first, and that you’ll look at it properly over the next two weeks.

title: Jesus, the only way
q: What did God do about it?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about why God can feel so far away, and about the wall that sin builds between us and Him.

Did anyone write down a way you’ve tried to earn God’s approval? You don’t have to share it, but I’d love to hear it if you’d like to.” Then ask: “When you read Genesis 3:8-13, what did you notice God doing when Adam and Eve hid?” Let someone find it. He goes looking for them and calls out, “Where are you?
Romans 3:23
Tonight’s question is the one we left hanging last week: what did God do about it?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for coming after us. Help us understand tonight what You did for us. Amen.

Let me start with a question. If you owed a debt you could never pay, and a stranger walked in and paid it for you, how would you feel about that person? Hold on to that thought. It’s close to what we’re going to see tonight.
God’s problem, and His answer

Last week we saw that sin separates us from God. Now here’s a puzzle. God is fair, and a fair God can’t pretend sin never happened. Sin has to be dealt with. But God is also loving, and He doesn’t want anyone to be far from Him. How can He be both? The answer is Jesus.
Romans 3:25-26

God presented Jesus as a sacrifice to pay for sin. That way God stays fair, because sin has been dealt with, and He is still able to forgive everyone who trusts in Jesus. The Bible calls Jesus the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). He was offered once to carry the sins of many (Hebrews 9:28).
What happened on the cross
On the cross, Jesus took our place. The punishment that belonged to us fell on Him.
2 Corinthians 5:21

God made Jesus, who never sinned, to be sin for us, so that in Him we could be made right with God. He carried our sins in His own body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24). Because He had no sin of His own, only He could pay for ours. That’s why our salvation rests on what Jesus did, and never on what we do for Him.
Romans 5:8
Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Remember the stranger who paid the debt? Nobody asked Him to.

And the story doesn’t end at the cross. Because Jesus never sinned, death had no hold on Him. He rose from the dead on the third day. Jesus is alive. We’ll come back to this next week, because it tells us how to respond.
Seven things only Jesus is
Some people say there are many ways to God. Let’s see what the Bible says. It names seven things that only Jesus can do. If you can, ask seven different people to read, one verse each.

x: Read aloud: John 3:16. Say: “He is the only Savior the Father sent.”
Read aloud: 1 Peter 2:24. Say: “He is the only one who died on the cross for our sins.”
Read aloud: Acts 4:12. Say: “His is the only name under heaven by which we must be saved.”
Read aloud: 1 Timothy 2:5-6. Say: “He is the only go-between for God and people.”
Read aloud: John 14:6. Say: “He is the only way to the Father.”
Read aloud: John 1:12-13. Say: “He is the only one who gives us the right to become God’s children.”
Read aloud: 1 John 5:11-13. Say: “He is the only source of eternal life.”

b.x: The Bible’s answer is clear. Jesus is the only source of forgiveness, salvation and eternal life. He is the only one who can connect us back to the Father.
Why “only one way” is good news

‘Only one way’ can sound narrow, even unkind. But think about it this way. If there were a hundred roads and none of them reached God, that would be hopeless. Instead, God Himself built one road and walked it first. That isn’t narrow-minded. It’s God making sure there’s a way at all. And the door is open to everyone who believes (John 3:16).
Next week we’ll talk about how to walk through it.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Why might “only one way” be good news and not bad news?
How would you kindly answer a friend who says all religions lead to God?
Think of the stranger who paid the debt. What does it say about God that He paid for our sin Himself?
Which of the seven “only” verses speaks to you most? Why?

b.x: Be kind and unhurried. If someone disagrees, thank them for saying so. You’re not here to win an argument. You’re inviting people to look at what Jesus said about Himself.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Memorize John 14:6. Write it on a card and put it where you’ll see it.
Keep praying for the person you’ve been praying for, and ask God to show them Jesus.

b.x: John 14:6

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for sending Jesus. Thank You that He took our place and rose again. Help us see that there’s no other way, and no better one. Amen.
What do I do with this?
Thinking of you. Have you got John 14:6 memorized yet?

x.q: Isn’t it arrogant to say Jesus is the only way?
x.a: Tell them it’s what Jesus said about Himself (John 14:6), and that it isn’t about who is better. All of us need the same rescue (Romans 3:23). We aren’t claiming we found the way. We’re saying Someone came to find us.

x.q: What about people of other religions?
x.a: Be kind and don’t argue. Say that the Bible’s claim is that salvation is found in Jesus alone (Acts 4:12), and that you’d be glad to talk more, or to take the question to your pastor.

x.q: Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn’t God just forgive?
x.a: God is fair, so sin has to be punished, and God is loving, so He took the punishment Himself (Romans 3:25-26).

x.q: How do I know Jesus really rose?
x.a: Tell them it’s a fair question. The Bible says He rose and is alive, and you’d like to look at it together or ask your pastor.

title: Receiving the gift
q: What do I do with all this?
notes: This is the decision lesson. Everything so far has been leading here. Go slowly, don’t pressure anyone, and leave real room for people to respond. The usual time for talking it over is replaced tonight by a quiet time to respond.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we saw that Jesus paid for our sin and that He’s the only way to God.
How did John 14:6 go? Would anyone like to say it from memory?
Then ask whether anyone has been praying for their friend.
John 14:6
Tonight’s question is the one most of us have been waiting for: what do I do with all this?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for Your gift. Help each of us hear You tonight, and keep our hearts open. Amen.
What’s the best gift you’ve ever been given? What did you do to earn it?
The answer is nothing, and that’s the point.
That’s very close to what we’re going to talk about tonight.
What being saved means
When the Bible says we’re saved, it means several things at once.
We are forgiven, and God gives us His own goodness in place of our sin (Colossians 1:13-14; 2 Corinthians 5:21).
We are saved from hell and sure of heaven (John 5:24; Philippians 3:20).
We are given a new nature. The old life is gone and a new one has begun (2 Corinthians 5:17; 2 Peter 1:3-4).
We are freed from Satan’s grip and brought into God’s kingdom (Colossians 1:13). And we are brought back to the Father (John 14:6; 1 John 2:23).
So salvation is more than escaping hell. It repairs the broken relationship we talked about two weeks ago.
It’s a gift
Ephesians 2:8-9

Notice the word gift. A gift has three parts. Someone gives it. It’s free. And the person receiving it has to accept it. God is the giver, the price has already been paid, and the only thing left is for us to receive it (Romans 6:23).

We can’t earn it, because even our best deeds fall short of what God requires (Isaiah 64:6; Titus 3:4-5). That’s good news. It means nobody here is too far gone, and nobody here is too good to need it.
Good deeds still matter. They just come after salvation, as the fruit of it, and never as the price (Ephesians 2:10).
Five steps
So how do we receive it? Here are five steps, in plain words.

x: Admit that you’re a sinner. Read aloud: 1 John 1:8 and 10. Say: “We can’t be forgiven for something we won’t admit.”
Ask God to forgive you. Read aloud: 1 John 1:9. Say: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us.”
Turn away from sin. Read aloud: Isaiah 55:7. Say: “This means turning around, and heading toward God instead.”
Trust His grace. Read aloud: Titus 2:11 and Ephesians 2:4-5. Say: “Grace means getting what we didn’t earn. A way to remember it is God’s Riches At Christ’s Expense.”
Receive Christ as your Lord. Read aloud: Colossians 2:6 and Romans 10:9-10. Say: “Jesus isn’t only the one who rescues us. He’s also the one we follow.”

b.x: Real faith, and now

A jailer once asked Paul and Silas, what must I do to be saved? They answered, believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. Believing in Jesus is more than agreeing that He existed. It includes handing Him the controls of your life (Galatians 2:20; Matthew 16:24-26).
2 Corinthians 6:2
Now is the time of God’s favor. Now is the day of salvation. ‘Someday’ isn’t a date. God is calling us now, and today is your day.
I’d like us to take a few quiet minutes. I’m going to ask three questions. You don’t have to answer out loud.

x: Are you ready to turn from your sins and give your life to Christ?
Are you ready to receive His grace, His forgiveness and the free gift of eternal life?
Are you willing to accept Him as your Lord, and to live for Him starting today?

b.x: If your answer is yes, I’d love to pray with you. You can say this prayer with me, or you can pray in your own words.

Prayer: “Lord Jesus, I believe You died for my sins and rose again. I admit that I’m a sinner. Forgive me and cleanse me. I turn away from my sin, and I need Your help. Come into my life by Your Holy Spirit. I receive You as my Lord and Savior. Write my name in the book of life. Thank You that I’m forgiven, that I’m Your child, and that heaven is my home. Amen.”

If anyone prayed, welcome them warmly. Tell them they’ve just been born into God’s family, that next week’s lesson is about exactly that, and that you’ll check in with them this week. Make a private note of who prayed so you can follow up.
If anyone isn’t ready, tell them that’s fine, and that you’re glad they’re here. Don’t pressure them. Offer to talk privately, and ask if they have questions about salvation.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: If you prayed tonight, tell one person what you decided. If you’re not there yet, that’s fine. Bring your questions next week.
Start reading the Gospel of John, a few verses a day.

b.x: Ephesians 2:8-9

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for the gift of Your Son. Thank You for everyone here. Meet each person where they are, and help us keep learning. Amen.
What just happened to me?
I’m so glad about what you decided. How are you feeling?

x.q: Do I have to pray out loud?
x.a: The Bible talks about believing in your heart and saying “Jesus is Lord” with your mouth (Romans 10:9-10). Encourage them to say it, even quietly.

x.q: I prayed something like this years ago. Do I need to pray again?
x.a: Nothing is lost by praying again. Ask what has happened in their life since, and listen. Lesson 8 talks about this.

x.q: Isn’t it enough to just believe the facts?
x.a: Knowing about Jesus is a start. The Bible describes faith that trusts Him and hands over control (Galatians 2:20).

x.q: What if I fail after I’ve prayed?
x.a: It’s a very honest question. Tell them lessons 7 and 8 are about exactly this.

title: Born again
q: What just happened to me?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week was a big one, and I want to thank everyone who took a step.
How has your week been? Did anyone tell someone about what they decided?
If someone prayed last week, ask how it felt, and give them room to answer. For anyone still thinking, tell them you’re glad they’re still here.
Ephesians 2:8-9
Tonight’s question is: what just happened to me?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for making us part of Your family. Help us understand what You’ve done. Amen.
What’s one thing a newborn baby can’t do for themselves?
Everything, of course.
People say ‘I was born again,’ but a lot of us aren’t sure what that means. Tonight we’ll clear up what it is, and what it isn’t.
What being born again is not
Let’s start with three ideas that aren’t right.
First, being born again isn’t joining a religion or a group. You can belong to a church your whole life and still not have been born again.
Second, it isn’t changing yourself by effort. People sometimes turn over a new leaf, and others may call them ‘born again,’ but self-improvement isn’t what the Bible means.
Third, it isn’t something water does. Baptism matters, and we’ll talk about it in lesson 9. But sprinkling a baby or immersing an adult isn’t what makes someone born again.
Two births, two families
John 3:3-7

Jesus told Nicodemus, a respected religious leader, that no one can see the kingdom of God unless they’re born again. Nicodemus was baffled. How can a grown man be born a second time? Jesus explained that flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit gives birth to spirit.

So there are two births. The first happens when we come out of our mother’s womb. With it we inherit a sinful nature, passed down from Adam (Psalm 51:5; Romans 5:12). The Bible says that without God we were spiritually dead (Ephesians 2:1), following the ways of this world (Ephesians 2:2).

The Bible is blunt that there are two families, the children of God and the children of the devil (1 John 3:10). That’s hard to hear. But it’s the reason Jesus said we must be born again. Our first birth made us sinners, and we need a second birth to be part of God’s family.
How it happens
To all who received Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God. Not by family line, not by human decision, not by trying harder, but born of God.
That’s what happened last week for those who prayed. It’s a miracle, and it’s God’s work, not ours. We simply received what He offered.
What comes next
1 Corinthians 3:1
Paul called the Christians in Corinth ‘infants in Christ.’ That’s what new believers are. And infants are meant to grow.
Ephesians 4:11-15

God gave us leaders and teachers to prepare His people so that the body of Christ is built up and becomes mature, no longer tossed around by every new idea, but growing up into Christ. Change has to follow the new birth. And nobody grows alone. That’s why this group exists: so we can grow together.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Are you sure you are God’s child? What makes you sure?
What’s the difference between someone young in faith and someone mature in Christ?
What are the benefits of being a mature believer?
What should we do to grow in God?

b.x: If someone isn’t sure yet, thank them for being honest. Don’t push. Lesson 7 is about how to be sure.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write a few lines about how you came to Christ, or about where you are in thinking about Him.
Ask someone who has walked with God for a while if they’d walk with you, a kind of spiritual parent (2 Timothy 2:2). If you can, help people find someone.

b.x: 2 Corinthians 5:17

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that we’re born into Your family. Help us grow, and help us not to grow alone. Amen.
Who is God to me now?
Thinking of you. Have you found someone to walk with?

x.q: I was baptized as a baby, or I grew up in church. Doesn’t that make me born again?
x.a: Be gentle. The Bible says being born of God isn’t by family line or human decision (John 1:13). The question is whether a person has received Jesus themselves (John 1:12). Ask, don’t argue.

x.q: Do I have to feel something to be born again?
x.a: Tell them it’s God’s work, not a feeling, and that lesson 7 looks at how to be sure.

x.q: What if I’m not sure it happened to me?
x.a: That’s normal, and worth talking about privately. Remind them that salvation is a gift received by faith (Ephesians 2:8-9), and that they can pray the prayer from last week again.

title: Our heavenly Father
q: Who is God to me now?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about being born again into God’s family.
Did anyone write a few lines about how you came to Christ? Would you like to share some of it?
Then ask whether anyone has found someone to walk with.
2 Corinthians 5:17
Tonight’s question is: who is God to me now?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to know You the way Jesus did. Show us who You are tonight. Amen.
When you hear the word ‘father,’ what comes to mind?
Be ready for mixed answers. Some people carry real hurt around this word, so don’t push and don’t try to fix anything.
For a lot of people, God feels like a judge or a boss. Jesus wanted us to know Him as a Father. Let’s see what that looks like.
Why Jesus came
Jesus came for two reasons. The first was to save us from sin and bring us back to God (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10; 2 Corinthians 5:19). The second was to show us what God is like.

Philip asked Jesus to show them the Father. Jesus said, anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father. Jesus didn’t only teach about the Father. He lived as a Son toward Him. In John 17, He prays and calls God Father again and again, and in John’s Gospel God is called Father more than a hundred times.
Matthew 11:27
No one knows the Father except the Son, and those to whom the Son shows Him. We only know God as Father because Jesus showed us.
Matthew 6:9 and Romans 8:15
Jesus taught His friends to begin their prayers with ‘Our Father.’ And the Spirit we’ve received doesn’t make us afraid. It lets us cry out, ‘Abba, Father.’ That’s the word a child uses.
Four sides of the Father
The Bible shows us four sides of the Father.
He’s good. Every good and perfect gift comes down from Him (James 1:17).
He’s generous. If an earthly father, imperfect as he is, knows how to give good gifts, how much more will our Father in heaven give to those who ask (Matthew 7:9-11).
He’s protective. How great is the love the Father has poured out on us, that we should be called children of God, and that is what we are (1 John 3:1).

And He corrects us, because He loves us. Hebrews 12 says God disciplines us like sons, for our good, so that we can share in His holiness. It isn’t pleasant at the time, but afterward it produces righteousness and peace (Hebrews 12:7-11).
What changes when you know Him as Father
Knowing God this way changes five things.
Our identity. We’re not strangers or servants. We’re children (John 1:12; Galatians 3:26).
Our sense of worth. If our Father loves us, we can learn to love ourselves too. We’re precious to Him (1 John 3:1).
Our security. We don’t have to be anxious, because our Father knows what we need (Matthew 6:25-33).
Our motivation. Children want to please their father. Jesus did only what pleased the Father, and the Father was pleased with Him (John 4:34; 8:28-29).
And our home. Heaven isn’t only a place full of wonderful things. It’s a home full of love (John 14:2).
A story Jesus told

A younger son asks for his share of the inheritance, goes far away, and wastes everything. When he hits bottom, he decides to go home, hoping to be hired as a servant. But while he’s still a long way off, his father sees him, runs to him and embraces him. He gives him a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast.
Notice what the father doesn’t do. He doesn’t make the son earn his way back. That’s what our Father is like.
How to know Him as Father

Three simple things help. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to see God as a good and loving Father (Romans 8:15). Start calling Him Father when you pray (Matthew 6:9). And go deeper through prayer, in your own quiet time with Him (Matthew 6:6).
And two cautions. Don’t let serving God replace walking with Him. Your closeness to Him comes first. And look for His face before His hand. Seek Him for who He is, not only for what He gives.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Do you picture God more as a judge, a boss or a Father? What’s the difference?
Where did your picture of God come from?
What makes it hard for some people to see God as a Father?
Which of the four sides of the Father, good, generous, protective or correcting, do you most need right now?

b.x: If someone shares something painful about their own father, listen. Don’t rush to fix it, and don’t rush to defend God.
This week I’d like to ask you to do one thing.

x: Each morning, pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, and thank God as your Father.

b.x: 1 John 3:1

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You’re our Father. Help us to know You the way Jesus did. Amen.
How do I know this is real?
Thinking of you. How’s the morning prayer going?

x.q: My own father hurt me. How can I call God Father?
x.a: Listen first, and don’t hurry to give an answer. Tell them Jesus shows what a good Father is like, and that they can go at their own pace. Suggest they talk privately with your pastor.

x.q: Is it okay to call God Father when I’ve only just become a believer?
x.a: Yes. The Spirit we receive lets us call Him Father (Romans 8:15).

x.q: Isn’t discipline just punishment?
x.a: Read Hebrews 12:10-11 together. It’s for our good, so that we can share in His holiness, and it produces righteousness and peace for those trained by it.

title: Assurance and the life of a child of God
q: How do I know this is real?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about God as our Father.
How did praying the Lord’s Prayer go this week? Did anything change as you prayed it?
1 John 3:1
Tonight’s question is one many new believers ask quietly: how do I know this is real?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for making us Your children. Help us be sure of it, and help us live like it. Amen.
How do you know someone loves you?
They show it.
New believers often wonder, is this real? Am I really saved, or was I just caught up in the moment? Tonight we’re going to look at something firmer than a feeling.
God wants you to be sure
1 John 5:13

John wrote this letter so that believers could know they have eternal life. Not hope, not guess, but know. Assurance clears away doubts and fears and steadies our relationship with God. And it rests on what God has said in His word, not on how we happen to feel on a given day.
The Bible gives us seven signs of a person who truly belongs to God. Some of them may not be obvious yet in a new believer. Mature believers live them out. Let’s go through them.
Seven signs
First, the Holy Spirit tells us inside that we belong to God.
Romans 8:16
When we receive Jesus, the Holy Spirit comes into our hearts and quietly confirms that we’re God’s children (Ephesians 1:13-14). There’s no shadow of doubt in the heart that our faith has saved us.
Second, we want to obey.
John 14:23-24 and 1 John 2:3-4
Many people say they love God and still resist Him. Obedience is the sign of a real relationship. It doesn’t mean being perfect. It means that the desire of our hearts is to please our Father.
Third, we love people.
Love for others, even for those who hate us (Luke 6:27), shows that we’ve passed from death to life. A child of God forgives and blesses (1 John 4:7-8).
Fourth, we keep growing.
1 Peter 2:2
Babies grow, and growth is a sign of life. Spiritual growth can be slow, but a steady pace is a sign of a life that won’t end.
Fifth, we can hear God’s voice.
John 10:4
The Bible calls God’s people sheep. A sheep knows its shepherd’s voice. The Holy Spirit guides, teaches, encourages and corrects us (Romans 8:14; John 14:26).
Sixth, we serve God.
Malachi 3:18

We aren’t saved by service (Ephesians 2:8-10), but people who belong to Him want to serve Him. Jesus said that whoever loses their life for Him and the good news will save it (Mark 8:35). If you haven’t yet found a way to serve, don’t worry. You’re young in faith. The desire is what matters at this point.
Seventh, we care for people in need.
James 1:27
Someone who knows God begins to look like Him. People who were once self-centered find mercy and generosity overflowing (Matthew 25:31-46).
How a child of God lives day to day

These signs show up in everyday habits. A child of God wants to show the Father’s character to the people around them (Matthew 5:16). They want to please God, not to impress people (Matthew 6:1-4; John 8:29). They make time alone with Him (Matthew 6:6; Mark 1:35). They want to do what He asks (Matthew 7:21). They trust Him for daily needs (Matthew 6:11, 25-33). They keep their hearts clean and forgive others (1 John 1:9; Matthew 6:14-15; Ephesians 4:32). They ask for His protection (Matthew 6:13). And they serve (John 4:34; Matthew 6:19-21).
Nobody does all of this perfectly. If these signs aren’t clear in your life yet, that’s normal. Babies don’t do everything at once. They grow.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which of these signs do you already see in yourself? Which are missing?
Are you growing in your faith? Why or why not?
Why is spiritual growth important? Will faith get stronger without good deeds?
Which habit would you most like to start?

b.x: Don’t let anyone leave feeling they’ve failed an exam. The point of these signs is encouragement, and each person is a baby in the faith or a growing child, never a failure.
This week I’d like to ask you to do one thing.

x: Pick one habit to start, like ten minutes a day with God, and tell someone in the group which one you chose.

b.x: 1 John 5:13

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that we can know we belong to You. Help us grow and help us live like Your children. Amen.
What if I fail? Can I lose it?
Thinking of you. How’s your new habit going?

x.q: I don’t feel anything. Am I really saved?
x.a: Remind them that assurance rests on what God has said, not on feelings (1 John 5:13). Offer to talk privately.

x.q: I see so few of these signs in myself.
x.a: Tell them growth takes time, and that the signs grow as they grow. Don’t turn it into a checklist.

x.q: Do I have to serve to be saved?
x.a: No. Salvation is a gift (Ephesians 2:8-9). Serving flows from it. Those who haven’t started simply haven’t taken the step yet.

x.q: How do I hear God’s voice?
x.a: The Spirit guides, teaches and corrects us (John 14:26; Romans 8:14). Encourage them to keep reading the Bible and praying, and ask your pastor to say more.

title: Staying the course
q: What if I fail? Can I lose it?
notes: Churches teach this topic differently. This lesson follows the position that salvation is not easily lost, but it can be forfeited by choosing to keep sinning on purpose. Check that this matches your pastor’s teaching before you lead it.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about how we can know we belong to God.
How did your new habit go this week? Did anything get in the way?
1 John 5:13
Tonight’s question is one every believer faces sooner or later: what if I fail? Can I lose it?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we’re glad You hold on to us. Help us hold on to You. Amen.
What’s something you started with great energy and then let slide?
Let people laugh, then connect it to faith.
Sooner or later, every new believer fails at something and wonders whether they’ve ruined everything. Tonight we’ll be honest about that.
Three parts of salvation
The Bible describes salvation in three parts, and it helps to see all of them.

The first is being made right with God. That happens the moment we believe, and it’s complete. We’re forgiven, and God sees us as righteous because of Jesus (Romans 3:22; 5:1). We could never earn this ourselves (Romans 10:2-4).

The second is becoming more like Jesus. After we’re saved, a process of change begins from the inside. We’ve been rescued from the power of sin, but we still need to leave behind the habits of the old life. It’s like being brought out of Egypt but still having Egypt’s ways in us. That’s why Paul says to keep working out our salvation (Philippians 2:12).

The third is when Jesus returns. We will be changed, and our bodies will be made new (1 Corinthians 15:51-55; Philippians 3:20-21). Those who belong to Him will be taken to be with Him (1 Thessalonians 4:16). And those who hope for that day keep themselves clean, just as He is clean (1 John 3:2-3; Hebrews 12:14).
Two wrong ideas
There are two common ideas about this that aren’t right.
The first says that your salvation can be lost easily. Sin once, and it’s gone, and you have to start over. That’s not what the Bible teaches.
The second says that once you’re saved, you’re saved no matter how you live, even if you walk away completely. That isn’t right either. The Bible’s teaching sits between them.
Secure as a child
If we belong to God, our relationship with Him is secure. When we sin, we may lose closeness with Him, but we don’t lose our place as His children.

So why do believers keep sinning? There are two main reasons. Some are still young in faith (1 Corinthians 3:1-4). Most of the sins we commit after we receive Jesus come from immature faith, and not from rebellion. Others have been walking with the Lord and have turned back (2 Peter 2:20-22). That’s what the Bible calls a backslider.

And why do some stay immature? There are two reasons. They weren’t nurtured by someone further along. We need a spiritual father or mother to grow (2 Timothy 2:2; 1 Corinthians 4:14-17). And they didn’t discipline themselves. Growing takes prayer, Bible reading, church, holy living and fellowship, and all of that takes effort.

The good news is that God doesn’t give up easily. He’s determined to finish what He started in us (Philippians 1:6). He may send someone to encourage, advise or even correct us. He may allow problems that wake us up, as He did with Jonah. He may discipline us so we return to Him (Hebrews 12:5-11). No one can snatch us out of His hand (John 10:29).
But the warnings are real
Hebrews 10:26-27

If we deliberately keep on sinning after we’ve known the truth, there’s no sacrifice left for sins, only a fearful expectation of judgment. The Bible says that a person who does this is mocking the Son of God, treating His blood as worthless, and grieving the Holy Spirit (Hebrews 10:29).
John 15:1-6

Jesus compares us to branches. It isn’t enough to be connected to the vine. We have to stay in it and bear fruit. Even Paul disciplined himself, so that after preaching to others he wouldn’t be disqualified himself (1 Corinthians 9:27). And it’s God, not us, who decides when someone has truly turned away.
When you sin
It’s never God’s will that we sin. But if we do, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ (1 John 2:1).
1 John 1:9

If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us. So come to Him quickly, with a repentant heart. If you feel the Holy Spirit convicting you, repent right away (Romans 6:12-14). Don’t let sin settle into your heart. And don’t treat this as permission to sin, because we are God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16-17).
You can’t grow alone
This is where everything we’ve said comes together. You need someone further along the road, and you need habits that keep you close to God. That’s what the next part of this program is for.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What do you think “work out your salvation” means?
Are you ready to give yourself to the Lord so that you can bear fruit?
What can we do so that we don’t drift away?
If you noticed yourself drifting, what would you do?

b.x: Some people may worry they’ve already failed. Reassure them that if they’re troubled by sin and want to come back, that’s the Spirit’s work, and that God is pursuing them.
This week I’d like to ask you to do one thing.

x: Write down three daily or weekly habits that will keep you close to God, and show them to your spiritual mentor or to someone in the group.

b.x: Philippians 1:6

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You finish what You start. Help us stay close, and bring us back quickly when we drift. Amen.
Why get baptized, and am I ready?
Thinking of you. Did you write down your three habits?

x.q: I sinned this week. Am I lost?
x.a: No. Walk them through 1 John 1:9 and 2:1. Tell them to come to Jesus quickly, and not to let it settle in.

x.q: Someone I know has left the faith.
x.a: Listen to the person’s pain. Don’t pass judgment. God is the one who judges, and He keeps pursuing people.

x.q: Isn’t it true that once you’re saved, you’re always saved?
x.a: Say that churches differ on this. Give them what you teach, and the verses behind it, and tell them you’d be glad to look at it more with your pastor.

x.q: How do I know if I’ve gone too far?
x.a: If they’re troubled and want to return, that is the Holy Spirit’s conviction. Tell them to repent right away and come back.

title: Baptism, the public step
q: Why get baptized, and am I ready?

b.x: Welcome back. This is our last lesson in this first stretch, and I’m so glad you’re here.
How did writing down your habits go? Which one has been the easiest to keep?
Philippians 1:6
Tonight’s question is: why get baptized, and am I ready?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for everything You’ve done in us these weeks. Help us take the next step with joy. Amen.
What’s a moment in your life you wanted everyone to know about?
A wedding or a graduation, maybe.
Baptism is the moment a private decision becomes public. I’d like you to hear it as a happy step, and not a test.
What baptism is
Matthew 28:19

Jesus told His followers to go and make disciples and to baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. So baptism is a command for everyone who believes in Him. The word itself means to immerse, to put under the water.
What it means
Romans 6:3-4
Baptism is a picture of Jesus’ death, burial and resurrection, and of our share in them. When we go under the water, we bury the old self. When we come up, we rise with Christ to a new life.
Colossians 2:12-13
We were dead in our sins, and God made us alive with Christ and forgave us everything.
What it doesn’t do

Baptism doesn’t save anyone. Salvation comes through faith in Jesus (Acts 16:31; Ephesians 2:8-9). Some people in the Bible were saved before they could be baptized. Zacchaeus, a cheat, was saved because of his repentant heart (Luke 19:8-10). And the thief who was crucified next to Jesus received eternal life because he believed in Him (Luke 23:40-43).
Baptism is a fruit of salvation, and not the root of it.
Why we get baptized
There are three reasons.
To obey God’s command (Matthew 28:19).
To show our faith. Baptism is the way a believer says so in public (Mark 16:16; Acts 8:12-13). Faith without action is dead (James 2:26).
And to follow Christ fully. Jesus Himself was baptized in obedience to the Father, and He set an example for us (Matthew 3:13-15).
Who, and when
Acts 2:38 and Mark 16:16

Baptism is for people who have repented of their sin, who believe in Jesus, and who have committed themselves to follow Him. Babies aren’t baptized, because they can’t yet understand what it means. The Bible doesn’t mention an infant being baptized. Instead, babies are dedicated to God, as Jesus was in the temple (Luke 2:21-22).

So when are we ready? When we understand what it means and we’re willing to bury the old self and live a new life in Jesus. You don’t have to be perfect or sinless first. And if you sin afterward, remember that you are dead to sin and a new creation in Christ.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What would baptism mean to you personally?
Why do you think baptism is for those who understand and believe?
Do you have to be perfect before you’re baptized? Why or why not?
Is anything holding you back?

b.x: End with a quiet moment and one question: “Are you ready to follow God’s command to be baptized?” Don’t ask for answers out loud.
This week I’d like to ask you to do three things.

x: Prepare a three-minute story of how you came to Christ.
Pick a date for your baptism, and talk with your pastor about it.
Invite your family and friends to come and see.

b.x: Romans 6:4

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for the new life You’ve given us. Help us follow You all the way, starting with this step. Amen.
This is the end of the first phase. Plan a simple celebration for your group, like a shared meal. The next phase is about the daily walk, and it starts the following week.
Thinking of you. Have you picked a date?

x.q: Does baptism save me?
x.a: No. Salvation comes through faith (Ephesians 2:8-9), and the thief on the cross was saved without being baptized (Luke 23:40-43). Baptism shows that we are saved.

x.q: I was baptized as a baby. Does that count?
x.a: Be gentle. Say that the Bible describes baptism for people who have repented and believed, and that babies are dedicated instead. Encourage them to talk with your pastor.

x.q: I’m afraid of the water, or of what my family will say.
x.a: Don’t push. Pray with them, and suggest they talk with your pastor about how and when.

title: Talking with God
q: Why pray, and how do I start?

b.x: Welcome back. We’re starting the second stretch of our time together, and I’m glad you’re here. This stretch is about the daily walk, the everyday habits that keep us close to God.
How did the last few weeks go? Did anyone pick a date for baptism, or tell their story to someone?
Then ask who has kept up their time with God in the morning.
Romans 6:4
Tonight’s question is: why pray, and how do I start?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to talk with You and hear from You. Teach us to pray. Amen.
Think of a friend you’re really close to. How did you get that close?
Let people answer. It usually comes down to time together and plenty of talking.
A friendship grows through time and conversation. Our friendship with God works the same way. Prayer is how we talk with Him. Tonight I’d like to show you why it matters and how to begin.
What prayer is

Being a Christian is more than joining a religion. It’s a living relationship with a living God, and every relationship needs conversation. Prayer is that conversation, and it goes both ways. Sometimes we talk. Sometimes we just listen.
Hebrews 4:12
God speaks to us in many ways, but the clearest is His word. It’s alive, and it speaks to us as we read it. We’ll spend a whole lesson on the Bible in a few weeks.
Two reasons to pray
There are two main reasons.
James 4:8

The first is to know God better. Being His child doesn’t make us close to Him automatically. Closeness grows. Moses spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks with a friend, and he knew Him because he kept coming back (Exodus 33:11).
Matthew 7:7

The second is to receive from Him. God’s promises fill the Bible, and prayer is where we bring our needs to Him. Paul says to bring everything to God, with thanks, and not to worry about anything (Philippians 4:6).
Seven simple guides
Jesus and the apostles gave us a few simple guides for praying. There are seven, and none of them is hard.

Pray in private, at least some of the time. Jesus said to go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who sees what is done in secret (Matthew 6:5-6). Prayer is a conversation, and it was never meant to be a performance.
Pray knowing who God is. He knows what you need before you ask (Matthew 6:7-8). You don’t have to use a lot of words, and you don’t have to talk Him into caring. He already does.

Pray with faith. Come believing that He is there and that He rewards those who look for Him (Hebrews 11:6). Your faith doesn’t need to be big. One man told Jesus, ‘I believe, help my unbelief,’ and Jesus helped him (Mark 9:24).
Pray to the Father. Jesus taught His followers to begin with ‘Our Father in heaven’ (Matthew 6:9). He wants us to speak to the Father directly.

Pray in the name of Jesus. He is the one who paid for our sins, and He is the only go-between for us and God (1 Timothy 2:5-6). Because of Him, we can come into the Father’s presence (John 16:23; Ephesians 5:20).

Pray with the Holy Spirit’s help. Sometimes we don’t know what to pray, and the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26). You can start by simply saying, ‘Holy Spirit, help me pray.’ Bring your wants honestly, and then ask for what God wants too. Jesus did that in the garden when He said, ‘Not my will, but yours’ (Luke 22:42; 1 John 5:14).
And pray from the heart. God isn’t impressed by polished words. He looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). When you look for Him with all your heart, He says you will find Him (Jeremiah 29:12-13).
Starting small

So how do you begin? Find a quiet place. Ask the Spirit to help you. Talk to your Father the way you’d talk to someone who loves you. Then stop and be quiet for a minute and listen. Simple, honest words are enough.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Have you ever sensed God speaking to you? When, and what was it like?
When you pray, do you picture God as strict or as caring? Why?
Which of the seven guides do you most take for granted?
What makes it hard for you to pray right now?

b.x: If someone says they’ve never heard from God, that’s fine. Don’t push. Tell them that listening is a skill, and it grows with practice.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose a time and a quiet place, and pray there every day this week, even if it’s only ten minutes.
In that time, spend one minute just listening, and write down anything you sense.

b.x: Philippians 4:6

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that we can talk with You. Help us to make time for You this week. Amen.
What do I actually say when I pray?
Thinking of you. Where did you pray today?

x.q: I don’t know what to say. Is it okay to just use my own words?
x.a: Yes. Tell them that plain, honest words are what God wants, and that next week you’ll look at a pattern Jesus gave.

x.q: Do I have to pray out loud or kneel?
x.a: No. God hears silent prayers and spoken ones. Posture matters less than a sincere heart.

x.q: My family prays to Mary or the saints. Is that wrong?
x.a: Be gentle, and don’t criticize their family’s faith. Tell them what Jesus taught: pray to the Father, in Jesus’ name, and Jesus is the one go-between (Matthew 6:9; 1 Timothy 2:5). Invite them to try praying this way and see what happens.

x.q: Does God hear me if I haven’t prayed in a long time?
x.a: Yes. Read James 4:8 again with them. He says to come near, and He’ll come near.

title: Praying the way Jesus taught
q: What do I actually say when I pray?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about why we pray.
Where did you pray this week? Did anything get in the way, or did anything surprise you?
Philippians 4:6
Tonight’s question is: what do I actually say when I pray?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray. We’re asking too. Amen.
Have you ever stood in front of someone important and had no idea what to say?
Let people laugh and tell a story or two.

Many of us feel that way when we pray. The first followers of Jesus did too. One day one of them asked Him, ‘Lord, teach us to pray’ (Luke 11:1). Jesus didn’t give them a lecture. He gave them a pattern. Tonight we’ll walk through it.
A pattern to follow
Matthew 6:9-13

This is called the Lord’s Prayer. Many of you have prayed it all week, and it’s a good prayer to pray word for word. But Jesus also meant it as an outline. If you follow the order, your prayer covers everything. It has seven steps.
Worship
Matthew 6:9

The first step is the most important. Before we ask for anything, we worship our Father. We thank Him for what He has given (Psalm 95:2). We praise Him for who He is (Psalm 103:1-5). And we honor His greatness (Psalm 95:6-7).

In this step we’re not asking for anything. We’re giving Him something. He is looking for people who will worship Him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). Start here, and your heart settles down before you bring your list.
His kingdom and His will
Matthew 6:10

Next we pray that God’s kingdom and God’s will come on earth as they are in heaven. Not everything that happens around us is God’s will. People do wrong, and the enemy works against us. So we ask for God’s will to be done.
A simple way to pray this is to start close and move outward. Pray for yourself, your family, your work, your church, your neighborhood, your leaders and your country, and the whole world.
Daily bread
Matthew 6:11

Then we ask for what we need today. If a human father wants to give his children good things, how much more does our Father in heaven (Matthew 7:9-11)? James says some of us don’t have because we don’t ask (James 4:2).

What about the prayers that don’t seem to be answered? Sometimes the answer is yes, sometimes wait, and sometimes no. Paul asked three times for something to be taken away, and God said, ‘My grace is enough for you’ (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). But the Bible also gives us some things to check in our own hearts. Unconfessed sin can get in the way (Isaiah 59:1-2). So can doubt (James 1:6-7), selfish motives (James 4:3), quarrels at home (1 Peter 3:7), and a distance from Jesus (John 15:7).
Use these as a checklist for your heart, and not as a verdict on you. God is a Father, and He isn’t looking for reasons to turn you away.
Forgiveness, received and given
Matthew 6:12

Next we ask God to forgive us, and we forgive others. When we’ve sinned, we go to Jesus, who speaks for us with the Father (1 John 2:1). We admit it, and we turn from it (Proverbs 28:13). And God promises to forgive us and clean us (1 John 1:9). Don’t confess a sin you’re planning to keep. Ask for help to let it go.

Then we forgive others, because God has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32). Jesus says that if we won’t forgive, our own prayer for forgiveness is blocked (Matthew 6:14-15). Forgiving doesn’t mean what happened was okay, and it doesn’t mean you feel nothing. It means you decide to let go of the debt, and you can ask God to help you do it. Some of you will need to do that more than once.
Protection
Matthew 6:13

Then we ask God to keep us from temptation and from the evil one. He wants to protect us (Psalm 91:9-11). We cooperate by staying out of places where we know we’re weak, and by not giving the enemy a foothold (Ephesians 4:27).
End with praise
We end the way we began, with praise. Everything is His, the kingdom, the power and the glory. We thank Him that He hears us and answers, in His way and in His time (Philippians 4:6).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Of the seven steps, which one do you skip most often?
Who do you pray for besides yourself?
What have you asked God for that hasn’t been answered yet? How are you handling the wait?
Is there someone you need to forgive? You don’t have to say who.

b.x: If someone has been deeply hurt by another person, don’t press them to forgive on the spot. Pray with them, and suggest they talk privately with your pastor.

title: A prayer life that lasts
q: How do I make prayer a habit?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we learned the pattern Jesus gave us for prayer.
How did praying through the seven steps go? Which one felt the most natural, and which one felt strange?
Matthew 6:9
Tonight’s question is: how do I make prayer a habit?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to be people who pray, and we know we need Your help. Amen.
What’s a habit you’ve managed to keep for a long time? How did you do it?
Let people answer. Exercise, a morning coffee and a daily call to family are good examples.

Almost every habit that lasts has a time, a place and a reason. Prayer is no different. Wanting to pray isn’t always enough, because life gets busy and we get tired. Tonight we’ll look at seven things that help a prayer life grow and last.
Put God first
Mark 1:35

Jesus got up very early, while it was still dark, went to a quiet place and prayed. And this was a busy time in His ministry, with crowds looking for Him. Before He did anything else, He spent time with His Father.

We have long days and many things to do. The first thing we can do is turn to our Father. When we wake up, we can think of Him before we think of work and family. And before we sleep, we can talk to Him again.
A set time

The Bible shows people praying at different times. David talked to God every morning (Psalm 5:3). Daniel prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10). Peter and John went to pray at three in the afternoon (Acts 3:1). So there’s no single correct hour, though the early morning, before the day pulls at you, is a good time if you can manage it.
What matters is that you choose a time, and set it. A fixed time gives your prayer some backbone. Without one, prayer is the first thing to be pushed out.
How long

Jesus once asked His friends to pray with Him for one hour (Matthew 26:40). That’s a good goal to grow toward, but please don’t start there. Start with what you can keep. If ten minutes is realistic, begin with ten. Then add a few minutes each week as your heart wants more. Many people find that, in time, an hour goes by fast.
Training the body
Matthew 26:41

Jesus said the spirit is willing and the body is weak. Our spirit wants to be with God, but our body wants to sleep, eat, work or play. This is why prayer feels forced at first. Paul talked about training his body like an athlete (1 Corinthians 9:27).
Give it time. The first weeks feel like effort, so plan on six to eight weeks before it starts to feel natural. If you skip a day, start again the next day. A missed day isn’t the end of anything.
A place

Jesus went to a quiet place (Mark 1:35). Daniel prayed in his room (Daniel 6:10). Peter prayed on the roof (Acts 10:9). Find a spot where you won’t be interrupted. If your home is crowded, that might be a corner, a rooftop or a walk outside.
Knowing God’s word

The more of God’s word you know, the more you have to say to Him. The writers of the Psalms prayed using words from God’s own promises (Psalm 119:47-48; 149; 164; 170). Read a few verses before you pray, and use them. That’s why Bible reading and prayer belong together, and it’s what we’ll look at next week.
Prayer all day long
1 Thessalonians 5:17

Paul tells us to pray continually. We can’t be on our knees all day, but we can keep talking to God. A short prayer on the way to work or in the middle of a hard conversation counts. As we do this, prayer becomes part of who we are, and not only something we do at one time of day.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Do you have a regular time to pray right now? When is it, and how long?
What gets in the way most often? Tiredness, noise, phones, busyness?
Do you read the Bible during your prayer time? How does that change your prayer?
Can you pray anywhere during your day? Where have you talked with God lately?

b.x: Help each person write a plan on a card or in their phone: when, where and how long. Keep it small enough that they can keep it.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

Tell one person in the group what your plan is, and ask them to check in on you.

Thinking of you. Did you keep your prayer time today?

x.q: I fall asleep when I pray.
x.a: Tell them that’s common. Suggest a different time of day, or praying while standing or walking, or praying out loud in a whisper. Encourage them to keep going.

x.q: I missed a few days. Have I failed?
x.a: No. Tell them to begin again the next day, and not to carry guilt about it. The goal is to return to God, and not to keep a perfect record.

x.q: I don’t have any quiet place at home.
x.a: Suggest a corner, a time when others are asleep or out, or a walk. Jesus often went to a quiet place, and any quiet place works.

x.q: My mind keeps wandering.
x.a: That happens to everyone. Suggest praying out loud or writing the prayer down. When the mind wanders, gently bring it back and keep going.

title: The Word, your daily bread
q: How do I feed on the Bible?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about building a prayer habit.
How did your prayer plan go? What helped you keep it, and what got in the way?
Mark 1:35
Tonight’s question is: how do I feed on the Bible?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to hear You as we read. Open our eyes and our hearts. Amen.
What happens to your body if you skip meals for a few days?
Let people answer. Weakness, headaches and a short temper are common answers.

Our spirits need food just as our bodies do. Jesus said that people don’t live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). Tonight I want to give you a way of eating that you can start tomorrow morning.
What happens when we don’t eat
If we skip God’s word, three things tend to happen.
We get weak. The Scriptures give us strength (Psalm 119:28).
We get sick. A person who is cut off from God’s word often becomes sour in attitude and spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit doesn’t grow. God’s word heals us from the inside (Psalm 107:20).

And over time, love for God can grow cold. Paul told Timothy to watch his life and his teaching closely, so that he and those who heard him would be saved (1 Timothy 4:16). A person who thinks about God’s word day and night is like a tree planted by a stream, whose leaves never dry up (Psalm 1:2-3).
How to feed on God’s word
There are seven simple habits that help us take in the Bible.

First, own a Bible. Choose one in a language and a version that you find easy to read. Print that is large enough to read comfortably will help too. Treat it as your most valuable possession, because it tells you what God is doing and what He wants for you.

Second, give it your best time. A Bible on a shelf doesn’t feed anyone. Read when your mind is fresh, if you can. If you’re new to reading the Bible, start in the New Testament, with the Gospel of Mark or John. The Old Testament is easier to understand after that.
Hebrews 4:12

Third, listen for what God is saying to you. Reading is not only for learning facts. God wants to speak to us through the Bible. You’ll find that sometimes a verse seems to stand up off the page and speak to you in your situation. The Bible’s Greek word for this is ‘rhema,’ a word spoken to you for now. When that happens, stop and receive it as God’s message.

Fourth, think it over slowly. This is called meditation. It means turning a verse around in your mind and asking what it means for your life today (Psalm 119:98-100). Ask five simple questions of a passage. Is there a command to obey? Is there a principle to follow? Is there a sin to turn from? Is there a promise to claim? Is there an example to follow?

Fifth, memorize verses. God told His people to keep His words in their hearts and minds (Deuteronomy 11:18). Pick a verse that spoke to you, say it out loud several times, and carry it with you. These verses become the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17).
James 1:22
Sixth, do what it says. A person who hears the word but doesn’t act on it is fooling themselves. Knowing without doing doesn’t help anyone.
And seventh, keep going. Plenty of people start well and stop. Application is the sign of a true disciple, and it doesn’t end when we’ve been believers for a long time (John 8:31; 1 John 2:24).
Try it together
Ephesians 4:31-32
Let’s practice the five questions on this short passage. Take a minute on your own, then we’ll share.

Is there a command? Be kind and forgiving. Is there a principle? We forgive because God forgave us. Is there a sin to turn from? Bitterness, rage, anger and harsh words. Is there a promise? In Christ, God has forgiven us. Is there an example? Christ Himself forgave us.
That took about two minutes. You can do this with any short passage.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

Has a verse ever seemed to speak straight to you? What was it?

What gets in the way when we know what God’s word says and still don’t do it?

x.a: Tell them to choose a version that’s easy for them to read, in a language they understand well. Ask your pastor which ones your church recommends.

x.q: I read and I don’t understand.
x.a: That’s common. Suggest they start with the Gospels, read a small amount, and write down questions to bring to the group.

x.q: No verse speaks to me when I read.
x.a: Tell them not to worry. Not every day has a stand-out verse. Keep reading, keep asking, and expect God to speak over time.

x.q: Can I read the Old Testament first?
x.a: Yes, but it’s usually easier to understand after the New Testament. Suggest starting with a Gospel.

title: Building on the rock
q: What will hold when life gets hard?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about feeding on God’s word.
What did you read this week? Did a verse stand out? Would anyone like to share the one they memorized?
Matthew 4:4
Tonight’s question is: what will hold when life gets hard?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want our lives to stand on You. Show us where we’ve been building on the wrong ground. Amen.
If you were building a house, what’s the first thing you’d think about?
Let people answer. Someone will probably say the foundation.

A house stands or falls on its foundation. You can’t see it once the house is built, but when the storm comes, you find out whether it was good. Jesus told a short story about exactly that. Let’s listen to it.
Two builders
Matthew 7:24-27
Two men build houses. One builds on rock, and one builds on sand. The rain falls, the floods rise, the wind hits both houses. The house on the rock stands, and the house on the sand falls hard.

Notice why Jesus called the first man wise. He wasn’t smarter or better educated. He simply chose the right ground to build on. The house in this story stands for our lives, and for our families, our work and everything else we are building.
The rock
1 Corinthians 3:11

The rock is Jesus Christ. He is strong, and He never changes. He is the same yesterday, today and forever (Hebrews 13:8). He is the cornerstone God chose (1 Peter 2:6), and God has given us no other foundation to build on (Isaiah 26:4).
The sand
Sand is anything other than Christ that we lean our lives on. People build on five kinds of sand.
Religion. Some people trust their church, their group or their rituals more than they trust Jesus. Their hope rests on belonging to the right place.
Money. Some people build their lives on what they own, and they measure their worth by how much they have.
People. Some of us lean so hard on a spouse, a parent or a friend that we feel we couldn’t go on without them. Those people are gifts, and they are not meant to be our foundation.
Human ideas. Some people base their beliefs on teachings that don’t come from the Bible, and they trust what they’ve always heard more than what God says.
And ourselves. Some people trust their own strength and make their own rules, and live as if God isn’t needed.
The storm comes to both
John 16:33

Look again at the story. The storm hit both houses. Being close to God doesn’t mean we won’t have trouble. Jesus said we would have trouble in this world. There will be pressure in our families, our money, our work and our health. The storm will come either way, and what counts is what we’re standing on when it does.
How to build on the rock
Jesus tells us exactly how in Matthew 7:24. Hear His words and do them. The two parts go together.
First, hear. Take time to read, study and listen to God’s word. We can’t obey what we don’t know. That’s why prayer and Bible reading matter so much.
Then, do. Hearing alone isn’t enough. Jesus called the man who hears and doesn’t act foolish (Matthew 7:26). Be a doer of the word, and not only a listener (James 1:22).

The more you hear and obey, the deeper your roots go, and the more strength you find inside. When storms come, you’re steady, because your heart rests on Jesus. And if God is for us, who can be against us (Romans 8:31)? Apart from Him we can do nothing (John 15:5). With Him, we can stand.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

Think of a storm you’ve been through. What held you up, or what didn’t?

Is there something you’ve heard from God that you haven’t acted on yet?

Thinking of you. Did you take that step?

x.a: No. They’re gifts from God. The problem comes when we put them where only God should be.

x.q: Is it wrong to trust in my church?
x.a: We’re called to be part of a church, and we’ll talk about that later. But our hope is in Jesus, and no church can take His place.

x.a: Listen first. Pray with them. Remind them that Jesus is with them in it, and encourage them to keep praying and reading. Make sure your pastor knows.

title: Turning around
q: How do I really change?
notes: Lesson 8 covered whether a believer can lose salvation, and this lesson picks up from there. It is about how a believer returns to God and changes. If someone raises the question of losing salvation again, go back to Lesson 8, and encourage them to talk with your pastor.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about building our lives on the rock.
Did anyone take the step they wrote down last week? What happened?
Matthew 7:24
Tonight’s question is: how do I really change?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to be changed by You. Show us what You see, and give us courage to follow. Amen.
Have you ever said sorry for something and then done it again?
Let people smile, because everyone has.

Becoming a Christian began with repentance, and that was a start. Repentance is also something we practice all through our lives. Tonight we’ll look at what real repentance is, because many of us have been taught to think of it as feeling bad.
What God is looking for
Isaiah 5:1-4

A man plants a vineyard in good soil. He takes great care of it, and then he looks for sweet grapes and finds sour ones. The Lord says the vineyard is His people (Isaiah 5:7). God has been good to us, and He hopes to see good fruit in our lives.
Galatians 5:19-23

Paul lists two kinds of fruit. There are the acts of our old nature, like hatred, jealousy, anger, selfish ambition, drunkenness and sexual sin. And there’s the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. A changed character is the sign that a person has truly turned to the Lord, and it grows out of real repentance.
Two kinds of sorrow

People repent for different reasons. Some are sorry because they were caught and feel ashamed. Some feel heavy guilt, and some just want the consequences to stop. Some repent hoping God will bless them in return. All of these are really about us.
Psalm 51:4

David prayed this after he sinned terribly. He knew that his sin hurt people, and he also knew it hurt God. That’s the second kind of repentance, the kind that sees what sin does to God and wants to make things right with Him. Paul calls it godly sorrow, and he says it leads to change (2 Corinthians 7:10).
Sorry isn’t enough

Feeling sorry is not the same as repenting. Esau cried bitterly over what he lost, but nothing in him changed (Hebrews 12:16-17). Judas felt such regret that he returned the money, but he never turned back to God (Matthew 27:3-5). That is why so many of us repeat the same sins we say we hate. We have felt bad, and we haven’t changed direction.
Three steps
The New Testament uses three words that help us see what repentance really involves.

The first is revelation. The Greek word means to remove a covering. God lifts the veil from our eyes so that we see our sin the way He sees it. We can’t make this happen. We ask for it, and God does it.
The second is repentance. The word means a change of mind. We take on God’s view of the thing, and we agree with Him about it. Our thinking changes first.
Acts 3:19

The third is turning. The Greek word means to turn onto a new path. After God shows us and our mind changes, we take a step in the other direction. God does His part, which is to show us His mind. We do ours, which is to accept it and live it out.
In real life, turning might mean an apology you owe, a habit you hand over, a friend you stop spending time with, or help you finally ask for. It’s something specific and visible.
Every day, and without fear
Repentance isn’t a one-time event. It’s how a child comes back to the Father, again and again. If you sin, come quickly (1 John 1:9). Don’t hide from God, and don’t wait until you feel better.

One more thing. When the Holy Spirit shows us something, He’s specific, and He points us toward Jesus. There’s no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). If you find yourself lying awake under a vague, heavy sense of being no good, that doesn’t sound like the Spirit. Bring that to Jesus too.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

What’s the difference between feeling bad and changing your mind?
What could turning look like in practice? Can you give an example?
Is there something the Spirit has been showing you lately?

Tell God about it, and ask Him to change your mind about it.

x.a: Encourage them. Ask whether they’ve told anyone, because confessing to a trusted believer often helps (James 5:16). Encourage them to keep coming to Jesus quickly, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.a: We confess to God, and He forgives us (1 John 1:9). But James 5:16 also encourages us to share our struggles with a trusted believer. It brings healing.

x.a: Yes. Read Isaiah 1:18 together. He says that though our sins are like scarlet, they will be white as snow.

title: Faith that waits
q: How do I trust God when I can’t see?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about repentance and turning around.
How did the step you took go this week? Was it harder or easier than you expected?
Acts 3:19
Tonight’s question is: how do I trust God when I can’t see?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
