b.x: Father, we can’t see everything You’re doing, and we choose to trust You anyway. Strengthen our faith. Amen.
Have you ever had to trust someone before you could see how things would turn out?
A doctor, a driver or a friend with a loan are all good examples.

Trusting someone is a normal part of life. Faith in God is trust too. It’s the trust that the One who made a promise will keep it. Tonight we’ll look at where faith comes from, what it rests on, and what it looks like when we have to wait. We’ll use the story of Abraham and Sarah.
What faith is
Hebrews 11:1

Faith is being sure of what we hope for, and certain of what we can’t see. It’s not wishing, and it isn’t a way of forcing God’s hand. It’s trusting that what God has said is true, even before we see it with our eyes. That’s why Paul says we walk by faith and not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7).
Where faith comes from
Romans 10:17

Faith comes from hearing, and what we hear is the word of Christ. Abraham didn’t just decide to believe. God first gave him a promise (Genesis 12:7; Hebrews 11:11). So when God speaks to us, whether through the Bible or by the Spirit, faith begins to grow. This is why we’ve spent the last weeks on prayer and the Word. They’re how we hear.
What faith rests on

Faith isn’t strong because we try hard. It’s strong because of who God is. Abraham trusted God because he considered the One who made the promise to be faithful (Hebrews 11:11). There are three things we know about God.
He never changes (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). He never fails (Job 42:2). And He never lies (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). If you know that about Him, you can lean on what He says.
Faith acts
James 2:17

Faith that never shows up in action is dead. Even demons believe God exists (James 2:19). Real faith shows in how we live. It leads us to ask God for help and for guidance (Proverbs 3:5-6). It leads us to lean on His strength when we’re weak (2 Corinthians 12:9-10). And it leads us to care for those in need, and to obey Him (James 2:15-17, 21-22).
A caution. Fruit grows slowly, and it grows differently in different people. Don’t judge someone else’s faith by your own, and don’t judge your own by theirs.
Faith waits
Hebrews 6:12-15

God promised Abraham a son. It took about twenty-five years from the first promise until Isaac was born. Abraham and Sarah were too old to have a child, and there was nothing they could do about it. God used that waiting to shape their character, and He’s interested in who we are becoming as well as what we receive.

Along the way they got impatient. Sarah suggested that Abraham have a child with her servant Hagar, and Ishmael was born (Genesis 16:1-4). Their own plan brought a lot of pain into their home (Genesis 21:8-14). We do this too. When God seems slow, we run ahead and make our own plan. If we’ve made an ‘Ishmael,’ the way back is the same as always. Tell God, and ask Him to help us start again.
Faith when it doesn’t turn out the way we hoped
Hebrews 11:35-39

Some people in Hebrews 11 saw amazing things. Others were beaten, jailed and killed, and they didn’t receive what had been promised while they lived. The same chapter calls all of them people of faith. So faith isn’t a guarantee of an easy road. It’s trust that God is good and that He has the last word.
Feeding your faith

When Abraham’s faith wavered, God came back and reminded him of the promise (Genesis 17:1-22). We need that too. Go back to the promises God has given you. Read them, think about them, and pray them. When the promise is fulfilled, there’s joy. Isaac’s name means laughter (Genesis 21:6).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Where is it hardest for you to trust God right now?
Is there a promise from the Bible that you’re holding on to?
Is there a place in your life where you’ve been running ahead of God, building your own Ishmael?
What helps you remember that God has been faithful to you before?

b.x: If someone says they’ve been praying and waiting for a long time, don’t hurry to explain it. Pray with them, and remind them that waiting is part of the story for many people in the Bible.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one promise from the Bible. Write it on a card, read it every day, and pray it back to God.
Tell someone in the group one way God has been faithful to you in the past.

b.x: Hebrews 11:1

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You never change, never fail and never lie. Help us trust You while we wait. Amen.
Why give, and where do I start?
Thinking of you. How’s the waiting going?

x.q: Does faith mean God will always give me what I ask for?
x.a: No. Faith trusts God’s goodness, and it doesn’t make Him obey us. Paul asked for something to be taken away, and God said no (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). Ask for what is in line with His will (1 John 5:14).

x.q: My faith is very small.
x.a: That’s okay. Jesus said even faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains (Matthew 17:20). Mark 9:24 is a good prayer: help my unbelief.

x.q: I prayed for a long time and nothing happened.
x.a: Don’t explain it away. Stay with them. Encourage them to keep praying, to keep reading the Bible, and to talk with your pastor.

x.q: Does faith mean I shouldn’t see a doctor?
x.a: No. God works through doctors too. Luke, who wrote one of the Gospels, was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Paul told Timothy to take something for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Using medicine doesn’t mean you lack faith.

title: Giving back to God
q: Why give, and where do I start?
notes: This lesson teaches the tithe the way our church does, as a tenth of income brought to the local church. Check that it matches your pastor’s teaching before you lead it. Some people in your group may be in debt, out of work or have been pressured about money before. Teach this as an invitation, and never as a bill.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about faith and what it looks like to wait on God.
Which promise did you hold on to this week? Did anything change because of it?
Hebrews 11:1
Tonight’s question is: why give, and where do I start?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, everything we have came from You. Give us glad and open hearts. Amen.
What’s the best gift you ever gave someone? What made it good?
Let people answer. It’s usually about the person, and not the price.

Giving can be a touchy subject, especially around money. So let me say right away that I’m not here to put pressure on anyone. Giving is one of the ways we say thank you to God, and the Bible has a lot to say about it. Let’s see what it says.
It all belongs to God
Psalm 24:1

The earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it. The air we breathe, the food we eat, the clothes we wear and the homes we live in all come from Him (Psalm 89:11). We don’t own anything in the way we sometimes think we do.
We are managers
1 Corinthians 4:1-2

God put us in charge of what He made. He has trusted us with time, abilities, family, work and money, each according to what we can handle (Matthew 25:14-15). The Bible calls us stewards, people who look after something that belongs to someone else. And one day we’ll give an account of how we managed it (Luke 12:48).

Think of David’s prayer when the people gave for building the temple. He said that everything comes from God, and that they had only given back what came from His hand (1 Chronicles 29:14). Once we see it that way, giving is easier. We aren’t parting with our things. We’re returning a little of what was His to begin with.
Three ways to give
The Bible mentions many kinds of giving. Three of them are for every believer.

The first is helping the poor. Jesus said that what we do for those in need, we do for Him (Matthew 25:35-40). The Bible says that whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord (Proverbs 19:17). Jesus also said to do it quietly, without announcing it (Matthew 6:2-3).

The second is the tithe. A tithe is a tenth. Our church teaches that the first tenth of our income belongs to the Lord and is brought to our local church (Leviticus 27:30; Malachi 3:10). In Malachi, God invites His people to trust Him with the first part and see how He provides. Since the tithe is already His, we’re returning it.

The third is offerings. An offering is what we give beyond the tithe, and we decide the amount ourselves (2 Corinthians 9:6-7). It may go to our church, to missionaries or to others in need as the Spirit leads (Philippians 4:18).
How to give
2 Corinthians 9:7
God loves a cheerful giver. We give with joy, not grudgingly and not out of pressure.
We give with faith. Abel’s gift pleased God because he gave it in faith (Hebrews 11:4).

We give with the right motive. Jesus said that when we give privately, our Father who sees what is done in secret will reward us (Matthew 6:1-4). If we give to be noticed, we’ve already received that reward.

And we give according to what we have. If the willingness is there, the gift is accepted according to what a person has, and not according to what they don’t have (2 Corinthians 8:12). Jesus noticed a poor widow who gave two small coins, and He said she gave more than all the rest (Mark 12:41-44).
What about the rewards?
Luke 6:38

The Bible does say that a generous person will be cared for. Those who refresh others will be refreshed (Proverbs 11:25), and God will supply what we need (Philippians 4:19). But giving isn’t a way to get rich. If we give to get something back, we’ve missed the point. The love of money is a danger, and Paul warns us about it (1 Timothy 6:9-10). Give because He gave first.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What changes if everything we have belongs to God, and we only look after it?
Of the three kinds of giving, which have you not started? What’s holding you back?
Why do you think some people find it hard to give?
What is one practical step you could take this month?

b.x: If someone shares a hard money situation, listen. Don’t give financial advice, and don’t suggest they give beyond what they can. Offer to pray with them, and tell them your pastor can help.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Pray about what to do with your income. Write down one step you will take, such as starting to tithe, giving an offering, or helping someone in need.
Do one act of giving in secret this week, and don’t tell anyone.

b.x: 2 Corinthians 9:7

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for all You’ve given us. Make us cheerful and generous givers. Amen.
Why gather every week?
Thinking of you. Did you take a step in giving?

x.q: I’m in debt, or I don’t have enough money. Do I still have to give?
x.a: Don’t add to their burden. Tell them God looks at the heart and accepts what a person is able to give (2 Corinthians 8:12). Encourage them to start small and to talk with your pastor.

x.q: Will God make me rich if I give?
x.a: No. God promises to care for us, and He doesn’t promise wealth. Give because you love Him.

x.q: Is the tithe from my gross pay or my take-home pay?
x.a: Say that churches see this differently, and tell them what your pastor teaches.

x.q: I missed my tithe for a long time. Am I in trouble with God?
x.a: Don’t frighten them. God is a Father who welcomes a fresh start. Encourage them to begin now.

title: Gathering on the Lord’s Day
q: Why gather every week?

b.x: Welcome back. This is our last lesson in this second stretch, and I’m so glad you’re here.
How did your step in giving go? Did anything surprise you?
2 Corinthians 9:7
Tonight’s question is: why gather every week?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for the family You’ve given us. Help us to love gathering with Your people. Amen.
What’s a family gathering you look forward to every year? What makes it special?
Let people tell a few stories.
Families need time together. A family that never gathers slowly grows apart. God’s family is the same. Tonight we’ll look at why believers set aside a day to gather, and what happens when we do.
Do we need a special day?
Romans 14:5-6

Paul says that one person considers one day more sacred than another, and another person treats every day alike, and each should be fully convinced in their own mind. All days are made by God (Psalm 118:24). Still, it helps to set one day apart from the others, a day when we stop our usual work and worship with our family and other believers. Most Christians choose Sunday, and it’s called the Lord’s Day.
Why Sunday
There are three reasons.
John 20:1

First, Sunday is the day Jesus rose from the dead. It was the first day of the week when Mary came to the tomb and found it empty. John calls it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). We gather on that day because it’s the day death was defeated.
Second, it’s the first day of the week. When we give the first day to God, we show that He comes first in our lives (Matthew 6:33; Matthew 28:1).

And third, the early believers met on that day. They broke bread together and listened to Paul teach (Acts 20:7), and they brought their gifts for God’s work (1 Corinthians 16:2). They also met nearly every day in the early years (Acts 2:46).

A word about rest. Sunday is not the Old Testament Sabbath. Our rest is found in Jesus Himself. He said to come to Him, and we will find rest for our souls (Matthew 11:28-30; Colossians 2:16-17). So Sunday is a day of worship and fellowship. It’s no rule to keep so that God will think well of us.

If you work on Sundays, perhaps in a hospital, a shop or a factory, don’t feel condemned. Paul says each person must decide for themselves. Find another time in the week to gather with believers, and talk to your pastor about it.
What happens when we gather
The Bible shows four things that believers do together.
Psalm 100:1-2
We sing. We worship God with gladness and come before Him with joyful songs.
We give. Our tithes and offerings are an act of worship (1 Corinthians 16:2; Malachi 3:10).
We listen to God’s word. We hear teaching from the Bible, and it feeds us (Acts 20:7).
And we care for each other. When someone is sick or in need, the elders pray, and the family comes around them (James 5:14-15).
What to look for in a church family
Where we gather matters. There are three things to look for.
A place where we are fed. Jesus said that people live on every word that comes from God (Matthew 4:4). Look for a church where the Bible is taught clearly.
A place where we sense God’s presence. David said he had seen God’s power and glory in the sanctuary (Psalm 63:2).

And a place where we can grow and serve. Psalm 92:12-14 says that those who are planted in the house of the Lord flourish and keep bearing fruit. Look for a place where you’ll be changed and where you can be useful. We’ll say more about the church in the last part of this program.
Putting it all together

Look back at the last nine weeks. We started with prayer, a pattern for it, and a habit to keep it. We learned to feed on the Bible and build on the rock. We learned how to turn back to God, trust Him while we wait, and give back to Him. And tonight we’ve talked about gathering with His people.

That is a rhythm of life. Prayer and the Word every day. Obeying what we hear. Turning quickly when we go wrong. Trusting God when we can’t see. Giving. And gathering every week. None of these makes us good enough for God. They’re the way we stay close to Him, and Hebrews 10:25 says we shouldn’t give up meeting together, but should encourage one another, even more as the day draws near.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Is gathering with believers a regular habit for you? What helps, and what gets in the way?
When has a gathering encouraged or changed you?
Why do you think some people stay away? What would you say to a friend who did?
Looking back over these nine weeks, which habit has taken root for you, and which one do you still need to work on?

b.x: Help each person see one thing that has grown. Some will feel they’ve done poorly, so point out what has changed, even if it’s small.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write a one-page weekly rhythm: when you pray, when you read the Bible, when you gather and how you give. Show it to your spiritual mentor or to someone in the group.
Invite someone to come with you to a gathering this Sunday.

b.x: Hebrews 10:25

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for these weeks and for Your family. Help us to keep walking with You every day. Amen.

This is the end of the second phase. Plan a simple celebration for your group, like a shared meal, and take a few minutes to share what has changed. The next phase is about living with the Holy Spirit’s help, and it starts the following week.
Thinking of you. Who did you invite?

x.q: Do I have to go to church on Sunday?
x.a: The Bible doesn’t give a rule about the day, but it does tell us not to give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:25). Encourage them to find a regular time to gather. Sunday is the most common choice.

x.q: My job doesn’t let me off on Sundays.
x.a: Don’t condemn them. Romans 14:5 says each person should be convinced in their own mind. Help them find another time to gather, and encourage them to talk with your pastor.

x.q: Is Sunday the same as the Sabbath?
x.a: No. The Sabbath was Saturday under the old law, and our rest now is in Jesus (Colossians 2:16-17). Sunday is the day we gather to celebrate His resurrection.

x.q: I don’t feel anything when I go to church.
x.a: Don’t judge them. Ask what they hope for, and encourage them to prepare by praying before the gathering and by sitting near someone they know. Suggest they talk with your pastor.

title: Who the Holy Spirit is
q: Who is the Holy Spirit?

b.x: Welcome back. We’re starting the third stretch of our time together, and I’m glad you’re here. This stretch is about living with the Holy Spirit’s help.
How did your weekly rhythm go? Did anyone invite someone to a gathering?
Hebrews 10:25
Tonight’s question is: who is the Holy Spirit?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for sending Your Spirit to live in us. Help us to know Him. Amen.
When you hear the words ‘Holy Spirit,’ what comes to mind?
Let people be honest. Some will say a power, a feeling or a mystery. A few may say they aren’t sure at all.

A lot of Christians feel unsure about the Holy Spirit, even after years in church. Jesus told His friends that it was good for them that He was going away, because He would send another Counselor to be with them (John 16:7). Tonight we’ll look at three things about Him.
He is God
Matthew 28:19

The Bible shows us one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Jesus told His followers to baptize in the name of all three. Paul closes a letter by naming all three together (2 Corinthians 13:14). We can’t fully understand how this works, and we don’t have to. God has told us what He wants us to know (Deuteronomy 29:29).

The Bible tells us the Holy Spirit is God. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter said he had lied to God (Acts 5:3-4). The Spirit is everywhere at once (Psalm 139:7). He knows everything, even the deep things of God (1 Corinthians 2:10-11). He has great power (Psalm 104:30), and He has no beginning and no end (Hebrews 9:14).
Because He is God, we can honor Him, thank Him and worship Him. The Father and the Son aren’t jealous when we do. They’re glad when we know the Spirit for who He is.
He is a person
Some people think of the Holy Spirit as only a force or a power. He does have power, but first, He is a person. He doesn’t have a body, but He has a personality.

He has a mind (Romans 8:27). He has a will, and He gives gifts as He decides (1 Corinthians 12:11). He has feelings, and He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30). And He speaks. In Antioch, the Holy Spirit told the church to set Barnabas and Saul apart for the work He had called them to (Acts 13:2).

That’s why the Bible gives us a few warnings. Don’t lie to Him (Acts 5:3). Don’t grieve Him (Ephesians 4:30). Don’t put out His fire (1 Thessalonians 5:19). Don’t keep resisting Him (Acts 7:51). Warnings like these only make sense about someone who can be hurt.

And because He’s a person, we can have a friendship with Him. Paul prays for fellowship with the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14), and he says that since we live by the Spirit, we should walk with Him step by step (Galatians 5:25). We can’t see Him, but we can sense His presence and learn to hear Him.
He is with us now

Jesus is with the Father in heaven (Mark 16:19). The Holy Spirit is the one who is here with us, and He lives inside every believer (1 Corinthians 3:16). He’s the God who is close. The world can’t receive Him, but you know Him, because He lives with you and will be in you.

Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. And as we look to Jesus, the Spirit slowly changes us to be more like Him (2 Corinthians 3:17-18). The fruit He grows in us is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23).
Getting to know Him

How do you get to know a person? You spend time with them, and you talk. So start by speaking to Him. Greet Him in the morning. Thank Him. Ask for help with the day. And then stop and listen for a moment. You don’t need special words.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What picture of the Holy Spirit did you have before tonight? What has changed?
Is it hard to think of Him as a person who can be pleased or grieved? Why?
Can you think of a time when you sensed His help?
What could you do this week to know Him better?

b.x: Don’t worry if some people say they’ve never felt anything. Remind them that the Spirit is with them because Jesus promised it, and not because of a feeling.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Each morning, greet the Holy Spirit by name, thank Him and ask for His help with your day.
Read Galatians 5:22-23 and pick one fruit of the Spirit. Ask Him to grow it in you this week.

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Holy Spirit, thank You for living in us. Teach us to know You, and help us follow You. Amen.
What does the Holy Spirit do in my life?
Thinking of you. Did you greet the Holy Spirit today?

x.q: Is the Holy Spirit just God’s power?
x.a: No. He has power, but He is a person. He thinks, wills, speaks and can be grieved. Walk them through the verses in Part 2.

x.q: Can I pray to the Holy Spirit?
x.a: Yes, because He is God. Many believers pray to the Father in Jesus’ name and ask the Spirit to help them, and that is a good pattern too.

x.q: I’m afraid I’ve sinned against the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31-32).
x.a: Be gentle. Tell them that a person who is troubled about this and wants to be close to God is not showing a hard heart. Encourage them to come to Jesus, and suggest they talk privately with your pastor.

x.q: I don’t feel anything. Is He really with me?
x.a: Feelings come and go. Jesus promised that the Spirit would be with us and in us (John 14:16-17). Keep talking to Him, and trust the promise.

title: What the Spirit does in us
q: What does the Holy Spirit do in my life?
notes: Your church may teach more about being baptized in the Holy Spirit and about spiritual gifts. This lesson covers what the Spirit does in every believer’s daily life. Add your pastor’s teaching on those other topics where it fits, or ask your pastor to teach them to the group.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about who the Holy Spirit is.
Did you greet the Holy Spirit this week? What happened, and did you notice anything?
Tonight’s question is: what does the Holy Spirit do in my life?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Holy Spirit, we want to know You more. Teach us, guide us and help us. Amen.
If you had a guide who knew the whole road, would you rather walk it alone or with the guide?
Let people laugh. Most will say with the guide.
That’s what the Holy Spirit is for us. He’s with us every step of the way. Tonight we’ll look at what He actually does. There are seven things.
He tells us we belong
Romans 8:16
If you’ve received Jesus, the Holy Spirit already lives in you, and He whispers deep inside that you are a child of God. On days when you doubt, this is the voice that says you’re His.
He helps us pray
Romans 8:26

We don’t always know what to pray, or how. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, and He speaks to the Father for us, even when we have no words. That’s why it helps to start prayer by asking, ‘Holy Spirit, help me pray.’
He helps us with God’s word
John 14:26

He helps us in two ways. First, He helps us understand and remember what we read. The Bible is hard to understand on our own, and the Spirit is our teacher. Second, He helps us live it out. God promises to put His Spirit in us and move us to follow His ways (Ezekiel 36:27). So when you feel a nudge to obey something you read, that’s often Him.
He helps us live a holy life
Galatians 5:16

The Holy Spirit makes us clean and keeps us growing. By Him, we can say no to what pulls us the wrong way (Romans 8:13). The Bible says to live by the Spirit, and then we won’t give in to the old desires. This is a daily choice, and He gives the strength.
He guides us in everyday life
John 16:13

Jesus said that the Spirit would guide us into all truth. His guidance isn’t limited to church matters. He’s a counselor for our families, our work, our studies, our marriages and our money. When we can’t tell what’s godly and what’s only our own desire, He helps us see.
He shows us the things of God
1 Corinthians 2:10

God reveals His wisdom and His will by His Spirit. If the Spirit is a close friend, we receive wisdom and understanding that we couldn’t get any other way. The more time we give Him, the more we hear.
He helps us see ahead

Jesus also said the Spirit would tell us what is yet to come (John 16:13). God may give us a sense of direction for our families, our work or our ministry. It won’t be a full picture. Next week and the week after, we’ll talk about how to tell whether something really comes from God.
And one more thing. The Bible tells us to keep on being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). It’s something we ask for again and again, because we need Him every day.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which of these seven things have you already experienced? What was it like?
Is it possible to be friends with someone you can’t see? How?
Can we live a Christian life without the Holy Spirit? Why or why not?
What could you do this week to grow closer to Him?

b.x: If someone feels they’ve never experienced any of these, don’t hurry. Encourage them to keep praying, reading the Bible and asking the Holy Spirit to help them. If they want to know more about being filled with the Spirit, invite them to talk with your pastor.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Before you pray and before you read the Bible, say, “Holy Spirit, help me,” and then pay attention to what stands out.
Pick one part of your life where you need guidance, and ask the Spirit for it each day. Write down what you sense.

b.x: Romans 8:14

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Holy Spirit, thank You for being our helper and guide. Lead us this week. Amen.
How do I make good decisions with God?
Thinking of you. Where did the Spirit help you today?

x.q: How do I know it’s the Holy Spirit and not just my own thoughts?
x.a: Say that this is a good question, and that you’ll spend the next two lessons on it. For now, tell them that what the Spirit says always agrees with the Bible.

x.q: What does it mean to be filled with the Holy Spirit?
x.a: Say that Ephesians 5:18 tells believers to keep being filled. Tell them what your church teaches, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: Does the Holy Spirit leave me when I sin?
x.a: Sin grieves Him (Ephesians 4:30), and sin harms our closeness to Him. But He is the one who convicts us and brings us back. Remind them of what Lesson 8 taught, and encourage them to confess quickly.

x.q: What about the gifts of the Spirit?
x.a: Tell them what your church teaches, and invite them to talk with your pastor. It’s a good topic for a future meeting.

title: Listening before doing
q: How do I make good decisions with God?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about what the Holy Spirit does in us.
Where did you notice the Spirit’s help this week? Did you pray for guidance in one area?
Romans 8:14
Tonight’s question is: how do I make good decisions with God?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to hear You before we act. Make us humble and willing to listen. Amen.
Think of a big decision you made in the last year. How did you decide?
Let people answer. Most of us weigh the facts, ask a friend or two, and pray, usually after we’ve already leaned one way.
That’s a normal way to decide. Tonight we’ll look at a better way, which is to ask God first and then act.
Why we go it alone
James 4:6

God gives grace to the humble and stands against the proud. At its root, pride is living without God. It means doing what I want and deciding for myself what’s right and wrong. The Bible traces this back to the first rebellion in heaven (Isaiah 14:12-14; Ezekiel 28:12-17). It entered our world when Adam and Eve wanted to be like God and live on their own terms (Genesis 3:4-5). And it has been passed on to all of us (Romans 5:12; Isaiah 53:6).
A proud person trusts their own ability, their own wisdom and their own experience. They may believe in God, and still live as if He isn’t needed.
Two ways to live
Jeremiah 17:5-8

God describes two kinds of people. The first trusts in human strength. That person is like a bush in the desert, with no sense of when good things come. The second trusts in the Lord. That person is like a tree planted by water. The roots reach the stream, the leaves stay green in a dry year, and the tree keeps bearing fruit.
Trust and ask
Proverbs 3:5-6

Trust in the Lord with all your heart, don’t lean on your own understanding, and in all your ways acknowledge Him. He’ll make your paths straight. People who trust God keep asking Him. Asking before we decide is a sign of a humble heart.

One clarification. We don’t need to ask God whether to do what He has already told us in the Bible, or whether to do our basic duties to our family, our work and our church. Those are settled. We ask about the choices that aren’t settled.
Listening before doing

David is called a man after God’s own heart. He had weaknesses and failures, but he learned to ask God first. When the Philistines attacked a town, he asked the Lord whether to go, and the Lord told him (1 Samuel 23:2-5). When his camp was burned and his family taken, he asked again before he chased the raiders (1 Samuel 30:7-8).
John 5:19

Jesus did the same. He said He could do nothing on His own, and that He only did what He saw the Father doing. Needs all around Him did not push Him. He moved when the Father moved (John 14:10). If the Son of God lived this way, we need to as well (1 John 2:6). Even good work that God hasn’t asked us to do can end up wasted.
God wants to speak

Does God still speak? The God of the Bible hasn’t changed (Malachi 3:6). He spoke to people then, and He wants to speak to us. In Revelation, the Spirit tells every church, ‘Whoever has ears, let them hear what the Spirit says’ (Revelation 2:7).

And He gives us the ability to hear Him. He puts a new spirit in us (Ezekiel 36:26), and Jesus says that His sheep know His voice (John 10:27). All of God’s children can be led by His Spirit (Romans 8:14).
Why we need to hear Him

There are three reasons. The first is a closer friendship. A relationship without conversation never gets close. Isaiah described waking each morning with God opening his ear to listen (Isaiah 50:4). The second is to obey. Sheep follow the shepherd because they know his voice (John 10:4), and we’re told to understand what the Lord’s will is (Ephesians 5:17). The third is to understand what we couldn’t learn on our own. The Spirit searches even the deep things of God, and He shares them with us (1 Corinthians 2:10).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Where have you made a decision without asking God? How did it go?
What would it look like to ask God before you decide? How would you do it?
Do you ever notice pride in the way you make choices?
Have you ever sensed God’s voice? Is it something that happens often or rarely?

b.x: For the third question, give the group a quiet moment, and don’t ask for answers out loud.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one decision you’re facing. Bring it to God every day this week before you decide. Write down what you sense, and what the Bible says about it.
Ask one wise, mature believer what they think about it.

b.x: Proverbs 3:5-6

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, we trust You with our decisions. Teach us to listen before we act. Amen.
Can I really hear God, and how do I know it’s Him?
Thinking of you. Did you bring your decision to God today?

x.q: Do I have to ask God about everything?
x.a: No. We don’t need to ask about what the Bible has already told us, or about our everyday duties. We ask about the choices that are still open, especially the big ones.

x.q: What if I don’t hear anything?
x.a: Don’t panic. Keep praying and reading the Bible, do what you already know is right, and seek the advice of mature believers (Proverbs 15:22). God may be silent for a while, and He is still with you.

x.q: Is asking other people for advice a lack of faith?
x.a: No. God often speaks through wise people. The Bible encourages us to seek counsel.

x.q: I have to make decisions quickly at work. What do I do?
x.a: Pray a short prayer as you go, and ask for wisdom (James 1:5). Over time, you’ll find it becomes a habit.

title: Hearing God’s voice
q: Can I really hear God, and how do I know it’s Him?
notes: This lesson is about how to recognize God’s voice and test it. Some people in the group may have strong experiences, and some may worry they hear nothing. Keep the tone calm. Whatever someone says they heard, it is weighed against the Bible and shared with mature believers. If anyone describes voices that frighten them or tell them to hurt themselves or others, take it seriously. Stay with them and get them to your pastor or a doctor right away.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about listening before we act.
Did you bring a decision to God this week? What did you sense, and what did the Bible say about it?
Proverbs 3:5-6
Tonight’s question is: can I really hear God, and how do I know it’s Him?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You speak to Your children. Open our ears and keep us from being fooled. Amen.
Can you recognize a family member’s voice on the phone, even without hearing their name?
Let people say yes. Say that we know voices we’ve listened to over time.
The same is true of God’s voice. We learn it the way we learn anyone’s, by spending time with Him. Tonight we’ll look at the ways He speaks, how to test what we hear, and what gets in the way.
How God speaks
The Bible shows seven ways God speaks to His children.
Through the Bible. As we read, the Holy Spirit makes certain words come alive for us. They can pierce the heart (Hebrews 4:12).
Through an inner voice. Since the Spirit lives in us, we can sense His leading from within (1 Corinthians 6:19; Romans 8:14).
Through peace. Sometimes God leads us by a settled peace that tells us we’re on the right path (Colossians 3:15).
Through a vision. God can give a picture in the mind, as He did for Peter (Acts 10:9-13).
Through a dream, as He did for Joseph (Matthew 1:20).
Through spiritual leaders. God uses mature leaders to speak to us, and He asks us to respect them (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13).
And through circumstances, as He did with Jonah (Jonah 1:12).
Test what you hear
1 Timothy 4:1
Not every voice comes from God, no matter how loud or clear it is. Some voices are deceiving. So we test them, and there are four tests.
Is it biblical? The voice will never contradict the Bible. Scripture is the measure of everything we hear (2 Timothy 3:16-17).
Does it lift up Jesus? The Holy Spirit always points to Jesus (1 Corinthians 12:3). If a voice makes a person, a group or a ministry bigger than Jesus, it isn’t from Him.
Is there a settled peace? God’s voice brings peace, even when it asks something hard (Colossians 3:15). The enemy’s voice tends to bring confusion and dread (Psalm 55:2-3).

And is there confirmation? Every matter is to be established by two or three witnesses (Matthew 18:16). If it’s an important decision, share what you sensed with a mature believer or your leader, and see whether they agree.
A dream or a vision on its own is never enough to make a major decision. Test it the same way.
What gets in the way
There are three hindrances.
The first is worldliness. If we’re holding on to things that grieve God, our ears get clogged. When we turn from them, we hear more clearly.

The second is unbelief. Everything in the Christian life runs on faith, and so does hearing from God. We believe He speaks when we call to Him (Jeremiah 33:3), and we trust that what we hear may be from Him, and not only our own thinking (1 Samuel 3:4-10).

The third is busyness. It may be the biggest one. Many of us believe God speaks, and we simply never stop to listen. When we pray, we do all the talking. Mary sat at Jesus’ feet and listened, while Martha was worried and worn out by all her tasks (Luke 10:38-42). We need time to be still.
Anywhere, anytime

The more we walk with God, the more we notice that He speaks in the middle of ordinary life. We’re told to pray at all times (1 Thessalonians 5:17). In Acts, Philip was told to go to a desert road (Acts 8:26-30), Ananias was sent to pray for Saul (Acts 9:10-17), and the church at Antioch heard the Spirit while they worshiped (Acts 13:2). None of them were looking for a special moment. Their friendship with God was strong, so they recognized Him.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Have you ever heard God’s voice? Is it something you hear often, or rarely?
Which of the three hindrances is most true for you?
Why is it wise to test what we hear, and to share it with others?
Is it a good idea to make a big decision based on one dream or one feeling? Why or why not?

b.x: This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Set aside ten minutes of silence. Read a short Bible passage, then sit quietly and listen. Write down what you sense.
Test what you wrote against the four questions: biblical, lifts up Jesus, peace, confirmation. Share it with a mature believer.

b.x: John 10:27

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, we want to know Your voice. Speak, Lord, we’re listening. Amen.
How do I live close to God every day?
Thinking of you. Did you get some quiet time with God today?

x.q: I’ve never heard God. Is something wrong with me?
x.a: No. Hearing God is a skill that grows with time and practice. Encourage them to keep reading the Bible, and to take the quiet time seriously.

x.q: What if I hear something that scares me or tells me to hurt myself or someone else?
x.a: That is not God. Stay with them, and get help right away from your pastor or a doctor. Don’t leave them alone with it.

x.q: I had a dream. Is it from God?
x.a: Maybe, and maybe not. Test it against the Bible, ask whether it lifts up Jesus, and share it with a mature believer before acting on it.

x.q: Why does God sometimes seem silent?
x.a: There are quiet seasons, and they are not always a sign of anything wrong. Keep walking with Him, do what you already know is right, and ask your pastor to pray with you.

title: Walking in His presence
q: How do I live close to God every day?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about how God speaks and how we test what we hear.
How did your ten minutes of quiet go? What did you sense, and did anyone test it with a mature believer?
John 10:27
Tonight’s question is: how do I live close to God every day?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to live in Your presence, not only visit it on Sundays. Draw us close. Amen.
Is there a place where you feel most at home? What makes it feel that way?
Let people share. It’s usually the people there.
God made us to be at home with Him. Tonight we’ll look at what it means to live in His presence, how to stay there, and what it looks like to walk with Him day by day.
Made for His presence

God made people in His own image, and He made a place for them to live. In the Garden of Eden, God walked with Adam and Eve in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8). The name Eden means delight. It was a place where God loved to be with the people He had made.

That’s what we were made for. David asked for one thing above all, to live in the Lord’s presence all his days (Psalm 27:4). In His presence there is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11). Moses said that without God’s presence, there was no point in going anywhere (Exodus 33:15-16). A person can be busy and successful and still be missing the thing they need most, which is God Himself.
Two kinds of presence
Psalm 139:7-8
God is present everywhere at all times. We can’t escape Him, and we never need to look for Him as if He were far away.

But the Bible also talks about God making His presence known in a way people can feel. He did it with Moses, with the Israelites, with the early church on the day of Pentecost, and with Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3-6). Christianity isn’t only a set of ideas about God. It’s a relationship with a living God who meets us.
What His presence does
2 Corinthians 3:17-18
When we spend time in His presence, we change. Saul went from a persecutor to an apostle after meeting Jesus. You can’t be changed by an idea. You get changed by meeting Him.
His presence also draws others. We can’t bring anyone to Christ by our own cleverness, but people notice when God is with us (Isaiah 60:1-3). Wherever we go, we carry the light with us.
Staying near
How do we stay in His presence? Four things help.
A heart that is willing to obey. Sin pushes us to hide from Him, as Adam and Eve did. Repentance brings us back (Psalm 24:3-4; Psalm 51:10-11).
The people we spend time with. Some friends pull us toward God, and some pull us away. We’re not to cut people off, but we do need to choose carefully who shapes us (2 Corinthians 6:14-15).

A willingness to go where God leads. Jonah ran the other way and paid for it (Jonah 1:1-4). Paul wanted to go one direction, and the Spirit redirected him (Acts 16:6-10). We stay near Him by following where He points.
And joining Him in His work. Jesus’ promise to be with us always came with a commission to make disciples (Matthew 28:19-20).
Walking with God
Genesis 5:21-24

Enoch lived 65 years and then began to walk with God, and he walked with Him for the next 300. The Bible doesn’t tell us much about those years, but it tells us that God was pleased with him (Hebrews 11:5). Walking with God means two people going the same direction, staying in conversation.

It begins when we’re made right with God through Jesus (2 Corinthians 5:18-19). It means a real, close relationship, the way a child is close to a father (Romans 8:15-16). Our first call is to walk with Him, and not just work for Him. Martha did a great deal for Jesus and missed sitting with Him (Luke 10:38-42). We don’t want to lose our first love (Revelation 2:1-5).

It means a right relationship, too. Friendship with the world pulls us away from God (James 4:4), and still He keeps calling us back (Hosea 3:1-3). And it means being in His will, in the right place at the right time, as Paul was when God guided him to Macedonia.

Enoch kept walking all the way to the end. A good start is important, and so is a good finish. Keep walking, and don’t let people, problems or the enemy kill a relationship with God (Matthew 24:12-13).
Seek Him every day
Isaiah 55:6

Sunday isn’t the only time to be near Him. We can seek His face every day, like a deer panting for water (Psalm 42:1). Jesus invites anyone who is thirsty to come to Him and drink (John 7:37-39). Come each day, and come with expectation.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: When do you most sense that God is near? What are you usually doing?
What makes you drift from His presence?
Is your faith based more on what you’ve learned about God, or on meeting Him yourself?
Which is harder for you right now, walking with God or working for God?

b.x: This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Each day, take five minutes with no requests. Simply be with God, and tell Him you’re glad He’s there.
Look at your week. Ask whether you’ve left room to walk with God, or whether you’ve filled every hour with doing.

b.x: Psalm 16:11

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that we were made for You. Keep us close. Amen.
What is fasting, and why would I do it?
Thinking of you. Did you take your five quiet minutes?

x.q: I don’t feel God’s presence. Is He gone?
x.a: No. Feelings change, and God doesn’t. Keep seeking Him. Ask what has changed in their life, and pray with them.

x.q: Does God leave me when I sin?
x.a: Sin makes us hide, but He keeps calling us back. Remind them of 1 John 1:9.

x.q: Do I need to leave my friends who aren’t believers?
x.a: No. Jesus was called a friend of sinners. We love them and we also choose carefully who has the most influence over us.

x.q: I’m too busy to spend time with God.
x.a: Start with five minutes. Many people find that they begin to want more.

title: Fasting
q: What is fasting, and why would I do it?
notes: Fasting affects the body, so this lesson gives health guidance that the original material leaves out. Please read Part 4 carefully before you teach. Nobody in the group should feel pushed to fast.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about walking with God in His presence.
How did your five quiet minutes go? Did anything change in how your week felt?
Psalm 16:11
Tonight’s question is: what is fasting, and why would I do it?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want to hunger for You more than for anything else. Teach us. Amen.
Have you ever skipped a meal because you were too busy, too nervous or too focused on something else?
Let people share. Say that when something matters enough, our appetite takes a back seat.

Fasting is going without food, or some other comfort, for a time, so that we can give God our full attention. It’s an old practice, and it’s a little unfamiliar to many believers today. Tonight we’ll see what the Bible says about it.
What Jesus taught
Matthew 6:16-18

Jesus said, ‘When you fast.’ He didn’t say ‘if.’ He spoke about fasting alongside giving and praying (Matthew 6:2, 5). He fasted for forty days Himself (Matthew 4:2), and He said His followers would fast once He was gone (Matthew 9:14-15). Moses, David, Esther, Daniel, Anna and Paul all fasted.
He also told us how to do it. We fast for God, in private, and not to be noticed by other people. Our Father sees what is done in secret, and He rewards it.

And God cares about our hearts when we fast. In Isaiah, the people fasted and still treated their workers unfairly, and God was not impressed. The fast He wants leads us to loosen the chains of injustice and share what we have (Isaiah 58:3-7). Fasting doesn’t force God’s hand. It humbles us and opens us to Him.
Kinds of fasting
The Bible shows three kinds.
A normal fast means going without food and drinking water. Jesus did this in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2).
A partial fast means limiting what we eat, like Daniel, who ate only vegetables and water for ten days (Daniel 1:12) and later gave up rich food, meat and wine for three weeks (Daniel 10:3).

An absolute fast means no food and no water. Ezra and Esther did this for a short time in a crisis (Ezra 10:6; Esther 4:16). Please don’t do this one. Going without water is dangerous, and God doesn’t ask it of us.
Why we fast
People in the Bible fasted for many reasons.
To draw near to God and seek Him with our whole heart. God said through Joel, ‘Return to Me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping’ (Joel 2:12-14).

To hear Him more clearly. When the church at Antioch was worshiping and fasting, the Holy Spirit gave them direction (Acts 13:1-3). The early church fasted and prayed before choosing leaders (Acts 14:23).

To break the hold of something heavy. Isaiah describes a fast that loosens chains and sets the oppressed free (Isaiah 58:6). Jesus said that some spiritual battles need prayer, and some old copies of Mark 9:29 add the words ‘and fasting.’ Fasting helps us stay with a hard prayer and focus on God’s strength.
And to humble ourselves. When Israel faced a hard battle in Judges 20, they wept and fasted before the Lord, and He gave them direction (Judges 20:26-28).
How to begin
If you want to try fasting, here’s some simple advice.

First, check your health. If you’re pregnant or nursing, you take medication, you have diabetes or another medical condition, or you’ve ever struggled with eating in a way that harmed you, don’t fast from food. Ask your doctor first, or fast from something else, like social media, television or a favorite treat. Children should not fast from food.

Second, start small. Skip one meal and use that time to pray and read the Bible. Next time, try a half day or a full day with water. Longer fasts can come later, with guidance from your pastor and a doctor.
Third, give the time to God. Fasting without prayer is only hunger. Use the hours you’d have spent eating to read, pray and listen.
Fourth, keep it private, as Jesus said. And fifth, end the fast gently with a light meal, and not a feast.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What comes to mind when you hear the word fasting? Where did you learn that?
Why do you think Jesus said “when you fast” and not “if”?
What would you want to fast from, and what would you pray about while you did?
What makes you hesitate?

b.x: Reassure the group that there’s no pressure. If someone has a health condition, point them to the non-food options.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: If you’re able, choose one meal or half a day to fast. Spend that time in prayer and reading the Bible, and write down what you sense. If you can’t fast from food, choose something else to go without.
Keep it between you and God, and tell your mentor only if you’d like their prayers.

b.x: Joel 2:12

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, we want to seek You with our whole hearts. Help us hunger for You. Amen.
Why is living for God so hard?
Thinking of you. How is the fasting going?

x.q: Is fasting required to be a Christian?
x.a: No. We’re saved by grace, and fasting doesn’t earn anything from God. Jesus expected His followers to fast, and it’s a way to draw near to Him.

x.q: I get a headache or feel dizzy.
x.a: Drink water and rest. If you feel unwell, end the fast. It’s no sign of failure.

x.q: My job is physical. Can I still fast?
x.a: Choose a partial fast, or skip one meal on a lighter day, and keep drinking water.

x.q: Can I fast from something besides food?
x.a: Yes. Social media, television and other comforts can also be set aside to make room for God.

title: Three enemies, one victory
q: Why is living for God so hard?

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about fasting.
Did anyone try a fast, or go without something to make room for God? What was it like?
Joel 2:12
Tonight’s question is: why is living for God so hard?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we’re glad the battle is Yours. Help us stand in the victory Jesus won. Amen.
Has anyone ever said, ‘I know what’s right, and I still do the opposite’?
Let people laugh a little. Everyone knows this feeling.

Paul felt that too. He wrote that when he wanted to do good, evil was close at hand (Romans 7:21-25). If you’ve felt this since you came to Christ, you’re in good company. Tonight we’ll look at three things that pull against us, and the good news is that Jesus has already won.
The sinful nature
Romans 7:21-25
The first enemy is inside us. We inherited a pull toward sin from Adam (Romans 5:12). Paul cried out, ‘Who will rescue me?’ and answered right away, ‘Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.’
So how do we deal with it? Three ways.
We live in Jesus’ victory. When Jesus is our Lord, the old nature doesn’t get to run our lives.

We live under the Spirit’s control. God commands us to walk by the Spirit, and then we won’t give in to the desires of the old nature (Galatians 5:16-17). There’s now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because the Spirit of life has set us free (Romans 8:1-2). By the Spirit we put to death the habits of the body, and we live (Romans 8:13).

And we live as the new person God made us. Each day we say no to the old desires (Luke 9:23), because we’ve been crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20; 5:24). We’re a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). Our lives haven’t merely been patched up. We have a new life.
The devil
Ephesians 6:12
The second enemy is real, and it’s behind much of what we face. The devil uses three weapons.
Temptation. He offers us something that looks good, to pull us away from God’s will. He even tried it on Jesus (Matthew 4:1-10).

Accusation. The Bible calls him the accuser (Revelation 12:10). He tells us lies about ourselves, and he brings up sins God has already forgiven. He also uses other people to accuse us, and he can use us to accuse others. And he may accuse God to us, so that we begin to doubt that God is good. If you ever have a heavy, vague voice telling you that you’re worthless, remember that Jesus has not condemned you (Romans 8:1).

Deception. He feeds us false beliefs that lead us to wrong decisions, as he did to Eve (1 Timothy 2:14; 4:1). A deceived person can’t see that they’re wrong. This is another reason to know the Bible and to test what we hear.
James 4:7

How do we fight? We stay alert and pray (1 Peter 5:8-9). We submit to God. And we resist the enemy, standing firm in faith, until he leaves. Jesus used the word of God when He was tempted, and we can too (Ephesians 6:17; Matthew 4:1-10). We also resist in the name of Jesus.
The world

The third enemy is the world. John doesn’t mean the earth God made, or the people He loves (John 3:16). He means the systems and values that stand against God. He names three. The cravings of the flesh, which means living for pleasure. The desire of the eyes, which means wanting more and more things. And the pride of life, which means wanting to be admired and to be a big name.

How do we resist? We refuse to be pressed into the world’s mold, and we let God change how we think (Romans 12:2). We stay filled with the Spirit and with the word (Ephesians 5:15-18). And we stay connected to God’s people, who help us see what the world hides.
They work together
These three work as a team. The devil tempts us through the values of the world, so that we follow the old nature. If we see that, we won’t be surprised when it comes.
The victory is already won
Colossians 2:15

On the cross, Jesus defeated all three. We’re not fighting to win a battle that’s undecided. We fight from His victory. Everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world, and our faith is the victory (1 John 5:4-5). Thanks be to God who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which of the three enemies, the old nature, the devil or the world, do you feel most this week?
Of the devil’s three weapons, temptation, accusation or deception, which one is most familiar to you?
What lie about yourself do you most often hear in your head? What does God say instead?
What helps you stand firm when you feel pulled?

b.x: If someone shares a struggle, thank them and don’t try to fix it in the room. Pray for them, and suggest a conversation with your pastor.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one verse that answers the lie you hear most often. Write it on a card and say it aloud when the lie comes.
When you’re tempted this week, do three things in order: stop and pray, say “I belong to Jesus,” and move away from the situation.

b.x: James 4:7

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that Jesus has already won. Help us stand in His victory. Amen.
How do I leave sin behind for good?
Thinking of you. Which verse did you use today?

x.q: Does a Christian still have a sinful nature?
x.a: Tell them that the pull remains, and so does the struggle Paul describes. But we’re no longer slaves to it, and the Spirit gives us strength to say no.

x.q: Is every bad thing that happens the devil’s fault?
x.a: No. Some things are our own choices, some come from other people, and some come from living in a broken world. The devil is real, and we don’t need to blame him for everything.

x.q: I’m afraid of the devil.
x.a: Tell them that Jesus has already defeated him (Colossians 2:15), and that a child of God doesn’t have to live in fear. Pray with them.

x.q: I keep hearing a voice that says I’m worthless.
x.a: That is the accuser, and not God. Read Romans 8:1 with them, and pray together. If the thoughts are heavy or frightening, encourage them to talk with your pastor, and see a doctor if they feel unsafe.

title: Go and sin no more
q: How do I leave sin behind for good?
notes: This lesson is about holiness, and it is easy to teach it in a way that crushes people. Lead with grace. Jesus forgave first and then said, “Go and sin no more.” If someone is carrying heavy shame, listen and pray with them, and suggest they talk privately with your pastor.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about the three enemies we face and the victory Jesus has already won.
Which verse did you use this week when a lie or a temptation came? Did it help?
James 4:7
Tonight’s question is: how do I leave sin behind for good?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You that You forgive us. Give us the strength to walk in freedom. Amen.
Has anyone ever been in a situation where something promised to make them happy and left them feeling empty instead?
Let people share, and be gentle.
That’s the nature of sin. It rarely looks bad at first. Tonight we’ll look at why Jesus told us to leave it behind, and how.
Grace first
John 8:3-11

A woman caught in sin was brought to Jesus. Everyone else was ready to condemn her. Jesus said that anyone without sin could throw the first stone, and they all left. Then He said, ‘Neither do I condemn you. Go now and leave your life of sin.’

Look at the order. He forgave her first, and then He told her to go and sin no more. Forgiveness comes before the change, and it makes the change possible. God calls us to be holy because He is holy (1 Peter 1:15-16).
Why leave sin
Why should we leave sin behind? The Bible gives many reasons. Let me give you five.
Sin doesn’t satisfy. It can give real pleasure, but only for a while (Hebrews 11:25). Afterward, many people feel empty and ashamed. The thing that promised joy ends up taking it.

Sin grows. One sin leads to another, and the habit tightens its hold (Proverbs 5:22). A sinner may think they’re free and a believer is restricted. It’s really the opposite. Sin makes us slaves, and the Son sets us free (John 8:34-36). Give sin an inch, and it asks for a mile.

Sin steals our joy and our dignity. The joy of the Lord is our strength (Nehemiah 8:10), and sin pushes us away from the place where that joy is found (Psalm 16:11). It also leaves a stain, as a few dead flies spoil perfume (Ecclesiastes 10:1).

Sin leads to death. It promises happiness and pays out death (Romans 6:23). It dulls our hearts toward God, and if we keep going on purpose, it can lead to separation from Him (James 1:15; Hebrews 10:26-27). Remember what we said in Lesson 8. This is a warning to take seriously, and it’s no cause for panic in a believer who wants to follow Jesus.

And sin hurts people. It hurts God. When Peter denied Jesus, the Lord turned and looked at him, and Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61-62). It hurts us, in our health, our work and our minds. And it hurts our families, our friends and our church.
God looks at the heart
Jeremiah 17:10

God doesn’t only watch what we do. He looks at why we do it. He sees the motive behind our worship, our prayers, our giving and our fasting (Matthew 6:1; Luke 18:9-14; Luke 21:1-4). A right motive is aimed at God, and a wrong one is aimed at ourselves or at people’s approval (Galatians 1:10). Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God (Matthew 5:8).

How do we find out what’s in our hearts? Look at the fruit of our lives. Listen to the words that come out of our mouths, since the mouth speaks what the heart is full of (Matthew 12:34). And notice how we respond when things go very well or very badly.
How to leave sin behind
Four things help.

Watch yourself. Eve got into trouble when she lingered near the tree and listened to the wrong voice (Genesis 3:1-6). Know where you’re weak, and stay away from places and situations that make it easy to fall.

Change what you tell yourself. Many people keep sinning because they believe, ‘I’m only human, I can’t stop.’ That’s a lie. We’re a new creation, dead to sin and alive to God (2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 6:11). Sin is no longer our master (Romans 6:14).
Say no, and lean on grace. God’s grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness (Titus 2:11-12). We don’t fight in our own strength.

And change what you desire. God doesn’t tempt us. Temptation grows out of our own desires (James 1:13-14). We deal with these by filling our hearts with God’s word (Psalm 119:11) and with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), and by asking God to search us and make our hearts clean (Psalm 139:23-24; Psalm 51:10). We guard our hearts above everything else (Proverbs 4:23).
And when we do fall, we come back quickly. Jesus speaks for us before the Father (1 John 2:1), and He is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Of the five reasons to leave sin, which one speaks to you most? Why?
Why do you think some believers have a hard time saying no to temptation?
What is something in your life that isn’t pleasing to God? Are you ready to turn from it?
What do you think God sees when He looks at your heart?

b.x: The third question can be answered in silence. Don’t ask for answers out loud.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Ask God to search your heart. Write down anything He shows you, and take one clear step of turning.
Choose one place, person or habit that makes sin easy for you, and put distance between you and it this week.

b.x: Psalm 119:11

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You forgive us and set us free. Give us clean hearts and the strength to say no. Amen.
How do I stay fruitful when life is hard?
Thinking of you. How is the step going?

x.q: Can a Christian really stop sinning?
x.a: Tell them that sin no longer has to be our master (Romans 6:14), and the Spirit gives us strength. We still stumble sometimes, and when we do, we come back quickly (1 John 1:9).

x.q: I keep falling into the same sin. I feel hopeless.
x.a: Don’t lecture. Remind them of John 8:11, that Jesus forgives first. Encourage them to tell a trusted believer or your pastor, since we get free faster when we don’t carry it alone (James 5:16).

x.q: How do I know if my motives are right?
x.a: Ask yourself whether you’d still do it if no one would ever know. And ask God to show you (Psalm 139:23-24).

x.q: Is God angry with me when I sin?
x.a: It grieves Him, because He loves us. And He’s quick to forgive when we come to Him. Read Luke 15:20 together.

title: Good ground
q: How do I stay fruitful when life is hard?
notes: This lesson touches on persecution and on forgiving people who have hurt us deeply. Someone in your group may be facing rejection from their family, or may have been seriously wronged. Listen first. Forgiving someone never means staying in a situation that isn’t safe. If anyone is in danger, help them reach your pastor and the proper authorities.

b.x: Welcome back. This is our last lesson in this third stretch, and I’m so glad you’re here.
What step did you take this week to leave something behind? How did it go?
Psalm 119:11
Tonight’s question is: how do I stay fruitful when life is hard?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, we want our hearts to be good soil. Plant Your word deep in us. Amen.
Have you ever planted something and watched it die? What went wrong?
Let people share. It’s often the soil, the weather or the weeds.

Jesus told a story about exactly this. He said that if we don’t understand it, we won’t understand any of His other parables (Mark 4:13). It’s a good story to end this stretch on, because it asks what has happened to everything we’ve been planting in these weeks.
The sower and the seed
Mark 4:3-9

A farmer scatters seed, and it falls on four kinds of ground. Jesus explains that the farmer is God, the seed is His word, and the ground is our hearts (Mark 4:14). Good seed can still fail to grow if the soil is wrong.
Four kinds of ground
The first ground is the hard path. The word lands and is taken away before it can grow (Mark 4:15). This is a heart that has closed itself to the message.
The second is rocky ground. People hear the word and receive it with joy, but it has no roots. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they fall away quickly (Mark 4:16-17).

The third is thorny ground. The word grows for a while, and then it is choked by the worries of life, the love of money, the desire for other things and the pull of pleasure (Mark 4:18-19; Luke 8:14). These people stay stuck as spiritual babies and don’t bear much fruit.

And the fourth is good ground. These people hear the word, understand it (Matthew 13:23), accept it, live it (James 1:22) and hold on to it with patience (Luke 8:15). They bear fruit thirty, sixty or even a hundred times over. Success in the Christian life isn’t a matter of how strongly we started. What counts is how we endure.
Which ground are you? Be honest with yourself tonight. All of us have a bit of each.
When trouble comes
2 Timothy 3:12

The rocky ground gives way under pressure. Jesus and Paul said plainly that those who live for Christ will face opposition (John 15:18-20; 2 Timothy 3:12). The enemy wants to push us away from God (Revelation 2:10), and many people who don’t yet know God react against those who follow Him (John 15:21).

It can look like insults, false rumors, being left out, family members turning away (Matthew 10:35-36), and in some places, much worse. Jesus said, ‘Blessed are you when people insult you and say all kinds of evil against you because of Me. Rejoice and be glad’ (Matthew 5:11-12). The Spirit of glory rests on those who suffer for Christ’s name (1 Peter 4:14).

How do we respond? We expect it, since Jesus told us (Matthew 10:24-25). We guard our hearts from hatred and bitterness. We bless and pray for the people who treat us badly, and we don’t pay back evil with evil (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:17-21). And we remember that we share in what Christ went through, and that glory is coming (1 Peter 4:13).
This isn’t a call to look for trouble, or to stay in danger. If you’re being threatened, tell your pastor, and use wisdom to stay safe.
The thorn of unforgiveness
One of the thorns that chokes the word fastest is a heart that holds on to a grudge. We’ll spend a few minutes here because it affects so many of us.

How do you know if you haven’t forgiven someone? You don’t want to be around them or hear their name. You can only see their faults. You replay what they did again and again. You’d secretly like to see them get what they deserve. You speak badly of them. And in prayer, they keep coming to mind.

Why forgive? Because God has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32). Because Jesus told us that our own prayers are blocked when we refuse (Matthew 6:14-15; Mark 11:25). Because bitterness gives the enemy a foothold (Ephesians 4:26-27). And because a bitter root poisons others around us (Hebrews 12:15), while a person who has been healed can bring healing to others.

How do we forgive? Start by receiving God’s forgiveness for yourself. Then decide to forgive. Peter asked how many times, and Jesus said seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21-22). Then pray good things for the person who hurt you, and keep doing it until the heaviness lifts (Luke 6:27-28). The feelings follow the decision, and not the other way around.
Forgiving doesn’t mean saying that what was done was fine, and it doesn’t mean going back into a harmful situation. It means you let go of the debt and hand the person over to God.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which ground do you recognize most in your own life right now?
What are the thorns in your life? Worries, money, desires, pleasures?
Have you experienced opposition because of your faith? How did you respond?
Is there someone you haven’t forgiven yet? Are you ready to forgive them?

b.x: The last question can be answered in silence. Don’t ask for answers out loud.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Name one thorn in your life, and write down one step you’ll take to pull it out.
Write the name of someone you need to forgive. Pray for that person by name every day this week, and ask God to bless them.

b.x: Luke 8:15

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, make our hearts good ground. Give us roots that go deep, and fruit that lasts. Amen.

This is the end of the third phase. Plan a simple celebration for your group, like a shared meal, and take a few minutes to share what has changed. The next phase is about giving our whole lives to Jesus as Lord, serving in His church and reaching others, and it starts the following week.
Thinking of you. Are you praying for that person?

x.q: My family might reject me because of my faith.
x.a: Listen, and don’t hurry to reassure them. Pray with them. Remind them that Jesus said we’d face this, and that He is with them (Matthew 28:20). Make sure your pastor knows so the church can support them.

x.q: I’ve forgiven, but I still feel the hurt.
x.a: That’s normal. Forgiveness is a decision, and healing takes time. Keep praying for the person, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: Do I have to stay close to someone who keeps hurting me?
x.a: No. Forgiving a person doesn’t mean you have to be in harm’s way. Help them stay safe, and bring in your pastor.

x.q: Is every hard thing persecution?
x.a: No. Some hardship comes from our own choices or from living in a hard world. Persecution is trouble that comes because we follow Jesus.

title: All in
q: What does it mean to follow Jesus all the way?
notes: This lesson asks people to look hard at their own motives. Keep the tone gentle. Nobody should leave feeling they are a bad Christian. Jesus was honest with the people in this story, and He was also kind to them.

b.x: Welcome back. We’ve finished three stretches of this journey, and tonight we begin the last one. I’m glad you’re still here.
Last week we talked about two things, a thorn to pull out and someone to forgive. How did it go?
Don’t press anyone to share the second one.
Luke 8:15
Tonight’s question is: what does it mean to follow Jesus all the way?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Jesus, we want to follow You, not only when it’s easy. Show us what’s in our hearts tonight. Amen.
Have you ever started something with a lot of energy, like a diet, a course or a friendship, and watched it fade? What happened?
Let people laugh and share.

Many people start well with God and then cool off. Some go back to the life they left. Others still show up at church while their hearts are somewhere else. There are many reasons, and one of the biggest is a weak commitment. Tonight we’ll look at a short scene in Luke 9, where three people say they want to follow Jesus, and see what He says to each.
Following with a condition

One man said, ‘I will follow You wherever You go.’ It sounds wonderful. Jesus answered, ‘Foxes have dens and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.’ He didn’t say ‘Great, come along.’ He told the man what following would cost.

Why? Because Jesus knew the heart. Some people follow Him for what they can get. In John 6 a crowd followed Him because of the miracles (John 6:2) and because they were fed (John 6:26). When the hard teaching came, many turned back and stopped walking with Him (John 6:66).

A commitment that depends on blessings lasts only as long as the blessings do. Look at Peter. When others left, Jesus asked the twelve if they wanted to go too, and Peter said, ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life’ (John 6:67-69). That’s what lasts. It’s knowing who He is.
Following after my own plans

Another man was told, ‘Follow Me,’ and he answered, ‘Lord, first let me go and bury my father.’ Many Bible teachers think his father hadn’t died yet. The man was saying, ‘I’ll follow You after my family duties are finished, when life settles down.’ Jesus told him that the time to start is now.

We say the same kind of thing. After I finish school. After I get the promotion. After the children are grown. After I’ve had my fun. God’s will becomes something we fit in around our own plans. Jesus doesn’t ask us to neglect our families. He asks us not to put Him last.
Following with one foot back

A third person said, ‘I will follow You, Lord, but first let me say goodbye to my family.’ Jesus answered that no one who puts a hand to the plow and keeps looking back is fit for the kingdom of God. Imagine a farmer plowing a field and looking over his shoulder. The row comes out crooked.

This is the person who has started but keeps glancing back at the old life. They haven’t left it behind in their heart. If you feel that tug, you’re in good company. Lot’s wife looked back (Luke 17:32). The Israelites in the wilderness kept remembering Egypt. That pull tells us something still has a grip on the heart, and Jesus wants to loosen it.
The commitment God looks for
So what does a whole-hearted commitment look like? There are three marks.
Habakkuk 3:17-18

First, it comes without conditions. The prophet says that even if the fig tree doesn’t bloom and the fields give no food, and there are no sheep in the pen, ‘yet I will rejoice in the Lord.’ We follow Jesus whether He gives us what we ask or not. Job lost nearly everything in a day and still worshiped (Job 1:20-22). We follow Him because He is worth following.

Second, it’s committed to His will. Jesus said that whoever loses their life for Him will save it (Mark 8:35). When Jesus called Peter, James and John, they left their nets and followed Him right away (Matthew 4:18-22). When we know what He’s asking, we don’t put it off.

Third, it doesn’t turn back. When Elisha was called, he slaughtered his oxen and used the plow for fuel, so there would be nothing to go back to (1 Kings 19:19-21). He cut off his own way of retreat. What are the things that make it easy for us to turn back? Old friendships that pull us down. Habits. Places. Maybe an old way of thinking. Elisha didn’t just say yes. He made a clean break.

I want to be honest about one thing. Jesus is not asking for perfection. Peter denied Him three times and was restored (John 21:15-19). Whole-hearted means we keep turning toward Him, and when we fall, we get up and come back.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Why did you start following Jesus? Has your reason changed?
Of the four kinds of commitment, one with conditions, one after my own plans, one with a foot back, and one whole-hearted, which describes you right now?
Which of the three marks is hardest for you: no conditions, His will, or no turning back?
What is one thing you could cut off, so that it’s easier to keep following Jesus?

b.x: Don’t push anyone to answer the second question out loud. A quiet “I’m somewhere in the middle” is an honest answer, so thank people for it.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write down one thing that makes it easy for you to turn back, and one step you’ll take to put distance between you and it.
Tell Jesus in your own words, once a day, “I’m following You, whether or not You give me what I ask for.”

b.x: Luke 9:23

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Jesus, we say yes to You again tonight. Keep our hearts from turning back, and thank You for holding on to us. Amen.
What does it mean that Jesus is Lord?
Thinking of you. How is the step going?

x.q: I’m not sure my commitment is strong enough.
x.a: Reassure them. Wanting to follow Jesus is a good start, and He is patient. Remind them that Peter failed and was restored (John 21:15-19). Pray with them.

x.q: Does this mean God will make my life hard?
x.a: Not always. Jesus was honest that following Him costs something, and He also promised to be with us (Matthew 28:20). Some seasons are easy and some are hard.

x.q: I’ve gone back to my old life before. Is it too late?
x.a: No. Read Luke 15:20 together and tell them the Father is still watching the road. Suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: Do I have to give up my family?
x.a: No. Jesus asks that nothing and no one comes before Him. Following Him makes us better at loving our families, and He doesn’t ask us to neglect them (1 Timothy 5:8).

title: Jesus is Lord
q: What does it mean that Jesus is Lord?
notes: Some of the verses here, especially Luke 14, sound harsh. Take them slowly. Jesus is describing who comes first in our lives, and He never asks anyone to stop loving or caring for their family. If someone is carrying a lot of fear or pressure from home, listen to them before you teach.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we asked what it means to follow Jesus all the way.
What did you cut off, or put distance from, this week? Was it hard?
Luke 9:23
Tonight’s question is: what does it mean that Jesus is Lord?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Lord Jesus, You are Lord. Help us to say it, and mean it, in every part of our lives. Amen.
When you hear the word ‘lord’, what do you picture?
Let people answer. Some will think of kings, landlords or bosses.

The word ‘Lord’ means master, the one who decides. It’s one of the most common words for Jesus in the Bible. In the New Testament, He is called Lord over six hundred times, and Savior far fewer. That doesn’t make His saving less important. It shows that being saved and following Him as Lord go together.
Lord at the start
Romans 10:9

Paul says that if we declare with our mouths ‘Jesus is Lord’ and believe in our hearts that God raised Him from the dead, we will be saved. Notice the word. Lord. We aren’t only asking Jesus to rescue us. We’re saying that He is the one in charge.
