Think of a lifeguard and a captain. We’re glad when a lifeguard pulls us out of the water, and then we go home. A captain is someone we follow. Jesus is both, and He doesn’t want to be only the One we call in an emergency.
Lord means obedience
Luke 6:46

Jesus asks, ‘Why do you call Me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?’ Saying it isn’t enough. He says that not everyone who says ‘Lord, Lord’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of His Father (Matthew 7:21).

Let me be clear about what this is not. We aren’t saved by obeying. We’re saved by grace through faith, as we saw in Lesson 4. But the faith that is real shows up in how we live. Obedience is how we show Him that we love Him (John 14:15).
Lord starts in the heart and lasts
1 Peter 3:15

Peter says, ‘In your hearts revere Christ as Lord.’ It starts on the inside. We can go to church and keep all the customs and still keep our hearts to ourselves. Jesus is Lord when we give Him our hearts.
Colossians 2:6-7

And it lasts. Paul writes, ‘Just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live in Him.’ We don’t make Him Lord once and then take the controls back. We yield again each day, and the more we know Him, the easier it gets.
Lord of everything
Jesus wants to be Lord of every part of our lives. Let’s look at four of them.

Our relationships. Jesus said that whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter more than Him isn’t worthy of Him (Matthew 10:37). In Luke 14:26, He uses the strong word ‘hate’ to make the same point. He’s using a way of speaking that means ‘love so much less by comparison.’ He isn’t asking us to stop loving our families. God commands us to honor our parents and to care for our households. He’s saying that when love for family and love for Him point in different directions, He comes first.

Ourselves. ‘I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20). Our own plans, desires and pride have to be put under His. This is about trading the old driver for a better one.

Our money. Paul warned that the love of money has led some away from the faith and caused them many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10). Jesus said that no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). When Jesus says we must give up everything to follow Him (Luke 14:33), He means that we hold our things loosely and are willing to let go of any of them if He asks. It doesn’t mean everyone must sell all they own.
And our time. This is the one we forget. A person’s calendar usually shows who the real Lord is. Ask yourself: who gets the best hours of my week?

How do I know if money has become my master? Ask yourself a few questions. Do I worry about it more than I trust God? Do I find it hard to give? Would I disobey God to get more of it? If so, bring it to Jesus. He’s gentle with us when we do.
What happens when He takes charge

Here’s the good news. The Lord we are talking about is the One who died for us. He isn’t a tyrant. His commands protect us and lead us toward what is good (John 10:10). He says, ‘My yoke is easy and My burden is light’ (Matthew 11:30). When Jesus takes charge, we find that we’re finally free, because we stop being ruled by fear, by money and by what other people think.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What is the difference between having Jesus as Savior and having Him as Lord?
In which area is it hardest to let Jesus be Lord: relationships, myself, money or time? Why?
What do you think happens when Jesus takes charge of a life? What does Galatians 2:20 say?
How can you tell if money, or something else, has started to rule you?

b.x: The first question is the key one. Take your time with it.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Pick one area, relationships, myself, money or time, where Jesus is not yet Lord. Tell Him so, and surrender it in prayer.
Look at your calendar and your bank or wallet from last week. Ask Him what He thinks of them.

b.x: Luke 6:46

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Lord Jesus, we make You Lord of everything, our families, ourselves, our money and our time. We trust You. Amen.
What is my life for?
Thinking of you. How is your surrender going?

x.q: If I’m saved by grace, why does obedience matter?
x.a: We obey because we love Him and because He’s Lord. Obedience doesn’t earn our salvation. It shows that our faith is real (John 14:15; James 2:17).

x.q: Does Jesus really want me to hate my family?
x.a: No. The word is a strong way of saying that He comes first. He told us to honor our parents and to love our families. Read Matthew 10:37 together.

x.q: Do I have to give away all my money?
x.a: No. Jesus asks us to hold our possessions loosely and to put Him first. If He asks you for something specific, you’ll know, and you can talk about it with your pastor.

x.q: What if I fail to obey?
x.a: Say that He forgives, and that Lordship is a daily choice. Read 1 John 1:9 together.

title: Four ways to live
q: What is my life for?
notes: This lesson describes people living wasted or self-centered lives. Don’t use it to point at anyone, in the group or outside it. Present it as a mirror for each of us. Some of your people may carry real regret about years they feel they lost, so be especially kind with Part 1.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about Jesus being Lord of every part of our lives.
Which area did you surrender, and what did it feel like?
Luke 6:46
Tonight’s question is: what is my life for?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You made us for a purpose. Show us what it is, and give us courage to live for it. Amen.
If you could ask God one thing about your life, what would it be?
Let people share. Many will ask ‘why am I here?’

Everyone who lives on this earth is living in one of four ways. Three of them miss what God made us for. The fourth is the one He designed for us. I want you to see all four, and to ask which one is yours.
A wasted life

Remember the younger son who took his inheritance and spent it all. He wasted his money, his time and his strength, and ended up feeding pigs and wishing he could eat their food. Some people waste their lives on things like drinking, gambling, drugs or loose living. Those things take time and money, and they leave a trail of hurt in families.

But look at the end of the story. The son came to his senses and went home, and the father ran to meet him. No matter how much has been wasted, it’s never too late to come home. If that’s you, or if it was you once, hear this. The Father is waiting.
A life lived for self

In Jesus’ story, a rich man lived in luxury every day, and a poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores, hoping for scraps. The rich man’s sin was that he never saw the man at his gate. Being rich was not the problem.

Many people, rich or poor, live this way. They care about getting ahead and having a comfortable life, and they hardly notice anyone else. Jesus told of a farmer who had a great harvest and made plans to build bigger barns, then eat, drink and enjoy life. God said, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be demanded from you’ (Luke 12:16-21). He was rich in things and poor toward God.
Jesus said that what we do for the least of these, we do for Him (Matthew 25:40, 45). We care about people because He cares about them.
A life lived for earthly goals
Romans 10:1-3

The third way is harder to spot. Paul writes about his own people. They were zealous for God, but their zeal wasn’t based on knowledge. They tried to earn a right standing with God by their own effort and didn’t submit to God’s way.

Some people do a great deal of good. They serve and give and work hard. But underneath, they’re doing it for their own name, for their group, their church or their cause, or to feel that they’re good enough. Jesus warned that people can honor Him with their lips while their hearts are far from Him (Matthew 15:8-9). It looks very good from outside, and God sees the heart.
If you’ve served for a long time, ask yourself gently: who is this for? It’s a question for all of us, me included.
A life lived for God’s plan
Isaiah 6:8
Isaiah heard the Lord ask, ‘Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?’ And he answered, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ The fourth way is to give ourselves to God’s plan and to say yes.

That doesn’t mean everyone becomes a pastor or a missionary. God’s plan includes parents, teachers, nurses, drivers, shopkeepers and students. What matters is that we’ve asked Him what He wants, and we’re ready to do it. Paul says that if we cleanse ourselves from what dishonors Him, we’ll be useful to the Master and ready for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21).

There’s real freedom here. We were made for this, and we find real satisfaction only at the center of His will. Think of a key made for one lock. It works nowhere else. Jesus said, ‘Whoever loses their life for My sake will find it’ (Matthew 16:25).

And don’t worry if you don’t know the details yet. God’s plan usually unfolds one step at a time. We said in Lesson 21 that the first thing is to ask and to listen. The next thing is to take the step in front of us.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which of the four ways of living describes you best right now? Which has described you in the past?
Why do you think so many people live for themselves, even when they know it won’t satisfy?
How can you tell whether you’re serving for God or for your own name?
Are you ready to say, “Here am I. Send me”? What makes it hard?

b.x: Take the second question lightly and the fourth seriously. Don’t hurry the silence after the fourth.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Ask God one question every day: “What do You want me to do today?” Write down what comes to mind.
Do one thing for someone who can’t pay you back, and tell no one about it.

b.x: Isaiah 6:8

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, here we are. Send us. Use our lives for Your purpose, and keep us from living for ourselves. Amen.
Why do I need to be in a small group?
Thinking of you. Did you hear anything from God today?

x.q: I’ve wasted so many years. Is it too late for God to use me?
x.a: No. Read Luke 15:20-24 together. God uses people at every age, and He restores what has been lost (Joel 2:25). Pray with them.

x.q: How do I know what God’s plan for me is?
x.a: It usually comes one step at a time. Ask Him, read the Bible, listen to wise believers, and obey what you already know (Proverbs 3:5-6).

x.q: Is it wrong to want a comfortable life?
x.a: No. Rest and comfort are good. The warning is about a life that is only about us, and that doesn’t see others or God.

x.q: I serve a lot, but I’m tired and a bit resentful.
x.a: Listen first. Ask whose approval they’re serving for, and encourage them to rest, to talk with your pastor, and to remember that God loves them apart from what they do.

title: Meeting in homes
q: Why do I need to be in a small group?
notes: Your group is the example for this lesson. As you teach it, notice how your own meetings work, and let people say what this group has meant to them. Some people have been hurt in groups before, so make room for a quiet answer.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we asked what our lives are for, and we looked at four ways to live.
Did you ask God what He wanted from you each day? Did anything come to mind?
Isaiah 6:8
Tonight’s question is: why do I need to be in a small group?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for each person in this room. Make us a real family to one another. Amen.
Think of one person who has helped you most in your life. How did they do it?
Let people share. It’s usually someone who spent time with them.
Growing in faith is something we do with other people. Tonight we’ll look at why God’s people have always met in small groups, and what a group like ours is for.
Two places to gather
Acts 2:46

The first believers met in two places. They gathered in the temple courts, which was the large meeting, and they broke bread from house to house, which was the small one. We said in Lesson 18 that gathering every week matters. That’s the big gathering. Today we’re talking about the other one.

Many believers see each other only on Sunday. That’s good, and it isn’t enough. In a big gathering we can listen and sing, and nobody has to know our names. In a home, people can ask us how we are, and they notice when we’re missing.

The Bible shows this over and over. Paul taught ‘publicly and from house to house’ (Acts 20:20). The church met in the house of Priscilla and Aquila (1 Corinthians 16:19), in Nympha’s house (Colossians 4:15), and in Philemon’s (Philemon 1-2). The early church grew and was strengthened in homes.
Four purposes of a small group
A small group has a purpose, or it gradually fades. There are four.

First, to reach people who don’t know Jesus. A group in a neighborhood is a place where a friend or neighbor can come in, sit on a chair and hear about God without being intimidated. The group should have a heart for the people around it. If it only looks inward, it will slowly shrink.
Second, to help each other grow. Everyone in the group can be taught how to live as a Christian, how to pray, how to read the Bible and how to change old habits. We’re doing exactly this right now.

Third, to build each other up. There are weeks when every one of us is weak. Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 says two are better than one, because if one falls, the other can help them up. In a group, someone notices and lifts us.

And fourth, to raise up leaders. There are many people to reach and to help, and not enough workers. A small group is the best place to learn, since each member can watch, try, and grow. If you are in a group, you may one day lead one. We’ll talk more about that in the last lesson.
What a group does
A good small meeting has four parts. We call them welcome, worship, word and work.
Welcome. This is the time to make friends, to ask how everyone is, to share what God has done this week. It’s person to person.
Worship. We sing or pray to God. It’s person to God.
Word. We open the Bible and let God speak to us. It’s God to person, and we follow a lesson so that we hear it step by step.
Work. We pray together for the people around us who don’t yet know Jesus, and we plan how to reach out to them. This is the part we skip most often, and it’s the part that keeps the group alive.
You’ll notice that our meetings have all four. We start with a welcome and a question. We pray and sing. We have a lesson. And each week, there’s something to do.
What makes a group healthy

A few things are worth guarding. Keep it small enough that everyone can speak. Keep it open, with a chair for a new person. Keep confidences, so that what is shared stays in the room. And keep it pointed toward Jesus. A group that loses its center turns into a social club or a place for gossip.

If you’ve been hurt in a group before, I’d like to say something. A healthy group is a safe place. Nobody should be pressured or shamed there, and everyone should feel free to say no. If that isn’t how a group treats you, please tell your pastor.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: How has this group helped you? Can you name three ways?
What is the difference between meeting in a big gathering and a small group?
Who around you would feel at home in a group like this? What stops you from inviting them?
Do you think you might lead a group some day? What would you need first?

b.x: Let people answer the first question one by one. Hearing how the group has helped others is often the most encouraging part of the evening.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write the name of one person you could invite to our group. Pray for them every day, and ask them this week.
Send an encouraging message to someone in this group, telling them what they mean to you.

b.x: Acts 2:46

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for this family. Help us to welcome whoever You send. Amen.
What is the church, and why do I need one?
Thinking of you. Did you ask anyone to come?

x.q: I’m shy. I don’t like groups.
x.a: That’s okay. Say that many people feel the same, and that nobody has to talk much. Ask what would make it easier, and encourage them to stay.

x.q: I’ve been hurt in a group before.
x.a: Listen first. Don’t push them to explain. Remind them that a healthy group is a safe place, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: Do I still need a group if I go to church on Sunday?
x.a: Yes, as the early believers did both. Sunday is good for worship and teaching. A small group is where people know your name.

x.q: Can I invite a friend who isn’t a Christian?
x.a: Yes, please do. That’s one of the purposes of the group. Tell them what to expect, and ask them to come as they are.

title: The church
q: What is the church, and why do I need one?
notes: The original lesson sorts churches into “true” and “false.” That kind of language can hurt people who belong to other congregations, or whose families do. This lesson teaches the same marks as signs of a healthy church, and it asks the group to look at those signs without pointing at anyone. Some people may also have been hurt in a church. Listen to them. If anyone describes pressure, control or abuse, take it seriously and bring in your pastor.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about why a small group matters.
Did you invite someone? How did it go?
Acts 2:46
Tonight’s question is: what is the church, and why do I need one?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Jesus, You love Your church and gave Yourself for her. Help us to love her too. Amen.
When you hear the word ‘church’, what’s the first thing that comes to mind?
Let people answer. Most will say a building, a Sunday service, or a certain church they know.
The Bible means something different, and bigger. Tonight we’ll look at what the church really is, how we become part of it, and what to look for in a church family.
The called-out ones
Matthew 16:18

Jesus said, ‘I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.’ The word for church in the New Testament Greek is ekklesia, which means ‘the called out ones’. We’re the church because we’ve been called out of death into life, out of darkness into light, and out of the devil’s grip into God’s family (Colossians 1:13-14; 1 Peter 2:9-10).
So the church is a people, and the building isn’t the church. When we say ‘I’m going to church’, we mean we’re going to meet with the church.
How we become part of it
Acts 2:47

‘The Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.’ Notice who adds, and notice the order. People were saved first, and then they were added. We don’t join a church to be saved. We’re saved through faith in Jesus (Acts 16:30-31), and that makes us part of His family. Jesus is the door (John 10:9). We come in through Him, and He is the head of the body (Ephesians 1:22-23).
The whole church and the local church

The word is used in two ways. It can mean everyone in the world who belongs to Jesus, in every place and every century. That’s the whole church, and Jesus is its head. And it can mean a group of believers in one place, such as a house church (Romans 16:5), a congregation in a city (Acts 8:3) or a congregation with its leaders (Acts 20:28).

The whole church can’t be seen all at once. It becomes visible in local churches. And each local church has leaders who care for the people, as Peter writes, shepherding God’s flock willingly and by example (1 Peter 5:1-4).
Five signs of a healthy church
Not every group that uses the name ‘church’ is healthy, and I’m not going to point at any in particular. Let me give you five signs to look for. You can hold them up to any church, ours included.

One. Jesus is Savior. People in the church know they’re saved by grace and not by their own effort (Ephesians 2:8-9), and they share this good news. A church where people are always trying to earn God’s love and never feel sure of it is missing something.
Two. Only Jesus is lifted up. In a healthy church the Spirit points to Jesus (1 Corinthians 12:3). No leader, no group and no tradition takes His place at the center.

Three. Jesus is alive and at work. You can see changed lives, and the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience and kindness (Galatians 5:22-23). God’s presence is real, and meetings aren’t dry rituals.
Four. The Bible is followed. A healthy church treats Scripture as the final word (2 Timothy 3:16-17; Psalm 119:105). Leaders are respected, and they, too, answer to the Bible.

And five. God is worshiped in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). Worship comes from the heart, led by the Spirit, and it agrees with the Bible. It isn’t only tradition repeated without thinking (Matthew 15:8).

Use these signs to look at a church with love and not to attack one. Many wonderful believers belong to churches that are different from ours. They’re our brothers and sisters, and we’re one body in Christ. The signs help us choose a spiritual home, and they help us see where we need to grow.
Why we need a church family

We need a church the way a child needs a home. Many believers stay weak for years because they aren’t planted anywhere, even though they want to grow. Psalm 92:13-14 says that those who are planted in the house of the Lord will flourish and will still bear fruit in old age.

A good church gives us five things. We’re established. There is peace and rest in God’s presence (Haggai 2:9). We’re cared for, because the leaders and the people really look after us. We grow and change, because there is a steady supply of teaching and fellowship. We can endure, because we aren’t alone when things get hard. And we can be used, because a church equips its people for the work God has for them.
If you aren’t yet a member of a church family, I’d urge you to find one, and I’ll help. And if you are, ask what you can give to it as well as receive from it.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What did you think the word “church” meant before tonight? What do you think now?
Why does it matter that we’re saved first and then added to the church?
Which of the five signs do you most want to see in your own church?
What does being part of a church family give you? What could you give back?

b.x: If anyone has had a bad experience in a church, thank them for saying so, and don’t defend the church too quickly.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Look at your own church family with the five signs. Write down one thing you’re thankful for, and one thing you could help with.
Thank someone in your church who has cared for you, either with a note or in person.

b.x: Matthew 16:18

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Jesus, thank You for building Your church. Help us to be good members of it, and keep us close to one another. Amen.
How does my work fit with serving God?
Thinking of you. Did you thank someone from church?

x.q: Is my church a real church?
x.a: Don’t judge any church. Go through the five signs together, and ask what they see. Suggest they talk with your pastor if they’re unsure.

x.q: Do I have to belong to a church to be saved?
x.a: No. We’re saved by faith in Jesus. But once we’re saved, we belong to His family, and we need one another (Hebrews 10:24-25).

x.q: I was hurt by a church leader.
x.a: Listen, and don’t hurry to defend anyone. Tell them that this isn’t how Jesus treats people. Pray with them, and help them speak with your pastor or another trusted leader.

x.q: Can I belong to more than one church?
x.a: Many believers are members of one congregation and visit others. Talk about commitment, and encourage them to settle in one family where they can serve and be known.

title: Work that serves
q: How does my work fit with serving God?
notes: Work and money are tender subjects. Someone in your group may be out of work, in debt, caring for a sick relative, or too ill or too old to work. Say clearly that being without a job is not a sign of weak faith, and don’t let anyone feel judged. The original lesson also linked hard work to financial blessing. This version keeps the Bible’s encouragement to work well and leaves out any promise that work will make us rich.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about the church.
Whom did you thank from your church? How did they respond?
Matthew 16:18
Tonight’s question is: how does my work fit with serving God?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You gave us hands and minds to work. Help us to work in a way that honors You. Amen.
What do you do all day? It could be a job, studies, caring for a home or something else.
Let people say a little. Respect all kinds of work, including unpaid work at home.

We usually divide life into ‘spiritual things’, like prayer and church, and ‘ordinary things’, like work. The Bible doesn’t. Tonight we’ll see that our work is one of the main places where we serve God.
Paul the tentmaker
Acts 18:1-4

When Paul came to Corinth, he stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, who were tentmakers like him, and he worked with them. On the Sabbath, he reasoned in the synagogue. Paul was one of the greatest missionaries who ever lived, and he made tents for a living so that he wouldn’t be a burden to anyone.
Why work matters
The Bible gives several reasons to work well.

Work meets our needs. Paul told Titus that believers should devote themselves to doing what is good, so that they can provide for daily needs and not live unproductive lives (Titus 3:14). Proverbs says that diligent hands lead to plenty (Proverbs 10:4; 12:11). Work is one of the ways God provides for us.

Work sets an example. Paul told the Thessalonians that he and his team worked night and day so they wouldn’t be a burden, and to give the believers a model to follow. He told them, ‘The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat’ (2 Thessalonians 3:8-10). He wasn’t talking about people who can’t work, such as the sick, the elderly or those who can’t find a job. He meant people who could work and wouldn’t.

Work helps us serve God. Work isn’t a hindrance to serving Him. For Paul, it was what made his ministry possible. Our work can be a bridge to the people God has put around us. We get to meet them, show them respect, and share our faith through how we live.

Work lets us help people in need. God commands us to care for the poor (James 1:27; Matthew 25:35-40), and when we earn something, we can share it. Paul tells us to work with our hands so that we’ll have something to share with those in need (Ephesians 4:28). Good giving is wise. Sometimes we hand over a fish, and sometimes we teach someone to fish. We ask the Holy Spirit to guide us, because we can’t meet every need in the world.

And work lets us support God’s work. Our offerings help the local church and those who are sent out. The Philippians supported Paul when he needed it (Philippians 4:14-18). We said in Lesson 17 that we give out of love and not out of pressure.
Finding the right work
How do we find the right job? There are four steps.

Put our relationship with God right first (Romans 12:1-2). Notice what we enjoy doing, because God puts desires in us (Psalm 37:4). See what we have in our hands, such as our skills and abilities (Deuteronomy 8:18). And pray and watch for the doors God opens (Proverbs 3:5-6; Revelation 3:7-8).

Whether we’re employees or run our own business, the aim is the same. Colossians 3:23 says, ‘Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters.’ Our boss is a person, and our real Lord is Jesus.

And if you can’t find work right now, that’s a hard place to be, and it doesn’t say anything about your faith. Keep seeking, keep asking for help from your church family, and remember that God sees you. Many in the Bible waited a long time.
Warnings
Three warnings.
Watch out for the love of money, which Paul says is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10). Money is a good servant and a poor master.

Watch out that our work doesn’t push God out. Jesus said we can’t serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). If our job keeps us from God completely, we may need to find a way to change it, or to change how we manage our time. God doesn’t give us a job that is meant to separate us from Him.

And keep the order right. God comes first, then our family, then our work, and our service finds room around all of these. A person can lose their family or their health to their job, and a person can neglect their job in the name of ministry. We want a balanced life and we ask the Holy Spirit to help us.

A last picture. A church has people in four situations. Some have a job and no time for ministry. Some have a ministry and no job to support it. Some have neither. And some have both. The best place is to have both, to work well and to serve, and we help each other get there.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What stood out to you in tonight’s lesson? Why?
How can your work, or your studies, or your home, be a place where you serve God?
Is there a way your work currently gets in the way of God, your family or your health?
Which of the four situations, job without ministry, ministry without a job, neither or both, is closest to yours? What’s the next step?

b.x: If someone is out of work, treat the third and fourth questions gently. Offer to pray with them, and see if the church can help.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Pray over your work, or your studies, at the start of each day, and offer it to the Lord.
Look for one person at work, at school or at home you can serve this week, and do something kind for them.

b.x: Colossians 3:23

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for the work You’ve given us. Help us to do it well, and to do it for You. Amen.
What does it mean to serve God?
Thinking of you. How did the day’s work go?

x.q: I’m out of work. Does God not care about me?
x.a: He does. Listen, and don’t offer quick answers. Pray with them, and tell your pastor so that the church can help look for work and meet needs.

x.q: Isn’t ministry more important than a job?
x.a: Both matter. Paul worked and served at the same time. Work often supports the ministry, so we don’t put it down.

x.q: My job requires me to do something I think is wrong.
x.a: Take it seriously. Ask what’s being required, read Acts 5:29 together, and encourage them to talk with your pastor and pray about whether to stay.

x.q: What if I can’t work because of illness or age?
x.a: Tell them that their worth doesn’t come from work. They can serve God by praying, encouraging others and being part of the family.

title: Servants and soldiers
q: What does it mean to serve God?
notes: This lesson talks about commitment to service and about why people leave. Someone in your group may have walked away from a ministry because they were hurt, overworked or treated unfairly. Listen to them before you teach. God does not ask anyone to stay in a place where they are being manipulated or harmed, and serving Him never means serving a person’s ego.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about how our work fits with serving God.
Did you pray over your work this week? Did anything change?
Colossians 3:23
Tonight’s question is: what does it mean to serve God?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Lord Jesus, You came to serve. Give us Your heart, and show us where we can serve. Amen.
Who is the best servant you’ve ever known? What made them different?
Let people tell stories. It’s often a person who serves quietly and doesn’t want attention.
Tonight we’ll look at two pictures of the Christian life, the servant and the soldier. Both are about the same thing. They show what it looks like when someone has stopped living for themselves.
The mind of Christ
Philippians 2:5-8

Paul says, ‘Your attitude should be the same as that of Christ Jesus.’ Jesus was God, and He didn’t hold on to that. He made Himself nothing and took the form of a servant. He humbled Himself, and obeyed all the way to a cross.

He told His friends that He didn’t come to be served but to serve and to give His life for many (Matthew 20:28). He washed their feet (John 13:12-17). Everything He did was for the Father’s will, and that will was to save the world (John 3:16; Luke 19:10).

Our minds are filled with other ideas all the time, from the media, from friends, even from some of what we were taught as children. Paul says to be transformed by renewing our minds (Romans 12:2). We start by choosing to think as Jesus thinks.
A child who serves

We don’t serve to become God’s children. We serve because we are His children. Salvation is a gift, and service is the response. Jesus said that anyone who follows Him must deny themselves and take up their cross each day (Luke 9:23). Our cross is the part of His work He has given us to carry.
A mature believer shows it in a readiness to serve, more than in how long they’ve been a Christian or how much of the Bible they know.

Most of us start serving on our own terms. We serve when it suits us, in the way we like, and we hope someone notices. That’s a normal place to begin, and God uses it. As we grow, something changes. We begin to serve because we love Him, whether or not anyone sees.
The servant who chooses to stay
Exodus 21:2-6

In Israel, a servant went free after six years. But if the servant said, ‘I love my master and I don’t want to go free,’ his master pierced his ear at the door, and the man served him for life. It was a way of saying, ‘I’m staying because I love him.’
That’s the picture of a servant of God. Four things stand out.
Service comes from love. We aren’t forced. We serve because we know how much He loves us (1 John 4:19; Galatians 2:20).

A servant serves in the Master’s household. For us, that’s God’s family, the church. We give ourselves to the people He loves. This never means neglecting our own families. Caring for them is part of God’s family too (1 Timothy 5:8).
A servant listens for the Master’s voice. We try to hear God before we hear our own wishes, the crowd or the circumstances (Ephesians 5:15-17). Our aim is to obey Him in everything.
And a servant serves for life. There’s no retirement from loving God. As we get older, how we serve may change, from running things to praying and encouraging, but we never stop.
God’s soldiers
1 Samuel 22:1-2

When David was hiding in a cave, people came to him. They were in distress or in debt or discontented, about four hundred of them. These were the people who became his mighty men. God doesn’t look for people who’ve got everything together. He takes people in trouble and makes them strong. Don’t focus on who you are today. Think of what God can make of you.
Look at the three mightiest of David’s men (2 Samuel 23:8-12), and what each can teach us.

Josheb-Basshebeth used what he had. He fought eight hundred men with one spear. Many of us feel we have too little to give, such as little time, little money or little talent. God can use whatever we have, if we give it to Him. The enemy loves to make us think about what’s missing. Ephesians 1:3 says that we’ve been blessed with every spiritual blessing in Christ.

Eleazar stood his ground. The rest of the army retreated, and he fought until his hand was stuck to his sword, and the Lord brought a great victory. Pressure and problems come. We keep going, with the Lord’s help.

Why do people leave their place of service? Fear, whether of failing, of people or of more responsibility. Conflict with others. Disappointment with the church. Discouragement and drifting. A loss of trust in a leader. If any of these is true of you, please talk to someone before you walk away. Some of these hurts are real, and they can be healed, and some situations need a wise person to step in.

Shammah took ownership. When the rest of the army ran from a field of lentils, he stayed and defended it. It was his field. God has given each of us something to look after, and we answer for it. Jesus told a story about three servants who were given money (Matthew 25:14-30). Two used what they were given and heard, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant.’ One hid his and was afraid. Let’s not bury what God has given us.
And you may ask, what am I called to do? Start with what is near. Welcome a newcomer. Help set up. Pray for someone. Visit a sick person. The big callings often grow out of the small ones.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What does it mean to you that Jesus, who is God, chose to be a servant?
When you serve, are you looking for thanks or for His smile? Be honest.
Which of David’s three men do you relate to most: the one who used what he had, the one who stood firm, or the one who took ownership?
Is there something God has put in your hands that you haven’t used? What’s holding you back?

b.x: The second question is an honest look at motives. Say that every servant starts there, and that it’s fine to be somewhere in the middle.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one small way to serve in your church or group this month. Tell your leader or mentor, and begin.
Do one act of service this week that nobody will see.

b.x: Philippians 2:5

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Lord Jesus, give us Your mind and Your heart. Make us faithful servants and strong soldiers. Amen.
How can I be a blessing to people who don’t know Jesus?
Thinking of you. How did you serve this week?

x.q: I’m too young in the faith to serve.
x.a: Not at all. Everyone starts somewhere. Small tasks like welcoming, setting up chairs or praying for someone count, and they help us grow.

x.q: I served and burned out.
x.a: Listen. Tell them that Jesus invites the weary to rest (Matthew 11:28), and that serving doesn’t mean having no limits. Encourage them to take a rest and talk with your pastor.

x.q: I left a ministry because I was hurt.
x.a: Don’t push them to return. Listen, and pray for healing. Help them talk with a trusted leader, and if there was abuse or manipulation, help them reach your pastor or someone outside the situation.

x.q: I don’t think I’m good at anything.
x.a: Remind them of Josheb-Basshebeth, who used one spear. Ask the group what they see in that person, and encourage them to try something small.

title: Blessing others
q: How can I be a blessing to people who don’t know Jesus?
notes: This lesson is about telling others about Jesus. Some people in your group will be afraid of it, and some live where talking about faith can cause trouble with family or neighbors. Make clear that nobody is being pushed to argue or preach. Relationships and kindness come first, and wisdom matters (Matthew 10:16). Be ready to practice the short testimony in Part 4 together.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about serving God like servants and soldiers.
What small way of serving did you choose? How did it go?
Philippians 2:5
Tonight’s question is: how can I be a blessing to people who don’t know Jesus?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You’ve blessed us so that we can bless others. Give us love for the people around us. Amen.
Who first told you about Jesus, or showed you what He was like? What did they do?
Let people share. It’s usually a person who was kind to them, and often didn’t give a speech.

None of us found Jesus alone. Someone cared enough to share Him with us. Tonight we’ll look at five ways that we can do the same. God has blessed us so that we can be a blessing to others, and so that people who are still far from Him can come close.
Holiness
1 Peter 2:12

Peter says, ‘Live such good lives among those who don’t know God that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God.’ The first way to bless people is to live well. We’re joined to Jesus, the vine, and we bear the fruit of the Spirit (John 15:5; Galatians 5:22-23). Before people hear our words, they see our lives.
This doesn’t mean being perfect. It means being honest, kind, reliable and gentle at home and at work, and quick to say sorry when we get it wrong.
Friendship
1 Corinthians 9:19-22

Paul says he became ‘all things to all people’ to win some. He listened to people and met them where they were. This doesn’t mean he joined in their sin. He lived victoriously over it (1 Thessalonians 2:10). It means he was a friend.

Jesus did the same. The religious leaders called Him a friend of sinners (Luke 7:34), and He ate with them (Matthew 9:10-12). He was holy, and He wasn’t afraid of people. Light doesn’t run from the dark. It goes where it’s needed. Paul’s warning about being ‘yoked with unbelievers’ (2 Corinthians 6:14) is about joining in their ways, and partnerships where our faith would be compromised. It’s no command to avoid people.
Think of one person near you who doesn’t know Jesus. Could you be their friend, with no agenda?
Service
Matthew 5:16

‘Let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.’ Serving people opens doors. When we care for someone’s needs, whether physical, practical, emotional or spiritual, we touch their heart, and they become more open to hear about Jesus. Jesus washed feet, and He asks us to follow His example (John 13:14-15; James 1:27).
A meal for a neighbor, a lift to the clinic, help with a child’s school fees or a few hours of listening can say more than a sermon.
Testimony
1 Peter 2:9

You are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, so that you may declare the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His wonderful light. Everyone who belongs to Jesus has a story. Nobody can argue with your story.

Paul told his story several times, in Acts 22 and Acts 26. It has three parts. What my life was like before. How I met Jesus. And what my life is like now. That’s all it needs, and you can say it in two minutes.
Let’s try it. Turn to the person beside you, and take one minute each. Tell them what your life was like before you knew Jesus, how you met Him, and what is different now.
Give them a few minutes, then ask if anyone would like to share what they heard.
Notice how natural it feels. Peter and John said, ‘We cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard’ (Acts 4:20). When Jesus has really done something in us, we want to talk about Him.
Evangelism
Mark 16:15

Jesus said, ‘Go into all the world and preach the good news to all creation.’ Evangelism is bringing the free gift of salvation in Jesus to people who haven’t received it. The early church did it everywhere they went (Acts 5:42). It’s not only for pastors and missionaries. Everyone who follows Jesus is invited to join in.

How? Pray for your friend by name. Be a friend. Share your story when there’s a chance. Invite them to a meal, to our group or to a service. And when they ask a question, give a gentle, respectful answer (1 Peter 3:15). We don’t have to persuade anyone. We tell them about Jesus, and the Holy Spirit does the work in their hearts. Be wise about where and when you speak, especially around family, and ask the Spirit for the right moment.
A true disciple has two commitments. We stay close to God, and we help others come close to Him too. The two go together.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Who has been a blessing to you? What did they do?
Of the five ways, holiness, friendship, service, testimony and evangelism, which would you like to begin with?
What makes it hard to talk about Jesus with people you know? What helps?
Whom has God put on your heart? What’s one thing you could do for them this week?

b.x: Pray for the people whose names are mentioned. If someone is afraid, remind the group that they’re not alone, and that nobody has to do this in one big leap.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write your three-part story: before, how I met Jesus, and now. Practice it once out loud.
Pray for one person by name every day, and do one kind thing for them.

b.x: Matthew 5:16

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, make us a blessing. Give us love for the people we meet, and open a door for us to speak about Jesus. Amen.
How do I help others follow Jesus?
Thinking of you. How is it going with the person you’re praying for?

x.q: I don’t know enough about the Bible to share my faith.
x.a: You don’t have to. Tell them your own story, and say that you’ll find out the answer if you don’t know it. Read Acts 4:20 together.

x.q: My family would be angry if I talked about Jesus.
x.a: Listen. Remind them that living well and serving can speak even when words are risky, and suggest they ask your pastor for guidance. Their safety matters.

x.q: Shouldn’t I avoid people who aren’t believers?
x.a: No. Jesus spent time with them. The warning in 2 Corinthians 6:14 is about close partnerships that pull us from God. We love and befriend people, and we choose carefully who has the most influence over us.

x.q: What if they say no?
x.a: Keep being a friend. We’re responsible for loving and telling, and God works in their heart in His time.

title: Making disciples
q: How do I help others follow Jesus?
notes: Leave a little extra time for the celebration in the wrap-up. The original lesson says that every disciple must submit to a “spiritual father.” This version teaches the healthy form of that idea, a trusted, older believer who walks beside us. Nobody should be pressured to obey a person, and anyone who feels controlled by a mentor should be heard and helped by your pastor.

b.x: Welcome back. This is our last lesson in this fourth stretch, and I want to say how glad I am that you’ve come this far.
Whom did you pray for, and what did you do for them? How did it go?
Matthew 5:16
Tonight’s question is: how do I help others follow Jesus?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for these thirty-six weeks. Show us how to pass on what we’ve received. Amen.
If you could pass on one thing you’ve learned in these months to a friend, what would it be?
Let people answer. Say that the answers show what has taken root.
Tonight I want to go back to the beginning of the Bible, and see how God’s plan has always been to grow a family, and how He invites us to help.
God’s plan for a family
Genesis 1:27-28

God made people in His own image so that He could know us, and so that we could know Him. He told Adam and Eve to be fruitful and to fill the earth. God wanted a big family who would know Him and walk with Him.

Sin broke that. Adam and Eve listened to the wrong voice (Genesis 3:1-7), and the relationship with God was damaged. The image of God in people was marred, and people moved away from Him. Sin has touched every one of us (Romans 5:12).
Jesus comes to restore
1 John 3:8

‘The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the devil’s work.’ Jesus announced that the kingdom of heaven had come near (Matthew 4:17). He healed and forgave, and on the cross He took the punishment for our sins and defeated the powers of darkness (Colossians 2:15). The way back to the Father was opened.
How Jesus multiplied

Here is something striking. Jesus came to save the whole world, and He gave much of His time to twelve people. He appointed them ‘that they might be with Him’ and that He might send them out. He ate with them, taught them, corrected them and prayed for them. And then He gave them a commission.
Matthew 28:19-20

‘Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always.’ A disciple is a learner who follows Jesus and becomes more like Him (John 8:31; Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18).
Think about these months. We’ve learned about salvation, prayer, the Bible, the Holy Spirit and Jesus’ lordship. You’ve been a disciple. Now Jesus asks you to help someone else become one.
We need someone ahead of us

Nobody becomes a disciple alone. Joshua had Moses. Elisha had Elijah. Timothy had Paul, and Mark had Peter. We need people a little further down the road to walk beside us, to tell us the truth in love, and to pray for us.

A good mentor points us to Jesus, and doesn’t ask us to follow them. They listen, they encourage, and they care for us the way a good parent does. Paul said, ‘Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 11:1). That’s the pattern. If anyone ever pressures you to obey them instead of Christ, or makes you afraid to ask questions, tell your pastor.
If you don’t have a mentor yet, ask for one. And if you do, thank them.
Passing it on
2 Timothy 2:2

‘The things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others.’ Count the generations. Paul teaches Timothy, Timothy teaches reliable people, and they teach others. That’s four generations in one verse. This is how the gospel reached us, and how it will reach the next person.

What does it take? The Holy Spirit in us, and time. Discipling someone is mostly sharing life. We pray with them, answer their questions, show them how we read the Bible, and let them see how we handle hard days. We can only take people as far as we’ve gone ourselves, so we keep growing and stay honest about our failures.
You may be thinking, I’m not ready. Remember that the twelve weren’t ready either. You don’t have to be finished to help someone who is a step or two behind you.

Here’s a simple way to start. Find one person who’s newer in the faith. Meet them regularly, even once a week. Pray for them, and walk them through what we’ve learned, using these lessons as a guide. Invite them to your group, and in time to help others. That’s how a small group becomes two.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Who has helped you most in following Jesus? What did they do?
Looking back over the thirty-six weeks, what has changed in you? What’s one thing you want to hold on to?
Who could you help follow Jesus? What would be the first step?
What makes you hesitate, and what might help?

b.x: Spend time on the second question. It’s the heart of the evening. Let each person say what has changed, even if it’s small.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one person to walk with, someone who is newer in the faith. Pray for them by name, and invite them to meet with you.
Thank the person who has helped you most, and ask them to keep praying for you.

b.x: 2 Timothy 2:2

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for each person here. Send us out to make disciples, and keep us close to You and to each other. Amen.

This is the end of the fourth phase, and it deserves a real celebration. Plan a meal together, ideally with your pastor or church leaders there. Let each person say one thing they’re thankful for, pray over each person by name, and tell them what’s next in your church, such as a baptism, a membership class or a serving team. If you can, start a new group. The next phase is about knowing the Bible well, and it starts the following week.
Thinking of you. Who are you walking with?

x.q: I’m not mature enough to disciple anyone.
x.a: You don’t need to be finished. If you’re a step ahead of someone, you can help them. Encourage them to start small.

x.q: What if the person I help leaves?
x.a: That happens. Keep praying. Jesus lost followers too (John 6:66).

x.q: Do I have to obey my mentor?
x.a: You listen to them, and weigh their advice with the Bible and prayer. Your obedience belongs to Jesus. If a mentor pressures or controls you, speak to your pastor.

x.q: What do I do next?
x.a: Keep your rhythm of prayer, the Bible, church and service. Walk with one person. Join a serving team. Ask your pastor how you can keep growing.

title: Why we can trust the Bible
q: Can I trust the Bible?
notes: Some people in your group may have been told the Bible is full of mistakes, or may have doubts they are afraid to say aloud. Welcome those doubts. Jesus never turned away an honest question, and a faith that has been questioned usually stands firmer. You do not need to answer everything tonight. It is fine to say, “I don’t know yet. Let’s find out together.”

b.x: Welcome back. Tonight we begin a new stretch, and I’m glad you’re here.
Last week I asked you to choose one person to walk with and to thank the one who helped you most. How did that go?
2 Timothy 2:2
Tonight’s question is: can I trust the Bible?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for speaking to us. Open our eyes as we look at Your word. Amen.
Whose advice do you trust the most? Why do you trust that person?
Let people answer. Usually it’s someone who has been honest with them over a long time.

We trust a person when they’ve shown they’re truthful and that they know what they’re talking about. The Bible asks for that kind of trust. Tonight we won’t ask you to trust it blindly. We’ll look at why so many people through the centuries have found it worth trusting.
What the Bible says about itself
2 Timothy 3:16-17

Paul says that all Scripture is breathed out by God, and that it’s useful for teaching, for correcting, for setting us right and for training us in how to live, so that God’s people are fully equipped for every good work. In other words, the Bible isn’t a book of ideas about God that people came up with. It comes from God.

Peter adds that no prophecy came from someone’s own idea. People spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. God used real people, with their own voices and backgrounds, and He guided what they wrote. A shepherd like David wrote differently from a doctor like Luke, and a fisherman like Peter wrote differently from a scholar like Paul. God worked through all of them.
One story from many writers

The Bible is a library of sixty-six books, written by about forty authors over around fifteen hundred years. They were kings, shepherds, fishermen, a tax collector, a doctor and a tentmaker. They wrote in three languages, Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, in many places, from deserts to prisons to palaces.

And yet it tells one story, which is the story of how God made people, how they walked away, and how He went to rescue them through Jesus. Many of these writers never met each other. We’ll trace that story in Lesson 39. For now, notice how unusual it is for a collection like this to hang together.
How it came to us
People often ask, ‘Hasn’t it been changed over the years? Haven’t the copies gotten garbled?’ This is a fair question.

The New Testament was written in the first century, and we have thousands of ancient handwritten copies and fragments of it, many from within a few hundred years of the original writing. That’s far more than for almost any other writing from the ancient world. The copies do differ in small details, such as spelling or word order, and scholars compare them carefully. The differences don’t change any of the main teaching of the Christian faith.

For the Old Testament, there was a famous discovery in 1947. A shepherd boy found ancient scrolls in caves near the Dead Sea, including a whole scroll of Isaiah that is about a thousand years older than the copies we had before. When scholars compared it, the text was remarkably close to the one we already knew. Jewish scribes had copied it with great care.

That doesn’t mean there are no hard questions. There are passages that are difficult to understand, and different translations word things differently. But we have good reason to believe that what we read today is what the writers wrote.
Jesus trusted the Scriptures
Luke 24:44

For a follower of Jesus, this may be the strongest reason. Jesus trusted the Old Testament. He quoted it when He was tempted (Matthew 4:4). He said that Scripture can’t be set aside (John 10:35). After He rose from the dead, He told His friends that everything written about Him in the law of Moses, the prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled.

Hundreds of years before He was born, Micah said the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Isaiah described a servant who would be pierced for our wrongs and would carry our sins (Isaiah 53:4-6). Jesus’ life lined up with these words. And He promised that His own words would never pass away (Matthew 24:35). If we trust Jesus, we trust what He trusted.
It changes lives
Hebrews 4:12

The writer says that God’s word is alive and active. Many of us can say that it has been alive in our own lives. Look at what has happened in this group. People have been forgiven, freed from habits, comforted when they were grieving, and guided when they didn’t know what to do. A book that merely recorded old stories wouldn’t do this.

Finally, a word about doubt. A man once said to Jesus, ‘I believe. Help my unbelief’ (Mark 9:24), and Jesus helped him. You don’t have to have every answer to keep following Him. Bring your questions to God, to the Bible and to people you trust, and keep reading.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What have you heard about the Bible, good or bad, before you started following Jesus?
Which of tonight’s reasons makes the most sense to you? Which feels weakest?
Has the Bible ever spoken to you in a moment when you needed it? What happened?
What question or doubt about the Bible would you like to explore in the coming weeks?

b.x: Write down any question that comes up, and promise to return to it. If someone asks something you can’t answer, thank them and say you’ll look into it with your pastor.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write down one question or doubt you have about the Bible. Bring it to your pastor or to a mature believer, and listen to the answer.
Each day, read a few verses and ask one thing: “What does this tell me about God?”

b.x: 2 Timothy 3:16

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for the Bible. Give us honest hearts, and help us trust what You’ve said. Amen.
How do I study a passage on my own?
Thinking of you. What did the Bible tell you about God today?

x.q: Doesn’t the Bible contradict itself?
x.a: Some passages seem to, and many have well-known explanations, such as different writers describing the same event from their own angle. Look at one together, and bring your pastor in for the harder ones.

x.q: Which translation should I use?
x.a: Choose one that you understand. A plain, modern translation is good for reading, and it helps to compare it with a second one. Your pastor can recommend one.

x.q: Does the Bible disagree with science?
x.a: Many Christians see no conflict, and they read the early chapters of Genesis in different ways. Suggest they talk with your pastor, and don’t make it a test of faith.

x.q: I’m struggling to believe.
x.a: Thank them for being honest. Remind them of Mark 9:24, and pray with them. Suggest they keep reading the Gospels and talk with your pastor.

title: Reading for yourself
q: How do I study a passage on my own?
notes: This lesson is hands-on. Plan to read a short passage together in Part 3 and let the group do the work, with you only asking questions. Some people may not read easily or may not have a Bible they can follow. Offer to read aloud, share a phone app or lend a printed copy, and never make anyone read in front of others.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we looked at why we can trust the Bible.
Did anyone bring a question about the Bible to someone this week? What did you learn?
2 Timothy 3:16
Tonight’s question is: how do I study a passage on my own?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, open our eyes to see what is in Your word. Teach us to read it well. Amen.
Have you ever read a verse and thought, ‘I don’t know what that means’? What did you do?
Let people share. Many will say they skipped it or felt embarrassed.

That’s normal, and the Bible was written for ordinary people. In Lesson 13 we said to read it daily. Tonight we’ll learn a simple way to understand what we read. It has three steps, and you can use it for any passage.
Start with prayer and humility
Psalm 119:18

The psalmist prays, ‘Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in Your law.’ Before we read, we ask the Holy Spirit to help us. He’s the One who inspired the words, and He helps us understand them (John 16:13).
We also come ready to be changed. We don’t open the Bible to prove a point. We open it to hear from God.
The Bereans
Acts 17:11

The people in Berea were praised because they received Paul’s message eagerly and then examined the Scriptures every day to see if what he said was true. They were eager and careful at the same time. That’s how we want to read, with an open heart and a thinking mind.
Three steps
Here are the three steps. First, observe. Second, understand. Third, apply.

Step one is to observe. What does the passage actually say? Read it slowly, and read it more than once. Ask who is speaking, who they’re speaking to, what is happening, where and when. Notice repeated words and anything that surprises you. Write down what you see. At this stage, you aren’t deciding what it means. You’re just looking carefully.

Step two is to understand. What did this mean to the people who first heard it? Every passage has a setting. Read the verses before and after it. Ask what kind of writing it is, whether a story, a poem, a letter or a command. And ask how it fits with the rest of the Bible, because Scripture explains Scripture. If you have a study Bible, the notes can help.

Step three is to apply. What is God asking me to believe or do? Be specific. ‘Be a better person’ is too vague. ‘Call my brother and apologize this week’ is something you can do. James says we’re to do what the word says, not merely listen (James 1:22-25).
Let’s try it together.
Philippians 4:6-7
I’ll ask the questions, and you tell me what you see.
Take a few minutes for each step.
Observe. What does Paul say we should do, and what does he say will happen? What words stand out?
Let people answer. They’ll notice ‘do not be anxious’, ‘prayer’, ‘thanksgiving’ and ‘peace’.
Understand. Paul wrote this from prison, to a church he loved. How might that change how we hear it? What does it say about God?
Let people answer.
Apply. What is something you’re anxious about this week? What would it look like to give it to God with thanks?
Let people answer, or think quietly.
That took ten minutes. You can do the same on your own with any passage.
Common mistakes
Three things to watch out for.

Taking a verse out of its setting. Jeremiah 29:11 says God has plans for His people, plans for good. Many of us have it on posters. It was written to people living in exile, who were told to settle down and wait seventy years. It still shows God’s heart, and it’s good to know what it first meant. Philippians 4:13 says that I can do all things through Christ. Paul was writing about being content in hunger and in plenty, and it isn’t a promise that we can accomplish anything we want.

Twisting a verse to say what we want. Peter warns that some people twist Paul’s letters, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own harm (2 Peter 3:16). If an idea needs only one verse and ignores the rest of the Bible, be careful.

Reading alone and never checking. Paul writes that the church is a body, and we need one another (1 Corinthians 12:21). Bring what you read to the group or to a mature believer. If your understanding is very different from what believers have held for centuries, slow down and ask.
Simple tools

A few helpful tools. A Bible in a translation you understand. A notebook and a pen. A study Bible or a good commentary, which your pastor can recommend. And a reading plan, so you aren’t wondering where to begin. A good place to start is the Gospel of Mark, then Acts, then Philippians.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What makes it hard for you to understand the Bible? What have you tried?
Which of the three steps do you tend to skip: observe, understand or apply?
Can you think of a verse that people often use in a way that its setting doesn’t support?
What is one habit that would help you read the Bible more carefully?

b.x: If someone struggles to read, say that listening to an audio Bible is a good way to read too.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Choose one short passage, perhaps John 15:1-11. Use the three steps on it for five days, and write your answers in a notebook.
Bring one thing you noticed, or one question, to share next week.

b.x: Acts 17:11

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for giving us Your word. Help us to read it with care and to do what it says. Amen.
What is the Bible’s story from start to finish?
Thinking of you. What did you notice in your passage today?

x.q: I don’t understand what I read.
x.a: That’s common. Slow down, read the verses around it, and ask someone. Not understanding every passage doesn’t mean you’re doing it wrong.

x.q: I don’t have time to study.
x.a: Start with ten minutes and one short passage. A little each day adds up more than a long session once a month.

x.q: I can’t read well.
x.a: Offer an audio Bible, or a reading partner in the group. Many people learn by listening.

x.q: Two Christians read the same verse and disagree.
x.a: That happens. Look at the setting and the rest of the Bible together, stay kind, and ask your pastor about the harder cases.

title: The big story
q: What is the Bible’s story from start to finish?
notes: This lesson sweeps through the whole Bible in about twenty-five minutes, so it will feel fast. Don’t try to teach every detail. The goal is for people to see the shape of the story, so that every later passage has a place to land. A set of eight index cards, one for each scene, helps if you can prepare them.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we learned a simple way to study a passage.
What did you notice in your passage this week? Did anything surprise you?
Acts 17:11
Tonight’s question is: what is the Bible’s story from start to finish?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You that Your story includes us. Help us to see the whole of it. Amen.
If you were telling a friend what the Bible is about, in one minute, what would you say?
Let a few people try. It’s usually harder than it sounds.
People often read the Bible as a pile of separate stories and rules. It’s one story with one hero. Tonight we’ll walk through it in eight scenes, and you’ll see how Jesus stands at the center.
Creation
Genesis 1:26-27

God made everything, and it was good. He made people in His own image, to know Him, to care for the earth and to live with Him. Adam and Eve walked with God in the garden (Genesis 3:8). Everything was in its right place.
The fall
Genesis 3:1-7

A voice questioned what God had said, and Adam and Eve chose their own way. The result was shame, hiding and being sent from the garden. Sin entered the world, and death and pain came with it (Romans 5:12). Everything after this is God’s response to that break.
The promise
Genesis 12:1-3

God didn’t give up on the world. He called one man, Abraham, and promised to make him into a great nation, so that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. From Abraham came Isaac, Jacob and the people of Israel. This promise runs through the rest of the Bible.
Rescue and the law
Exodus 19:4-6

When Abraham’s descendants were slaves in Egypt, God rescued them with great power. He led them through the sea and brought them to Mount Sinai. There He gave them the law and said they would be His treasured people and a kingdom of priests. The law showed them how to live with God and with one another. It also showed that they couldn’t keep it perfectly.
Kings and prophets
2 Samuel 7:12-13

Israel got kings. David was the greatest, and God promised him that one of his descendants would rule forever. But most kings, and most of the people, drifted away from God. Prophets like Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel warned them to turn back. In the end, Israel and Judah were taken into exile.
Jeremiah 31:31-34

Yet even in exile, God made a promise. He would make a new covenant, one in which He would write His law on people’s hearts and forgive their sins. The prophets looked ahead to a king who would come and put everything right.
Jesus

After His resurrection, Jesus walked with two disciples and explained everything in the Scriptures about Himself, beginning with Moses and all the prophets. All of the story was pointing to Him. He is the descendant of Abraham through whom all nations are blessed. He’s the son of David who rules forever. On the cross, He paid for sin and began the new covenant (Luke 22:20). When He rose, He defeated death.
The church
Acts 1:8

Before Jesus went back to heaven, He promised that the Holy Spirit would come, and that His followers would be His witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria and to the ends of the earth. That’s what Acts describes. The good news spread from a small group of Jewish believers to people of every nation. We’re part of this scene. We live in the time between Jesus’ first coming and His return.
New creation
Revelation 21:1-5

The story ends where it began, with God living among His people. John sees a new heaven and a new earth. God wipes every tear from our eyes. There is no more death, mourning, crying or pain. The break that began in Genesis 3 is fully healed.
Putting it together

Let’s put the eight scenes in a line. Creation, fall, promise, rescue, kings and prophets, Jesus, the church, and new creation. If you like, you can remember it as God makes, we break, God promises, God rescues, God sends His Son, God sends His people, and God makes all things new.

When you read any passage, ask where it fits. A psalm of David belongs to scene five. A story about Jesus healing someone is scene six. A letter to a church is scene seven. Knowing where you are in the story makes the passage clearer.

And notice where you are. You aren’t an observer. The story invites you in. You were made by God, you’ve felt the break, you’ve been rescued by Jesus, and now you’re sent with the Spirit’s help until all things are made new.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Which of the eight scenes did you already know well, and which was new to you?
How does seeing the whole story change how you read a single passage?
Where do you see yourself in the story?
Which scene gives you the most hope right now?

b.x: If you have the index cards, hand them out in a mixed-up order. Ask the group to put them in sequence and say what happens in each one.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write the eight scenes on a card in your own words, and carry it in your Bible.
Tell the story to one person in a couple of minutes, and ask them what they think.

b.x: Luke 24:27

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for the story You’ve written, and for giving us a place in it. Help us to see Jesus on every page. Amen.
Why does the Old Testament matter?
Thinking of you. Did you tell the story to anyone?

x.q: Why is there so much suffering if God made everything good?
x.a: Point to scene two, and to the promise that it ends in scene eight. The Bible doesn’t say it’s easy. It says God has entered our suffering in Jesus, and He’ll end it.

x.q: Why did God choose one nation?
x.a: Not to leave others out. God called Abraham so that all families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).

x.q: Where do the dinosaurs or the age of the earth fit?
x.a: Christians understand these questions in different ways. Suggest they talk with your pastor, and keep the main story in view.

x.q: Is the Old Testament still for us?
x.a: Yes. We’ll look at that next week. It shows us who God is and prepares us for Jesus.

title: The law and the promise
q: Why does the Old Testament matter?
notes: Churches teach slightly different things about how the Old Testament law applies to Christians today. Teach what your church teaches, and use this lesson as a guide for the main shape. Part 4 also deals honestly with some hard passages in the Old Testament. You do not have to explain every one. It is better to say “that one is hard for me too” than to give an answer you are unsure of.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we walked through the whole Bible in eight scenes.
Did you tell the story to anyone? What did they say?
Luke 24:27
Tonight’s question is: why does the Old Testament matter?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for the whole of Your word. Show us Jesus in the Old Testament. Amen.
Be honest. When you open your Bible, which part do you tend to skip? Why?
Let people laugh. Many will say Leviticus, or the Old Testament in general.
The Old Testament is about three quarters of the Bible. If we skip it, we miss much of the story. Tonight we’ll see why it matters, how Jesus fits into it, and how to read it well.
It shows us who God is
Exodus 34:6-7

God passes in front of Moses and says who He is. He is compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and full of faithful love. And He doesn’t ignore sin. The God of the Old Testament is the same God we meet in Jesus (Hebrews 13:8). Some people think of the Old Testament God as angry and the New Testament God as kind. If you read both closely, you’ll see love and justice together in each.

The Old Testament also gives us the words that Jesus and the apostles used. Words like sacrifice, covenant, redemption, holy and Messiah come from it. Without it, much of the New Testament wouldn’t make sense.
What the law was for
Exodus 20:1-3

God gave Israel the law after He rescued them from slavery. Notice the order. He saved them first, and then He gave them the law. It wasn’t a ladder to climb to earn His love. It was a way to live as people who already belonged to Him.

Paul explains four purposes. It shows what a holy God is like. It shows us that we can’t keep it perfectly, and so we need a Savior (Romans 3:20). It protected and shaped the community of Israel. And it pointed to Christ. Paul says the law was our guardian until Christ came, so that we might be made right with God by faith (Galatians 3:24).

People often sort the law into three kinds. Some laws were moral, such as the Ten Commandments and the call to love God and our neighbor (Matthew 22:37-40). Some were civil, which governed the nation of Israel. And some were ceremonial, about sacrifices and the temple. Christians generally teach that the moral teaching continues, because it reflects God’s character. The civil laws were for Israel as a nation. The ceremonial laws pointed to Jesus and were fulfilled in Him. Your church may describe this a little differently.
Jesus fulfills it
Matthew 5:17

Jesus said, ‘Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.’ He lived the law perfectly, which none of us could. He was the sacrifice the law kept pointing to.

When John the Baptist saw Jesus, he said, ‘Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world’ (John 1:29). The writer of Hebrews explains that the old sacrifices were a shadow of the good things to come, and that they could never take away sin. Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (Hebrews 10:1-14). So we don’t offer animals any more. We trust in His sacrifice.

This also means that we aren’t saved by keeping the law. We’re saved by grace through faith in Jesus, as we saw in Lesson 4. But the law still teaches us who God is and what is good. Paul says the law is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12).
The hard parts

I want to be honest. There are passages in the Old Testament that trouble us. Wars like those in Joshua, harsh punishments, and stories that seem to go against what we know of Jesus. Let me say a few things, though I can’t answer everything.

First, God is patient. He told Abraham that He would wait four hundred years before judging the nations in Canaan, because their sin hadn’t yet reached its full measure (Genesis 15:13-16). Second, those events were a judgment on specific nations at a specific time, and they aren’t a pattern for how we treat people today. Jesus told us to love our enemies (Matthew 5:44). Third, Jesus is the clearest picture of God. Hebrews says He is the exact imprint of God’s being (Hebrews 1:3). When we aren’t sure what God is like, we look at Jesus.
And fourth, it’s fine to say, ‘I don’t understand this yet.’ Bring it to God, and to your pastor. Honest questions don’t offend Him.
How to read the Old Testament
Four tips.
Find out what kind of writing it is. The Old Testament has history, law, poetry, wisdom, and prophecy. You read a psalm differently from a list of laws.
Look for Jesus. Ask how this passage points ahead to Him, as in Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22. Not every verse does, but the whole story does.

Learn from the people. Paul says the things that happened to Israel were written down as examples and warnings for us (1 Corinthians 10:11). Abraham’s faith, David’s repentance and Daniel’s courage are still good teachers. Note that many Bible people are flawed, and the Bible tells us so. Their stories are descriptions, and not always instructions.
Be careful with promises. A promise God made to Israel as a nation isn’t automatically a promise to us. Read the setting, then ask what it shows about God’s character, which doesn’t change.
If you aren’t sure where to start, try Genesis, Exodus 1 to 20, a few of the Psalms, and Isaiah.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.
