title: Jesus in the Gospels
q: Who is Jesus in the four Gospels?
notes: You will get the most from this lesson if people have a Bible in front of them. Each of the four Gospels is introduced with one short reading. If your group has newer believers, keep the pace relaxed and let them notice things for themselves.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we looked at the Old Testament and how it points to Jesus.
What did you notice about Jesus when you read Isaiah 53?
Matthew 5:17
Tonight’s question is: who is Jesus in the four Gospels?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Jesus, we want to know You better. Show us who You are as we read about You. Amen.
If a friend asked you, ‘Who is Jesus?’, what would you say in one sentence?
Let a few people answer.

The New Testament begins with four short books about Jesus. They’re called the Gospels, which means ‘good news’. Why four? Think about four people standing around a statue, each describing it from where they stand. The statue is the same, and each person sees something the others don’t. That’s how the four Gospels work. Together they give us a fuller picture of Jesus.
Matthew, the promised King
Matthew 1:1

Matthew writes especially for a Jewish audience. He begins by tracing Jesus’ family line back to David and Abraham, to show that Jesus is the promised King. He often says ‘this happened to fulfill what the prophet said.’ He gathers Jesus’ teaching into five large sections, including the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5 to 7). If you want to know how Jesus fulfills the Old Testament, start here.
Mark, the Servant who acts
Mark 10:45

Mark is the shortest and the fastest. He uses the word ‘immediately’ again and again. He gives us a Jesus in action, healing, casting out evil, calming storms, on the move. Church tradition says Mark drew on the memories of Peter. His key verse is this one: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. If you’ve never read a Gospel, Mark is a good place to start.
Luke, the Savior of everyone
Luke 1:1-4

Luke was a doctor, and he writes like a careful researcher. He tells us he investigated everything from the beginning so that we can be sure of what we’ve been taught. His Gospel shows Jesus’ care for the people on the edges, the poor, women, children, the sick, tax collectors and outsiders. Only Luke has the stories of the good Samaritan, the lost son and Zacchaeus. He wrote a second book too, the Acts of the Apostles, which we’ll look at next week.
John, the Son of God

John is different from the other three. He tells us why he wrote. He chose some of the signs Jesus did so that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing we may have life in His name. His Gospel has seven ‘I am’ sayings. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. I am the good shepherd. I am the way, the truth and the life. He opens by saying that the Word was God and that the Word became flesh (John 1:1, 14).
What they agree on

The four Gospels tell the same story, with different emphasis. Take the feeding of the five thousand. It appears in all four. Each writer includes details the others don’t, and the core is the same. When accounts differ in small ways, it’s usually because the writers had different aims and different witnesses.

Across all four, we meet the same Jesus. He teaches with authority. He heals the sick and frees people from what binds them. He forgives sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:5-12). He calms a storm with a word (Mark 4:39-41). He says He and the Father are one (John 10:30). He’s welcoming to sinners and tough on pride. He dies on a cross, and He rises on the third day.
Notice how much space the Gospels give to the last week of Jesus’ life, His death and His resurrection. This tells us what the writers thought mattered most.
How to read a Gospel
Three suggestions.
Read a whole story at a time, not a verse. Notice who’s there, what Jesus does and what He says.
Ask one question of every passage: what does this show me about Jesus? Use the three steps from Lesson 38.
And don’t only study Him. Follow Him. Jesus said that if we love Him, we’ll keep His commands (John 14:15). After reading, ask what He’s asking you to do.

Try this. In pairs, pick a story you know, such as the calming of the storm, the woman at the well, or the healing of the paralyzed man. Take two minutes to tell each other what it shows you about Jesus.
Give them a few minutes, and invite a few to share.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

b.x: The fourth question is hard, so give people a moment. A good answer is that a good teacher wouldn’t claim to forgive sins, to be one with the Father, or to rise from the dead. He was either who He said He was or He wasn’t, and the Gospels invite us to look closely.

x.a: Mark is short and quick. John is good for understanding who Jesus is. Luke is rich in detail and compassion.

x.q: Was Jesus just a good man?
x.a: He claimed more than that. Look at Mark 2:5-12 and John 10:30 together, and let them think about what He claimed.

title: The early church in Acts
q: How did the first church grow?
notes: Acts describes what the first church did, and it does not always say what every church must do. Be careful not to turn every detail into a rule. The aim is to see what the Holy Spirit did through ordinary people, and to let it stir our faith. Some of the events involve persecution, so be sensitive to anyone in your group who is facing opposition.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we met Jesus in the four Gospels.
Did you read some of Mark? What did you notice about Jesus?
John 20:31
Tonight’s question is: how did the first church grow?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for the church that has gone before us. Do the same kind of work in us. Amen.
When you picture the very first church, what do you imagine?
Let people answer. Some will picture a great crowd, and others a small room.

The book of Acts was written by Luke, who also wrote the third Gospel. He tells us that his first book was about what Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1). Acts tells what Jesus kept doing, through His people, by the Holy Spirit. It’s the story of how a small group of frightened believers became a movement that spread across the Roman world.
The map of the book
Acts 1:8

This verse works like a table of contents. You’ll receive power when the Holy Spirit comes, and you’ll be My witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Chapters 1 to 7 are in Jerusalem. Chapters 8 to 12 move out into Judea and Samaria. Chapters 13 to 28 take the message to the wider world, ending with Paul in Rome.
The Spirit comes
Acts 2:1-4

On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came on the disciples. They’d been waiting and praying, as Jesus told them. Peter stood up and preached, and about three thousand people believed and were baptized (Acts 2:41). Notice that the church didn’t start with a plan or a building. It began with prayer and the Spirit’s power.
How they lived

Luke describes four habits. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to breaking bread and to prayer. They met in the temple and in homes. They shared with those in need. They enjoyed favor with the people, and every day the Lord added to their number those who were being saved.
Look at your own group. We learn from the Bible, we spend time together, we share meals and we pray. Without planning it, we’ve been living out Acts 2:42.

They were also generous. Acts 4:32-35 says that no one claimed their things as their own, and no one among them was needy. Believers sold property to help one another. This was voluntary, and it came from love.
Courage under pressure

The apostles were arrested and told to stop talking about Jesus. They went back to the church, and they prayed. They didn’t pray for the threats to stop. They prayed for boldness, and the place where they were meeting shook, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.

Stephen was stoned for his faith (Acts 7). After that, a great persecution scattered the church, and those who were scattered preached the word wherever they went (Acts 8:1-4). What looked like a disaster spread the message. If you or someone you know is facing opposition because of faith, remember that God is not absent, and that the church has always faced this.
That doesn’t mean we should look for trouble. Paul used wisdom. He escaped over a wall (Acts 9:25) and appealed to Caesar when it helped (Acts 25:11). Faith and wisdom go together.
Barriers broken

At first the church was almost entirely Jewish. Then God showed Peter, through a vision, that the good news was for Gentiles too. Peter went to the house of a Roman officer named Cornelius, and the Holy Spirit came on them as He had at Pentecost. Peter said that God shows no favoritism. The church in Antioch became a mixed community, and that’s where the believers were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).

A few chapters later, the church of Antioch worshiped and fasted, and the Holy Spirit said to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work He had called them to (Acts 13:1-3). The church prayed, laid hands on them and sent them out. This was the beginning of Paul’s journeys.
Problems too

The early church wasn’t perfect. In Acts 6, the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles didn’t ignore it. They gathered the church, chose seven trustworthy people to take care of it, and kept going. In Acts 15, a serious argument about whether Gentiles had to follow Jewish law was settled by the church gathering, listening and deciding together. Paul and Barnabas later disagreed so sharply that they parted ways (Acts 15:36-41), and God still used both of them.
So when we see problems in our own church, we needn’t be shocked. We should face them the way they did, with prayer, honesty and wise leaders.
What we learn

Four things. The church grows by the Spirit’s power, and we depend on Him. It grows through prayer, and through ordinary believers sharing their faith wherever they go. It grows through a community that teaches, shares and prays. And it grows through sending, when a church prays and releases people into the work. The book ends with Paul in Rome, preaching boldly and without hindrance (Acts 28:30-31). The story isn’t finished, and we’re in the next chapter.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

title: Reading the letters
q: How do I read Paul’s letters?
notes: Some of what Paul wrote about women, slaves and authority has been misused to hurt people. Part 5 gives a short, careful answer. If someone in your group has been harmed by how a verse was used, listen first and don’t defend the misuse. Invite them to talk with your pastor.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we looked at how the first church grew.
Which of the four habits from Acts 2:42 did you work on? What happened?
Acts 2:42
Tonight’s question is: how do I read Paul’s letters?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for the letters You’ve kept for us. Help us to read them as they were meant. Amen.
When did you last receive a letter or a long message that mattered to you? How did you read it?
Let people share. Most will say they read it slowly, more than once, and all the way through.

Twenty-one books of the New Testament are letters. Thirteen of them were written by Paul, and the rest by others, such as Peter, John, James and Jude. The letter to the Hebrews doesn’t name its writer. Tonight we’ll learn how to read them well.
Real letters to real people
Romans 1:1-7

Look at how Paul begins. He names himself, he names who he’s writing to, he greets them. These were real letters, sent to real churches and people with real questions and problems. The Corinthians were divided and disorderly. The Galatians were being pulled away from grace. The Philippians were Paul’s close friends, and he wrote to thank them.

Reading a letter is a bit like hearing one half of a phone call. We hear Paul’s side. We can sometimes tell what the other side said, but not always. That’s why it matters to find out the setting. A study Bible or the introduction to each letter helps.
Teaching first, then living
Romans 12:1-2

Many of Paul’s letters have two parts. The first half explains what God has done in Christ. The second half tells us how to live in light of it. Romans 1 to 11 teaches about sin, grace, faith and God’s plan. Then chapter 12 begins with the word ‘therefore’. In view of God’s mercy, offer your lives to Him. Ephesians works the same way. Chapters 1 to 3 describe what we have in Christ, and chapters 4 to 6 tell us how to walk.
So whenever you see ‘therefore’, ask what it’s there for. Go back and see what the writer is building on. Our behavior grows out of what we believe, and not the other way around.
Three questions for every letter
Here are three questions to bring to any letter.
Who wrote it, to whom, and why? Look for clues in the opening and closing.

What is the main point? Read the whole letter in one sitting if you can. Philippians takes about fifteen minutes, and 1 Thessalonians about ten. You’ll see the flow, which you can’t see when reading a verse at a time.
What does it ask me to believe or do? Use the steps from Lesson 38. Observe, understand, and apply.
Let’s try the first two with Philippians 1:1-11, and 1:12-14.
Read the passage aloud.
Who is writing and where is he? What is going on?” Let people notice that Paul is in prison. Ask: “What is his mood? What does he pray for them?
Let people notice joy, thanks and love.
Paul writes about joy from a prison cell. That tells us something about joy before we’ve read another line.
Hard passages and customs
Peter says that Paul’s letters have some things that are hard to understand, and that some people twist them. So you’re not alone if you find parts difficult. Here are three helps.
Don’t build a teaching on one hard verse. Look at what the rest of the Bible says about the subject. If a reading contradicts the clear teaching elsewhere, it’s probably not the right reading.

Separate the principle from the custom. Paul tells the Romans to greet each other with a holy kiss (Romans 16:16). Few of us do that, but the principle, warm greeting and care for each other, still applies. Ask what the writer wanted the first readers to understand, and what that looks like in our setting.
And bring hard passages to others. Ask your pastor or a mature believer, and read a good commentary.
Verses that have been misused
Some of Paul’s words about slaves, about women and about those in authority have been used to justify harm. I want to say something short and honest about that.

Paul wrote in the Roman world, where slavery was a part of life. His letters aren’t an endorsement of it. In the letter to Philemon, he asks a slave owner to receive his runaway slave Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a dear brother (Philemon 15-16). And in Galatians 3:28, he says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female. We are all one in Christ Jesus. Christians read other passages on the roles of men and women in different ways, and they sincerely differ. If a verse has been used to hurt you, or someone you know, please talk to your pastor or someone you trust. God doesn’t use His word to crush people.
Where to begin

If you haven’t read these before, here’s an order. Start with Philippians, a warm and short letter. Then read Ephesians for what we have in Christ. Read James for practical faith, and 1 John for love and assurance. After that, try Romans, which is longer and deeper. Read each one all the way through, and then go back and study it a section at a time.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

title: Psalms and wisdom
q: How do I use the Psalms and Proverbs?
notes: Some psalms speak of deep despair. Someone in your group may be going through depression, grief or a time when they feel nothing. If anyone says they feel hopeless or talks about harming themselves, stay with them, don’t leave them alone, and help them reach your pastor and a doctor or a crisis line that day. The psalms show that being honest with God is allowed, and they do not replace professional care.

Did you read Philippians? What stood out?

Tonight’s question is: how do I use the Psalms and Proverbs?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, thank You for giving us words to pray. Teach us to pour out our hearts to You. Amen.
Is there a song that you turn to when you’re happy, and one when you’re sad? What does it do for you?
Let people share.

Songs say things that plain talk can’t. The Bible has a whole book of songs and prayers, the Psalms, and a book of practical sayings, Proverbs. Tonight we’ll look at how to use them. They make a good pair, because the Psalms teach us how to speak to God, and Proverbs teaches us how to live.
The Psalms, a prayer book for every mood
Psalm 1:1-3

There are one hundred and fifty psalms, written over several hundred years, many by David. Psalm 1 opens the collection by describing the blessed person who delights in God’s law and thinks about it day and night. That person is like a tree planted by streams of water, with fruit in its season.

What sets the Psalms apart is how honest they are. There’s praise (Psalm 100), thanks (Psalm 136), trust (Psalm 23), confession (Psalm 51), and wisdom (Psalm 119). And there are many psalms of lament, where the writer cries out to God in pain. Some of the most honest words in the Bible are in the Psalms.
A pattern for pain
Psalm 13

Listen to the shape of this psalm. It begins with a complaint. ‘How long, Lord? Will You forget me forever?’ Then comes a request. ‘Look on me and answer.’ Then the writer remembers God’s love. And it ends with a decision to trust and sing.

That’s a pattern we can borrow. Say what hurts, honestly. Ask God for help. Remember what you know about Him. And choose to trust, even if the feelings haven’t caught up. Notice that David isn’t polite in verses 1 and 2. God can take our honest cries.

Some psalms never reach the comfort. Psalm 88 ends in darkness, and it’s still in the Bible. If you’re in a very dark place, those words are there for you. And please also tell someone, like your pastor or a friend. You don’t need to carry this alone.
How to pray the Psalms
Three simple ways to use them.
Read one slowly, and let it be your prayer. When you don’t know what to say, open a psalm, and say it to God as your own.
Put one in your own words. After reading Psalm 23, write a few lines about what it says to you. Who is your shepherd? What are you afraid of?
Pray one when you’re in a particular mood. Psalm 51 when you’ve failed. Psalm 139 when you feel unknown. Psalm 121 when you’re anxious about the road ahead. Psalm 23 when you need comfort.

A few things about reading poetry. Hebrew poetry often repeats an idea in different words, or sets two ideas against each other. When David says ‘The Lord is my rock,’ he doesn’t mean God is made of stone. He’s using a picture of strength and safety. And read a psalm as a prayer, not as a promise of what will happen in every situation.
Let’s try one. Read Psalm 13 again, and in the next two minutes, write four lines in your own words, one for each part. What is your complaint, your request, your reminder and your trust?
Give people time, and invite a few to read theirs aloud. Don’t press anyone.
Proverbs, wisdom for daily life
Proverbs 1:7

‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.’ Proverbs was written mostly by Solomon, and it collects short sayings about how to live well. The ‘fear of the Lord’ here means deep respect for God, and wanting to live His way. It’s the foundation of wisdom.

Proverbs speaks about everyday matters. Words (Proverbs 15:1: a gentle answer turns away anger). Work (Proverbs 10:4). Friends (Proverbs 27:17). Money, anger, laziness, pride and humility. It’s a practical book.

There’s an important thing to understand. A proverb states what is generally true, and it isn’t a guarantee. Proverbs 22:6 says to train up a child in the way he should go, and when he’s old he won’t depart from it. That’s a general principle. Many faithful parents have grieved over a child who walked away. Proverbs gives us wisdom about how life usually works, and not a promise that it will work that way every time.

The Bible balances it. The book of Job shows that suffering isn’t always punishment for something we did. Ecclesiastes asks hard questions about meaning and ends with the call to fear God and keep His commands (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Together with Proverbs, they give us a fuller picture.
A simple habit is to read one chapter of Proverbs a day. There are thirty-one chapters, and so one for each day of the month. Write down one saying that speaks to you.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Have you ever felt that you couldn’t say what you really felt to God? What held you back?
What does it mean to you that the Bible includes psalms of complaint?
Which psalm is your favorite, and why?
Which proverb do you most need right now?

b.x: If someone shares something painful, thank them, and don’t hurry to fix it. Pray with them, and make sure they know who they can talk to this week.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Read one psalm each day, and pray it back to God. You could use Psalms 1, 23, 51, 121 and 139.
Read the chapter of Proverbs that matches today’s date, and write down one saying you’ll practice.

b.x: Psalm 1:2

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for giving us words when we have none. Teach us to bring You everything, and to live wisely. Amen.
What does the Bible say about the future?
Thinking of you. Which psalm did you pray today?

x.q: Is it okay to be angry at God?
x.a: The psalmists were, and they told Him so, and God didn’t turn them away. Bring the anger to Him and not away from Him. If it feels too heavy, talk with your pastor.

x.q: Are the Psalms that curse enemies okay for us?
x.a: Some psalms ask God to judge those who do evil, and they leave the judgment to God. Jesus tells us to love our enemies and pray for them (Matthew 5:44). Pray the honest feelings, and then hand them to Him.

x.q: Proverbs says if I do right, things will go well. Why didn’t they?
x.a: Proverbs gives wisdom about how things usually go. Job and Ecclesiastes show that life is not always fair. Listen and pray with them, and don’t suggest that they’ve done something wrong.

x.q: I feel nothing when I read the Bible or pray.
x.a: This happens to many believers. Keep going, try a psalm like 42 or 88, and talk with your pastor. If they feel low for a long time, encourage them to see a doctor too.

title: The hope ahead
q: What does the Bible say about the future?
notes: Christians hold different views on the order of events at the end of time. This lesson teaches what all believers agree on, and names the places where they differ. Teach your church’s position where it has one, and keep your tone humble. Some people in your group may be afraid of the end of the world, or grieving someone who has died. Take your time with them, and let the comfort come first.

b.x: Welcome back. This is our last lesson in this fifth stretch, and I’m glad you’re here.
Which psalm did you pray this week? Did a proverb stand out?
Psalm 1:2
Tonight’s question is: what does the Bible say about the future?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You hold the future. Give us hope, and help us to live ready. Amen.
When you think about the future, what do you feel? Hope, worry, curiosity?
Let people answer. Many will say worry.

The Bible gives us a hope that doesn’t depend on how the world looks today. It doesn’t give us every detail, and God has kept some things to Himself. But it tells us enough to be sure of the ending. We’ll look at what we know, where Christians differ, and how to live in the meantime.
Jesus will return
Acts 1:9-11

As the disciples watched Jesus rise into the sky, two angels said that this same Jesus would come back in the same way. The New Testament speaks of His return again and again. It’s the great hope of the church. Paul called it our blessed hope (Titus 2:13).
Matthew 24:36

Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour, not even the angels, but only the Father. So be suspicious of anyone who sets a date. Many have, and every one has been wrong. What Jesus asked of us is to be ready (Matthew 24:42-44).
What we can be sure of
Christians of every tradition agree on these things.
1 Thessalonians 4:13-18

First, those who have died in Christ are with Him, and they’ll be raised. Paul writes this to comfort people who were grieving. We don’t grieve like people without hope. The Lord Himself will come down, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we’ll be with the Lord forever. Then Paul says, ‘Encourage one another with these words.’ If you’ve lost someone who belonged to Jesus, this is for you.

Second, our bodies will be raised and changed. Paul says that what is sown perishable is raised imperishable, and that we shall all be changed (1 Corinthians 15:42-44, 51-54). Jesus’ resurrection is the first fruits of it (1 Corinthians 15:20).

Third, there will be a judgment. We all must stand before Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), and the Bible warns that those who’ve rejected Him will be separated from Him (Revelation 20:11-15). For those who belong to Jesus, there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Our hope rests on what He has done.
Revelation 21:1-5

Fourth, God will make all things new. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the home of God among people. He’ll wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain. We said in Lesson 39 that the story ends where it began, with God living with His people. Our hope is to live in a renewed creation with Him (Romans 8:18-21).
Where Christians differ

There are some questions on which faithful, Bible-loving Christians disagree. When will Jesus gather His church in relation to a time of great trouble? What does the thousand years in Revelation 20 mean? Is it a literal period, a long age, or a symbol? And how are the symbols of Revelation to be read?

You may hear terms like premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial. These are names for different views of the thousand years. All three views agree that Jesus will return, that the dead will be raised, that there will be a judgment, and that God will make all things new.

My advice is to hold your own view with humility, and to teach what your church teaches. Don’t let these questions divide believers who agree on what matters most. Paul told Timothy to avoid pointless arguments (2 Timothy 2:23-24).
Reading Revelation
Revelation 1:1-3

Revelation is a hard book, and many people avoid it. A few tips. It’s a letter to seven churches facing real pressure (Revelation 1:4; chapters 2 and 3). It uses many symbols, such as beasts, bowls, horns and a dragon, and it’s written in a style that people at the time understood. We shouldn’t read every image as a literal prediction.

The main message is clear. Jesus is on the throne. Evil won’t last. God’s people are called to be faithful, and the Lamb wins. John says that those who read it and take it to heart are blessed. If you’re curious, read it as a whole, and keep your eyes on Jesus and not on a chart.
Living ready
1 John 3:2-3

‘Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as He is pure.’ A real hope changes how we live now. Jesus told stories to teach readiness. The ten bridesmaids in Matthew 25:1-13 show us that we need to be prepared and watchful. The servants who invested what they were given in Matthew 25:14-30 show that being ready means being faithful. And the sheep and the goats in Matthew 25:31-46 show that caring for people in need is part of it.

Being ready means loving God, loving people, obeying what we know, and telling others about Jesus. Peter says that the Lord isn’t slow. He’s patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9). The delay is mercy, and it’s our chance to bring others in.

And for anyone who’s afraid, hear this. Jesus said, ‘Do not let your hearts be troubled’ (John 14:1-3). He’s gone to prepare a place for us, and He will come back and take us to be with Him. The future is in good hands.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What do you feel when you think about Jesus’ return? Excitement, fear, something else?
Which of the four sure things, being with Christ, being raised, judgment or a new creation, gives you the most comfort?
What did you used to believe about the end times? Has anything changed?
How should hope for the future change how we live this week?

b.x: Leave space for anyone who has lost someone. Let them speak, and don’t hurry to give answers.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, and send it to someone who is grieving, with a kind word.
Ask yourself, “If Jesus returned today, what would I wish I had done?” Take one step toward it this week.

b.x: 1 Thessalonians 4:18

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You that You hold the future. Give us hope that lasts, and help us to live ready until You come. Amen.

This is the end of the fifth phase. Plan a simple celebration for your group, like a shared meal, and take a few minutes to share what you’ve learned from the Bible over these weeks. The next phase is about living out the character of Jesus at home, with friends, with money and in hard seasons, and it starts the following week.
Thinking of you. Who did you encourage with these words?

x.q: When will Jesus come back?
x.a: Nobody knows. Jesus said so (Matthew 24:36). We stay ready, live faithfully and tell others.

x.q: Will everyone be saved in the end?
x.a: Jesus taught that there is a judgment and that the way to life is through Him (John 14:6). Don’t argue the point, but say what the Bible says, and say it gently. Pray with them if it troubles them.

x.q: My loved one died, and I’m not sure they knew Jesus.
x.a: Be gentle, and don’t make promises the Bible doesn’t. We can trust that God is just and merciful (Genesis 18:25). Pray with them, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: I’m afraid of the end times.
x.a: Read John 14:1-3 together. Remind them that Jesus is Lord of the future, and that the church has always lived with this hope. Suggest they limit frightening videos and talk with your pastor.

title: Who I am in Christ
q: Who am I now that I belong to Jesus?
notes: Many people carry labels they were given by someone who hurt them, such as “worthless,” “dirty” or “a mistake.” This lesson speaks to those labels, so go slowly and let people feel safe. If anyone tells you about abuse, listen without interrupting, thank them for trusting you, and help them reach your pastor and a trained counselor. Don’t push anyone to forgive or to forget quickly.

b.x: Welcome back. Tonight we begin a new stretch, and I’m glad you’re here.

Last time we looked at what the Bible says about the future. Did you share 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 with anyone who is grieving? And what came to mind when you asked yourself, ‘If Jesus returned today, what would I wish I had done?’
1 Thessalonians 4:18
Tonight’s question is: who am I now that I belong to Jesus?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, tell us who we are in Your eyes. Quiet the other voices, and help us believe You. Amen.
If a stranger asked, ‘Who are you?’, what would you say first?
Let people answer. Most will give a job, a family role or a name.

We usually answer with what we do, or whom we belong to. Those things matter, and they can also change. People lose jobs, lose loved ones, make mistakes and grow old. If our whole sense of who we are rests on them, it shakes. Tonight we’ll look at what God says about us, which doesn’t shake.
Where our labels come from

Most of us collected labels along the way. A teacher said we were slow. A parent said we’d never amount to anything. An ex called us a failure. We said some things to ourselves after we messed up. Over the years those labels harden into a picture of who we think we are.
The Bible doesn’t ask us to pretend that those words never hurt. It asks us to put God’s words next to them, and to decide whose voice we’ll believe.
What God says about us
John 1:12

To everyone who received Him, to those who believe in His name, Jesus gave the right to become children of God. If you’ve received Him, you’re God’s child. That’s not a title we earn. We were adopted into a family (Ephesians 1:5), and we can call God our Father (Romans 8:15).
Here are some more of the things God says about those who belong to Jesus.
We’re forgiven. In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins (Ephesians 1:7). God has canceled the record of our debt and nailed it to the cross (Colossians 2:13-14).
We’re chosen and loved. Paul calls believers God’s chosen ones, holy and dearly loved (Colossians 3:12). God chose us before the world began (Ephesians 1:4).
We’re a new creation. We said early in the program that the old has gone and the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17).

We’re God’s handiwork. The word Paul uses in Ephesians 2:10 is the one from which we get ‘poem’ or ‘masterpiece.’ We’re created in Christ Jesus to do good works that God prepared in advance for us to do.
We belong to heaven. Our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). And God’s Spirit lives in us (1 Corinthians 6:19). The Holy Spirit makes His home in each believer.
Truth against the lies
Romans 8:1
Let’s put a few of the common labels against what God says.
‘I’m a failure.’ The Bible says there’s no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God doesn’t define us by our worst day.
‘I’m unlovable.’ God showed His love by sending Christ to die for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). Nothing can separate us from His love (Romans 8:38-39).

‘I’m what was done to me.’ People can do real harm, and it matters. But what was done to us doesn’t get the final word about who we are. God sees what happened, and He’s close to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).
‘I’m my past.’ If anyone is in Christ, the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17). We aren’t pretending the past didn’t happen. It just doesn’t define us any more.
This takes time. A lifetime of labels doesn’t vanish in one evening. Keep putting God’s words next to the old ones.
Raised with Christ
Colossians 3:1-4

Paul says that we’ve been raised with Christ, so we should set our hearts and minds on things above, where Christ is. Our life is now hidden with Christ in God. When Christ appears, we’ll appear with Him in glory. Our true identity is tied to Jesus, and no one can take it away.
Living from who we are
A few things follow.

We live from our identity and don’t live for it. We don’t obey God to become His children. We obey because we are His children. Paul calls us to live in a manner worthy of the calling we’ve received (Ephesians 4:1). It begins with who we are.
We renew our minds. Romans 12:2 says to be transformed by the renewing of our minds. Each day, say back to yourself what God says. Write it out, and put it where you’ll see it.

And we stay humble. Knowing we’re loved isn’t a reason to think we’re better than others. Paul says not to think of ourselves more highly than we ought (Romans 12:3). Everything we are is a gift. And everyone we meet bears God’s image too (Genesis 1:27).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What is something you used to believe about yourself that you now know is a lie?
Which of the things God says about us do you find hardest to believe?
Where do you tend to find your worth, in work, family, looks, or something else?
How would your week look different if you really believed what God says about you?

b.x: The second question may bring up pain. Don’t rush to fix it. Thank the person, and say that many people share it.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Write five sentences that start “I am,” using what God says: I am forgiven, I am loved, and so on. Read them aloud each morning.
When an old label comes to mind, answer it with one of those sentences.

b.x: John 1:12

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, thank You for calling us Your children. Help us to believe what You say about us, and to live like it. Amen.
What does the Spirit’s fruit look like day to day?
Thinking of you. Which ‘I am’ did you need today?

x.q: I don’t feel like God’s child.
x.a: Feelings change, and God’s word doesn’t. Read John 1:12 and 1 John 3:1 together, and keep reading them. Ask what is making them doubt, and pray with them.

x.q: I was told I’m worthless by my family.
x.a: Listen and don’t rush. Tell them that those words don’t come from God. Pray with them, and suggest they talk with your pastor or a counselor.

x.q: Isn’t it proud to say I’m special?
x.a: It’s humble to agree with what God says. Our worth comes from His love and doesn’t rest on our performance. It also means everyone else has the same worth.

x.q: I keep doing things that don’t match who I am.
x.a: That’s real, and Paul struggled too (Romans 7:15-25). We keep turning to Jesus, who forgives us and helps us grow. We’ll see more about this in the next lessons.

title: Love, joy and peace
q: What does the Spirit’s fruit look like day to day?
notes: Joy and peace are tender subjects for people who are depressed, anxious or grieving. Don’t suggest that a believer who feels low is lacking faith. Joy and peace can sit beside sorrow, and sometimes a person needs a doctor or counselor as well as prayer. Say that plainly when it fits.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we looked at who we are in Christ.
Which ‘I am’ sentence did you need most this week? How did it help?
John 1:12
Tonight’s question is: what does the Spirit’s fruit look like day to day?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Holy Spirit, grow Your fruit in us. Make us people who love, who have joy and who are at peace. Amen.
Think of someone you know who is a joy to be around. What is it about them?
Let people answer. They’ll mention kindness, calm, warmth and how that person listens.

People like that are rare, and they didn’t get that way by trying to look good. Something grows in them. Paul has a picture for it. Tonight and for the next two weeks, we’ll look at the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
A fruit, not a list of tasks
Galatians 5:22-23

The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Notice that Paul says ‘fruit’, in the singular. It’s one fruit with nine flavors. It’s a picture of a single character, and not a menu where we choose the ones we like.

And notice that it’s the fruit of the Spirit. Apples don’t grow by effort. They grow because the branch is joined to the tree. Jesus said, ‘I am the vine, and you are the branches. If you remain in Me and I in you, you’ll bear much fruit’ (John 15:4-5). We stay close to Jesus, and He grows the fruit in us. Earlier we said that the Spirit makes us more like Christ. This is what that looks like.
We can’t produce it by gritting our teeth. We can make room for it, by praying, reading the Bible, obeying and staying with God’s people. That’s how the branch stays joined.
Love
1 Corinthians 13:4-7

Love comes first, and the others grow out of it. Paul describes it. Love is patient and kind. It doesn’t envy or boast. It isn’t proud or rude, and it doesn’t insist on its own way. It isn’t easily angered, and it keeps no record of wrongs. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes and always perseveres.

Look at that list. Almost all of it is about what we do. Love is an action we choose, and not only a feeling we have. Jesus said, ‘A new command I give you: love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another’ (John 13:34). He loved us by giving Himself. We love because He first loved us (1 John 4:19).
A good test is to put your own name in place of the word ‘love’ in verses 4 to 7. ‘Maria is patient, Maria is kind.’ It’s humbling, and it shows where we need the Spirit’s help.
Joy
Philippians 4:4

Paul says, ‘Rejoice in the Lord always.’ He wrote that from a prison cell. Joy isn’t the same as happiness. Happiness depends on what’s happening to us. Joy comes from who God is and what He’s done. Jesus told His disciples not to rejoice that spirits obeyed them, but to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The joy of the Lord is our strength (Nehemiah 8:10).

That means joy can live next to sadness. Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’ tomb, and He still had joy (John 11:35; Hebrews 12:2). If you’re grieving or going through a dark time, you aren’t failing at joy. You can be both sad and held by God. Telling someone who is hurting to just be joyful isn’t what Paul had in mind.
Where does joy grow? In knowing that we’re forgiven and loved. In worship. In spending time with God’s people. In serving others. And in giving thanks.
Peace
John 14:27
Jesus said, ‘Peace I leave with you. My peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not be afraid.’ The Bible speaks of three kinds of peace.
Peace with God. We have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). Our sins are forgiven, and nothing stands between us.

The peace of God. When we bring our worries to God with thanks, the peace of God, which is beyond understanding, guards our hearts and minds (Philippians 4:6-7). God keeps in perfect peace those whose minds are fixed on Him (Isaiah 26:3).
And peace with people. As far as it depends on us, we live at peace with everyone (Romans 12:18). We’ll look at that in Lesson 51.

Peace doesn’t mean that nothing is wrong. It means that in the middle of what’s wrong, we aren’t alone. And God also uses doctors, counselors and friends to help. If anxiety is making it hard to eat, sleep or work, please see a doctor. That doesn’t mean you lack faith.
How the fruit grows
Four things help.
Stay close to Jesus. A branch bears fruit by remaining in the vine.
Accept pruning. A gardener cuts back the branches that bear fruit so that they’ll bear more (John 15:2). Hard seasons can be part of it, though not every hardship is sent as a lesson.
Be patient. Fruit takes a season. If you feel you haven’t changed, look back over a year, and ask someone who knows you.
And look for the fruit, not for how you feel. A person can feel flat and still be growing in love.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Who has shown you real love, and how did they do it?
How would you describe the difference between joy and happiness?
What steals your peace most often?
Of love, joy and peace, which one do you most want the Spirit to grow in you?

b.x: If anyone describes ongoing sadness or anxiety, thank them, and quietly suggest a doctor or counselor along with prayer.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 each day, putting your name in the place of “love.” Pick one line to practice.
Each evening, write down one thing you’re thankful for, and one worry you handed to God.

b.x: Galatians 5:22-23

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Holy Spirit, grow Your fruit in us. Make us people who love, who rejoice and who are at peace. Amen.
How do I treat people who test me?
Thinking of you. What were you thankful for today?

x.q: I don’t feel any joy.
x.a: That’s more common than people say. Ask how long, and listen. Joy can return in a quiet way, and low mood sometimes needs a doctor. Pray with them, and suggest they talk with your pastor.

x.q: I can’t love someone who hurt me.
x.a: Love doesn’t mean trusting them again or being near them. It starts with praying for them and treating them fairly. If they were abused, help them reach your pastor and a counselor.

x.q: Is it wrong to feel anxious?
x.a: Anxiety is a feeling many people have, and it doesn’t mean you’re a bad Christian. Give it to God, and see a doctor if it’s heavy.

x.q: Why do I not see fruit in me?
x.a: Look back over a year. Ask a friend what they see. Growth is often slow, and the Spirit is at work even when we can’t feel it.

title: Patience, kindness and goodness
q: How do I treat people who test me?
notes: Be careful that this lesson does not teach people to put up with mistreatment. Patience and kindness do not mean staying in danger or being used. If anyone in your group is being abused or threatened at home or work, listen, take it seriously, and help them reach your pastor and the proper authorities. Part 4 says this plainly.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we looked at love, joy and peace.
What was one thing you were thankful for this week? Did reading 1 Corinthians 13 with your name in it change anything?
Galatians 5:22-23
Tonight’s question is: how do I treat people who test me?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You’ve been patient and kind with us. Teach us to be the same toward others. Amen.
Who is the person who most tests your patience right now? Don’t name them, just think of them.
Let people laugh. Say that all of us have someone.

Patience, kindness and goodness are the next three flavors of the Spirit’s fruit. They’re the ones that show up in how we treat other people, especially people who aren’t easy to be around. Let’s look at each one.
Patience
Exodus 34:6

God describes Himself as slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness. The Bible’s word for patience means being long-tempered, taking a long time to boil. We know it first from God. He has been patient with us. Peter says the Lord is patient with us, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9).

A patient person doesn’t have a bigger supply of energy. They’ve learned to pause. Proverbs says that a person with understanding is slow to anger (Proverbs 14:29), and that it’s better to be patient than powerful (Proverbs 16:32). James compares us to a farmer who waits for the crop, knowing that the rain will come (James 5:7-8).

Where do we need it? Waiting in lines, dealing with children, relatives who say the same thing every visit, coworkers who are slow, and our own slow growth. The pause before we answer is where patience shows. In that pause, we can pray one sentence, such as ‘Lord, help me,’ before we speak.
Kindness
Ephesians 4:32

‘Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.’ Kindness is a warm and practical goodwill toward other people. We learn it from God, whose kindness leads us to repentance (Romans 2:4).

Jesus said to love our enemies and do good to them, and to lend without expecting anything back, because God is kind to the ungrateful and wicked (Luke 6:35). So we’re kind even when it isn’t returned.

Kindness isn’t the same as being nice. A nice person avoids hard truths to stay comfortable. A kind person cares enough to speak truthfully and gently (Ephesians 4:15). And kindness is often small. A word of encouragement, a meal, a ride, a note, remembering a name, a phone call to someone who’s alone. These small acts say, ‘You matter.’
Goodness
Acts 10:38

Peter says that Jesus went around doing good. Goodness is a kind of moral beauty, and it shows up as actions. It means wanting what is right and doing it, especially when it costs something. Paul says, ‘Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, especially to those who belong to the family of believers’ (Galatians 6:9-10).

Goodness is also quiet. Jesus said that when we give to the needy, we shouldn’t announce it, but let our left hand not know what the right is doing (Matthew 6:3-4). Real goodness doesn’t need an audience.
People who test us
Now the hard part. How do we practice these with people who are difficult? Let’s look at Jesus.
1 Peter 2:23

When they hurled insults at Him, He didn’t retaliate. When He suffered, He made no threats. He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. He’s our example. Paul adds that we shouldn’t repay evil with evil, but overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17-21).

Here are four practical steps. First, pause and pray before you answer. Second, ask what the other person might be dealing with, which often changes how we hear them. Third, do one small good thing for them. Fourth, bless them in prayer by name, even if it’s a short prayer.

Now an important word. Being patient and kind doesn’t mean putting up with abuse. If someone is hurting you or your children, or threatening you, or controlling you, you aren’t required to stay near them, and you aren’t being impatient when you protect yourself. Proverbs says the prudent see danger and take refuge (Proverbs 22:3). Jesus Himself sometimes walked away from those who wanted to harm Him (John 8:59). If this is you, tell your pastor and someone you trust, and get help from the proper authorities.
Patience also isn’t the same as silence. When a wrong has been done, it may be right to talk about it kindly and honestly. We’ll look at that in Lesson 51.
The Spirit does it

Here’s the good news. We aren’t trying to produce this by ourselves. When we reach the end of our patience, we pray, and the Spirit gives what we lack. Be quick to apologize when you slip. A sincere ‘I’m sorry I snapped’ does a great deal of good. And be patient with yourself. These qualities grow slowly.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: When do you most lose your patience? What do you usually say or do?
Who has been kind to you when you didn’t deserve it? What did that do for you?
What is one small act of goodness you could do this week that nobody will see?
How can you tell the difference between being patient with someone and being used?

b.x: The fourth question matters. Take your time, and let it lead to the point about safety.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Think of the person who tests you most. Pray for them by name each day, and do one small kind thing for them.
Pause before you respond whenever you feel irritation. Say a short prayer first.

b.x: Colossians 3:12

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, make us patient, kind and good, as You are. Help us to love the people who are hard to love. Amen.
How do I stay steady and gentle under pressure?
Thinking of you. How did the pause go?

x.q: My spouse or family member treats me badly. Should I just be patient?
x.a: Listen carefully. If there is abuse or fear, patience isn’t the answer. Help them reach your pastor and the proper authorities, and keep them safe.

x.q: I always lose my temper.
x.a: Say that it’s a common struggle, and that the Spirit can help. Suggest pausing, praying, stepping away, and saying sorry quickly. If it feels out of control, encourage them to talk with a counselor.

x.q: Do I have to be kind to people who are cruel?
x.a: We’re called to treat them fairly and wish them well. We don’t have to give them access to hurt us again. Read Romans 12:18 together, where Paul says, as far as it depends on you.

x.q: Aren’t I being fake if I’m kind when I don’t feel it?
x.a: No. Kindness is a choice, and the feeling often follows. You can be honest with God about how you feel and still choose to act kindly.

title: Faithfulness, gentleness and self-control
q: How do I stay steady and gentle under pressure?
notes: Self-control touches habits that some people struggle with deeply, such as alcohol, drugs, gambling, anger or screens. Nobody should be shamed in this lesson. If someone tells you they are caught in an addiction, thank them for trusting you, pray with them, and help them connect with your pastor and with a doctor or a recovery program. Willpower alone is rarely enough, and asking for help is a sign of strength.

b.x: Welcome back. This is the last of three evenings on the fruit of the Spirit.
Who did you pray for last week, and what small kind thing did you do for them? How did the pause go when you felt irritated?
Colossians 3:12
Tonight’s question is: how do I stay steady and gentle under pressure?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Lord, make us people others can count on. Make us gentle with others, and give us strength to govern ourselves. Amen.
When life gets stressful, what is the first thing in you to crack? Is it your temper, your words, your habits, or your promises?
Let people answer honestly. A little laughter helps.
Pressure shows what’s in us. Tonight we’ll look at the last three flavors of the Spirit’s fruit, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. They’re the ones that hold us steady when things get hard.
Faithfulness
Lamentations 3:22-23

‘Because of the Lord’s great love we are not consumed, for His compassions never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness.’ Faithfulness begins with God. He keeps His promises, and He doesn’t change. We can count on Him (Hebrews 13:8).

A faithful person is someone others can count on. They show up. They keep their word. They finish what they start. Paul says that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). Jesus said, ‘Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much’ (Luke 16:10).

Faithfulness mostly lives in small things. Being on time. Returning the call. Doing the job well when nobody’s watching. Keeping a promise to a child. Showing up to the group. These small things are how people learn whether we’re trustworthy.
And what if we’ve failed? Peter denied Jesus three times, and Jesus restored him (John 21:15-19). If we’ve been unreliable, we can say so, ask forgiveness, and start again today.
Gentleness
Matthew 11:29

Jesus said, ‘Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.’ Gentleness isn’t weakness. The old word describes a strong horse that has been trained, with its strength under control. Jesus was the most powerful person who ever lived, and He was gentle.

Gentleness shows in how we speak. ‘A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger’ (Proverbs 15:1). It shows in how we correct people: ‘If someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently’ (Galatians 6:1). And it shows in how we share our faith: ‘with gentleness and respect’ (1 Peter 3:15-16).
Gentleness doesn’t mean we never speak the truth. Jesus drove the traders out of the temple. Gentleness means that our strength serves other people, and doesn’t crush them.
Self-control
Proverbs 25:28

‘Like a city whose walls are broken through is a person who lacks self-control.’ In ancient times, a city without walls was open to anyone who wanted to come in. Self-control is our wall. It’s the ability to govern our desires, our words and our actions so that they serve what we truly want.

Where do we need it? Our temper, our tongue, food and drink, spending, screens and social media, sleep, anger, and our time. Paul said, ‘Everyone who competes in the games goes into strict training’ (1 Corinthians 9:25). He trained himself because he wanted to finish well.

Where does self-control come from? Not only from trying harder. Paul wrote to Titus that the grace of God teaches us to say no to ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled lives (Titus 2:11-12). Grace is where it starts. And Timothy was told that God gave us a spirit of power, love and self-discipline (2 Timothy 1:7).
Staying steady under pressure
Isaiah 40:31

Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not be faint. Here are some practical ways to stay steady.
Know your weak points. If you lose your temper in traffic, or overspend when you’re tired, plan for it before it happens. Jesus told us to watch and pray (Matthew 26:41).
Build small habits. Pray in the morning, sleep enough, eat, move, and keep your Bible reading steady. Pressure is much harder to carry when we’re worn out.
Slow down your responses. Count to ten. Breathe. Say a short prayer. Then speak.

Keep people close. Paul told the Galatians to carry each other’s burdens (Galatians 6:2). Ask a friend to check in on the area where you struggle. In James 5:16, we’re told to confess our sins to one another and pray for each other, so that we may be healed.

And if you’re struggling with something that feels stronger than you, such as alcohol, drugs, gambling or an angry temper, please ask for help. That may mean your pastor, a doctor, a counselor or a recovery group. Asking for help is a wise step, and it isn’t a failure of faith.
When we fall

We will fall. When we do, 1 John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just and will forgive us. The fruit grows over a lifetime. Get up, confess, and keep going. ‘Though the righteous fall seven times, they rise again’ (Proverbs 24:16).
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: Who in your life is most faithful, and what have they taught you?
When has someone’s gentleness changed how you responded to them?
Where does your self-control feel weakest right now?
What is one small step you could take this week to build a wall in that area?

b.x: The third question is sensitive. Let people answer in general terms, and don’t ask for details. Offer to talk privately afterward.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Pick one small promise you’ve been putting off, and keep it.
Choose one area where you need self-control. Tell one trusted person, and ask them to check in with you.

b.x: Proverbs 25:28

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, You’re faithful to us. Make us faithful, gentle and self-controlled. Hold us steady when the pressure comes. Amen.
How do I honor God in my home?
Thinking of you. How is the promise going?

x.q: I’ve tried to stop a habit many times and keep failing.
x.a: Listen kindly. Remind them of Proverbs 24:16 and 1 John 1:9. Encourage them to see a doctor or join a recovery group, and offer to go with them. Tell your pastor, with their permission.

x.q: Is gentleness the same as being a doormat?
x.a: No. Jesus was gentle and also spoke the truth and set boundaries. Gentleness is strength under control.

x.q: I can’t stop losing my temper with my children or spouse.
x.a: Take it seriously. Encourage them to talk with your pastor or a counselor, and to step away and pray when they feel it rising. If anyone is being hurt, help them get support right away.

x.q: What if I promised something and can’t keep it?
x.a: Go to the person, say so honestly, and ask what you can do. Honesty is part of faithfulness.

title: Marriage, singleness and family
q: How do I honor God in my home?
notes: This lesson will land differently for each person in the room. Some are married and happy, some are married and struggling, some are single by choice or by circumstance, some are divorced or widowed, and some grew up in painful homes. Speak so that every one of them feels included, and never as if one situation is better than another.

Please read this carefully. The Bible passages on marriage must never be used to tell someone to stay in a home where they or their children are being hurt. If anyone describes violence, threats, control or fear at home, listen, believe them, and help them reach your pastor and the proper authorities or a local support service right away. Safety comes first. Questions about separation or divorce belong with your pastor, and you shouldn’t try to settle them in the group.

b.x: Welcome back. Over the last three weeks we looked at the fruit of the Spirit. Tonight we begin to see how it shapes the places we live.
What small step did you take on self-control or on a promise you’ve been putting off? How did it go?
Proverbs 25:28
Tonight’s question is: how do I honor God in my home?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You set the lonely in families. Bless every home represented here, whatever it looks like, and teach us to love well. Amen.
What is one thing you learned about family growing up, good or bad, that still shapes you?
Let a few people answer. Say that all of us carry something.

God cares about the places where we live. Some of us are married, some are single, some are raising children, some are caring for parents, and some live alone. Whatever your home looks like, God has something to say to you. We’ll go through a few of them, and I’d ask you to listen for what applies to you.
God’s design for the family
Genesis 2:18, 24

‘It is not good for the man to be alone.’ God made people for relationship. Marriage is described there as a man and woman leaving their parents and becoming one flesh, a lasting, faithful bond. Jesus pointed back to this when he talked about marriage (Matthew 19:4-6). The Bible also says that God sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6), and that family can include the church.
Marriage
Ephesians 5:21
Paul begins the whole section with ‘Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.’ Everything that follows rests on that sentence. Both spouses give themselves to the other.

He tells wives to respect and support their husbands (Ephesians 5:22, 33). And he gives husbands the heavier command: ‘Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her’ (Ephesians 5:25). Christ’s love was sacrificial and served those He loved. It never controlled or hurt them. A husband who raises his hand, his voice or his power against his wife has abandoned this passage.

Here are some simple habits that build a marriage. Pray together. Listen without interrupting. Say thank you every day. Say sorry quickly. Keep promises. Spend time together without screens. And keep the marriage ahead of your phone, your work and your friends.
Marriages struggle at times, and the struggle doesn’t mean that it’s failing. If you need help, please ask. A pastor or a trained counselor can make a great difference.
Singleness
1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 32-35

Paul was single and called it a gift. He wrote that a single person can give undivided devotion to the Lord. Jesus was single too. So being single is not a lesser life, and it isn’t a waiting room. Some are single by choice, and some wish they weren’t. Both are real. If you desire marriage, it’s fine to ask God for it. And in the meantime, you can serve, be a friend, and grow.

The church is meant to be a family for the single, the widowed, and the divorced. Jesus said that whoever does God’s will is His brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35). If you’re married, invite someone to your table.
Children and parents
Ephesians 6:1-4

‘Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honor your father and mother.’ And then fathers are told, ‘Do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.’ Parents lead with patience. They don’t use harshness to get obedience.

How do we raise children well? Love them in ways they can feel. Spend time with them. Pray for them and with them. Let them see you read the Bible and say sorry. Set clear and fair limits. Proverbs 22:6 says to train up a child in the way they should go, though every child makes their own choices, and good parents can still have children who struggle.

Honoring parents looks different for adults. We can respect and care for our parents (1 Timothy 5:4, 8) without letting them control us. If your parents hurt you, honoring them doesn’t mean pretending that nothing happened, and it doesn’t mean staying near them. It can mean treating them fairly from a safe distance.
Wherever you are

Whatever your home is like, here are four things to try. Pray for the people you live with, by name. Serve someone in your home this week in a way they’ll notice. Forgive what you can and talk about what you can’t. And invite others in. Hospitality is a gift of the family of God (Romans 12:13).
If your family is broken, hurting or far away, God hasn’t forgotten you. Psalm 27:10 says that even if my father and mother forsake me, the Lord will receive me. His family is open to you.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What is one thing your family did well that you would like to pass on?
What is one pattern from your family that you want to change?
How can our group be a family to people who are single, widowed or far from home?
What is one thing you could do this week to serve the people in your home?

b.x: Keep an eye on people’s faces. If someone grows quiet or upset, check in with them afterward, privately.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Pray for each person in your home by name every day. If you live alone, pray for three people you love.
Do one unexpected act of service or encouragement for someone in your home or your church family.

b.x: Ephesians 5:21

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Father, bless our homes. Heal what is broken, and teach us to love one another as Christ loves us. Amen.
How do I handle a disagreement or hurt in a relationship?
Thinking of you. How did your home do this week?

x.q: My spouse is not a believer. What do I do?
x.a: Love them, serve them, and live well. Peter encourages believers to win a spouse without words by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1-2). Don’t preach at them. Keep praying, and invite them gently.

x.q: I’m divorced. Does God still love me?
x.a: Yes, without question. Romans 8:1 and 8:38-39 apply to you. If there’s pain or questions about the past, offer to arrange time with your pastor. Don’t try to judge it in the group.

x.q: My husband or wife hurts me.
x.a: Listen, believe them, and ask whether they’re safe. Help them reach your pastor and the proper authorities or a local support service. The Bible never asks anyone to stay in danger.

x.q: I want to get married and I’m not.
x.a: Listen without fixing. It’s a real ache. Pray with them, and include them in the life of the group.

title: Conflict and making peace
q: How do I handle a disagreement or hurt in a relationship?
notes: Forgiveness is a heavy subject for anyone who has been seriously hurt. Do not push someone to forgive quickly, to meet the person who hurt them, or to trust them again. The lesson says plainly that forgiving is not the same as trusting, and that safety matters. If anyone describes abuse, listen, and help them reach your pastor and a counselor. The steps in Matthew 18 are for ordinary conflict between believers and are not a way to confront a person who is dangerous.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we thought about our homes.
Who did you pray for, and what did you do to serve someone at home or in church? How did it go?
Ephesians 5:21
Tonight’s question is: how do I handle a disagreement or hurt in a relationship?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Prince of Peace, make us peacemakers. Show us anyone we need to forgive or talk to, and give us the courage to do it well. Amen.
What is your usual way of handling conflict? Do you fight, run, freeze, or smooth things over?
Let people smile at each other. Say that we all have a default.

Wherever there are people, there will be conflict. The question is how we handle it. Jesus said, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God’ (Matthew 5:9). A peacemaker isn’t someone who avoids conflict. A peacemaker works to make things right. Tonight we’ll look at how.
Start with yourself
Matthew 7:3-5

Jesus asks why we notice the speck in our brother’s eye while ignoring the plank in our own. Before we say anything to someone else, we ask ourselves a few questions. What is my part in this? Am I hurt, or am I just annoyed? Have I understood them correctly? Have I prayed about it?

Sometimes, after that honest look, we realize that it’s small and we can let it go. Proverbs 19:11 says that it is to a person’s glory to overlook an offense. Love covers over many sins (1 Peter 4:8). Not everything needs a conversation.
Go to the person
Matthew 18:15

‘If your brother or sister sins against you, go and point out their fault, just between the two of you. If they listen to you, you have won them over.’ The first step is to go directly and privately to the person. Not to a third person, not to social media, and not to the group chat. Gossip is the opposite of this. The goal is to win them back, and not to win the argument.

How do we do it well? Choose a good time, not in the heat of anger. Start by saying what you value in them. Describe what happened and how it affected you, using ‘I’ sentences: ‘When this happened, I felt hurt.’ Then listen. Ask them to tell you their side, and try to repeat it back before you respond. Proverbs 18:13 says that to answer before listening is folly and shame.

Ephesians 4:26-27 gives a warning: ‘In your anger do not sin. Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not give the devil a foothold.’ Being angry isn’t a sin. Holding on to anger lets bitterness grow. Deal with it soon.
If you are the one who hurt someone
Matthew 5:23-24

Jesus says that if you’re offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there. First go and be reconciled, and then come and offer your gift. Making things right with people matters to God as much as worship.

A good apology is simple. Say what you did without excuses: ‘I was wrong to say that.’ Say that you’re sorry for how it hurt them. Ask, ‘Will you forgive me?’ Offer to make it right if you can. And avoid the words ‘but’ and ‘if you felt’. ‘I’m sorry if you were offended’ isn’t an apology.
Forgiving
Colossians 3:13

‘Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.’ Jesus said we must forgive others, and that those who do not forgive will find it hard to receive God’s forgiveness (Matthew 6:14-15). He told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21-22).
What is forgiveness? It means we give up our claim to get even. We let go of the debt, and we trust God to deal with the wrong. It’s a decision first, and the feelings may take longer.

Here is what forgiveness is not. It isn’t pretending the wrong didn’t happen. It isn’t saying it was okay. It isn’t the same as trusting the person again. Trust is rebuilt over time by changed behavior. And forgiveness doesn’t mean staying near someone who is dangerous. You can forgive from a safe distance. If you were abused, forgiving is not something you owe on anyone’s timetable, and a counselor can walk with you.

When the other person won’t listen, Jesus describes taking one or two others with you, and then involving the church (Matthew 18:16-17). Bring in your pastor early if the matter is serious. If they still refuse to make peace, we do what Romans 12:18 says: ‘If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.’ We do our part, and the rest belongs to God.
Peace in the church

Conflict in a church family needs special care, because we represent Jesus. Jesus prayed that His followers would be one, so that the world would know the Father sent Him (John 17:20-23). Paul asked two women in Philippi, Euodia and Syntyche, to agree in the Lord (Philippians 4:2). Even great churches had disagreements. The aim is to work through them with love and honesty.
Ask these in order. After each one, let the silence sit for a few seconds.

x: What is your usual response to conflict, and where did you learn it?
Why is it so tempting to talk about someone, and not to them?
What makes it hard to say sorry?
What is the difference between forgiving someone and trusting them?

b.x: The fourth question is important. Take your time with it, and make it clear that no one is required to stay near someone who harms them.
This week I’d like to ask you to do two things.

x: Ask God whether there is someone you need to talk to, or to forgive. Write down the name, and take one step this week, such as a call, a message or a prayer.
If you’ve been talking about someone, stop, and say something good about them instead.

b.x: Romans 12:18

b.i: Close with a short prayer in your own words.
b.x: Lord, make us peacemakers. Give us the courage to go to those we need to, and the grace to forgive as You have forgiven us. Amen.
How do I honor God with my body and my desires?
Thinking of you. Did you take that step?

x.q: I forgave them, but I still feel angry.
x.a: That’s normal. Forgiveness is a decision, and the feelings often catch up slowly. Keep bringing them to God, and consider talking with a counselor.

x.q: Do I have to forgive someone who never apologized?
x.a: Jesus forgave from the cross while people were still mocking Him (Luke 23:34). We let go of the debt, and reconciliation requires both people. Safety still matters.

x.q: What if the person who hurt me is dangerous?
x.a: You don’t have to meet them. Tell your pastor, and get help from a counselor or the proper authorities. Matthew 18 is not meant for that situation.

x.q: Should I tell my pastor about a conflict with another believer?
x.a: If it’s serious or you can’t resolve it, yes. Bringing in a wise person early helps.

title: Purity and sexuality
q: How do I honor God with my body and my desires?
notes: This is one of the most sensitive lessons in the program. Please prepare carefully, and consider whether to teach it with men and women together, or in separate groups. Keep the language plain and respectful, and never ask anyone to share details of their struggles or their past. Many people in a group carry shame, and some carry the effects of abuse or assault. Say clearly that being sinned against is not a sin of theirs. If someone shares that kind of history, thank them, don’t press for details, and help them privately reach your pastor and a trained counselor. Some may struggle with pornography or other habits, and some may live with attractions or situations that feel hard to bring to the church. Treat every person with dignity, speak with grace and truth together, and remember that you are not the person’s judge. Your pastor can help with specific questions about what your church teaches.

b.x: Welcome back. Last week we talked about making peace. Tonight’s lesson is a delicate one, and I want to say up front that this is a safe place. Nobody here will be shamed or asked to share anything they don’t want to.
Did you take a step toward peace with someone this week? How did it go?
Romans 12:18
Tonight’s question is: how do I honor God with my body and my desires?

b.i: Pray, and sing or listen to one song together.
b.x: Father, You made us, and You love us. Teach us to honor You with our bodies and our hearts. Where we carry shame, bring Your freedom. Amen.

Our culture talks about sexuality constantly, and it often leaves people more confused, more hurt, or more ashamed. The Bible speaks about it honestly. It doesn’t treat the body as bad. God made it, and He called it good. Tonight we’ll look at what He says, and at the grace He offers.
God made us, body and soul
1 Corinthians 6:19-20

‘Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies.’ Our bodies belong to God. They aren’t just machines for pleasure, and they aren’t shameful. God made desire, and He made marriage as a place where sexual intimacy is a good gift (Genesis 2:24; Proverbs 5:18-19; Hebrews 13:4).
God’s call to holiness
1 Thessalonians 4:3-5

‘It is God’s will that you should be sanctified: that you should avoid sexual immorality; that each of you should learn to control your own body in a way that is holy and honorable, not in passionate lust like the pagans, who do not know God.’ The Bible’s picture is that sex belongs within the faithful, lifelong commitment of marriage. Outside of that, whether single or married, believers are called to purity.

Why? Because of what sex is. It is a deep joining of two people (1 Corinthians 6:16-18), and when it’s separated from commitment, it often leaves hurt, regret and broken trust. God’s boundaries are meant to protect us and the people we love. Paul says that sexual sin is a sin against our own bodies (1 Corinthians 6:18).

Jesus went to the heart. He said that anyone who looks at another person lustfully has already committed adultery with them in the heart (Matthew 5:28). So purity includes our eyes and our thoughts. That’s why guarding the heart matters.
Guarding the heart
Proverbs 4:23
‘Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.’ Here are some practical ways to do that.

Watch what you take in. What we watch, read and scroll shapes our desires. Job said, ‘I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully’ (Job 31:1). Pornography is a trap for many people, and it damages relationships and trust. If you struggle with it, you aren’t alone.

Set boundaries before you’re tempted. Decide ahead of time what you’ll do and where you won’t go. Think about the hours you spend alone on your phone, the people you spend time with, and the places you visit. Paul told Timothy to flee from youthful desires and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart (2 Timothy 2:22).
Ask for a way out. 1 Corinthians 10:13 promises that God is faithful, and that when we are tempted, He will provide a way out. Often the way out is a phone call, a walk, or leaving the room.

Don’t fight alone. James 5:16 says to confess our sins to each other and pray for each other so that we may be healed. Pick one trusted person of the same gender who will pray with you and ask you how you’re doing. Secrecy gives shame its strength.
When we have fallen
Psalm 51:10

David wrote this after a terrible failure. ‘Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.’ He didn’t hide, and he didn’t make excuses. He asked God for a new heart. And God forgave him (Psalm 32:5).

If you’ve fallen, whether last night or years ago, hear this clearly. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just and will forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Jesus didn’t condemn the woman caught in adultery. He said, ‘Neither do I condemn you. Go now and leave your life of sin’ (John 8:11). He offers both grace and a new way to live.

Shame says, ‘You’re ruined.’ God says, ‘You’re forgiven, and I’m making you new.’ The Corinthian church had people with all kinds of pasts, and Paul told them, ‘And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified’ (1 Corinthians 6:11).
If you were hurt

Some of us carry things that were done to us. If you’ve been abused, assaulted or taken advantage of, the shame isn’t yours. It belongs to the person who did it.
